We cannot do what we do without your support. Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the current leadership was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. Poland's right-wing opposition PiS party is set to split after a more moderate faction of over 30 MPs loyal to deputy leader @MorawieckiM refused to sign a loyalty pledge demanded by leader @OficjalnyJK, who says that means they have effectively resigned https://t.co/TuqYpGI5ak — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 24, 2026 On Tuesday, the party announced that instead, the committee had referred the cases of 44 members, who either failed to submit the required declarations or submitted them on the wrong form, to the party’s disciplinary officer for individual review, delaying a final decision. “From a formal and legal perspective, Mr Mateusz Morawiecki has not yet been removed from the list of members,” PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek said on Tuesday. PiS disciplinary officer Karol Karski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) he would examine each case individually. “I am open to speaking with each of them so they can present their positions,” Karski said. “At this point, I can initiate proceedings against the individual in question, refer the case to a peer disciplinary tribunal with a motion for punishment – this could include a temporary suspension or expulsion from PiS.” PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll at a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. The national-conservative opposition PiS party has named its candidate to be prime minister if it wins next year’s parliamentary elections. Przemysław Czarnek is a hardline conservative who played a prominent role in PiS's campaign against "LGBT ideology" https://t.co/sSJLON00hW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2026 They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Adam Szłapka, the spokesman of the current more liberal government, said Braun was “the ultimate playmaker in this whole game”, who had helped push far-right rhetoric into the political mainstream. “The worst thing about this whole situation is that Poland’s largest opposition party has, in effect, started to adopt Grzegorz Braun’s agenda from A to Z,” Szłapka told broadcaster TVN24. World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. Bidding consortia will have 15 weeks to submit proposals, contracts are due to be awarded in early 2027 and the facilities are scheduled to become operational in 2028. 🚀 Droga do Gigafabryki AI otwarta. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.title: UNESCO adds Poland’s modernist port city of Gdynia to World Heritage List
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. UNESCO has added the modernist city centre of the Polish port city of Gdynia to its World Heritage List, recognising its interwar urban planning and architecture. The designation, approved during the World Heritage Committee’s 48th session in Busan, South Korea, is Poland’s 18th World Heritage site and comes as Gdynia marks the centenary of gaining city rights. In its justification, UNESCO referred to “an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions”. Gdynia’s city centre “illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars”, it added. Granted city status in 1926, Gdynia was rapidly developed by the newly independent Polish state from a small fishing village into a major Baltic seaport, growing to more than 100,000 residents in under 20 years and providing Poland with a modern maritime gateway. It is now Poland’s 13th largest city by population, with just under 210,000 residents, and the third largest by area when including its maritime territory. Nowy tydzień zaczynamy od dobrych wieści! Komitet Światowego Dziedzictwa UNESCO oficjalnie uznał modernistyczne centrum Gdyni za dobro o wyjątkowym znaczeniu dla całego świata. Nie ma lepszego momentu niż 100-lecie Gdyni na to wyjątkowe wyróżnienie!https://t.co/L3WZZCJCAz — Gdynia (@MiastoGdynia) July 27, 2026 Oktawia Gorzeńska, Gdynia’s deputy mayor, who represented the city in Busan, celebrated the decision of the committee as “a wonderful gift for our anniversary and a tribute to the vision and determination of the people who created one of Europe’s great modernist cities”. The city’s mayor, Aleksandra Kosiorek, added that the decision “confirms that the vision which launched the history of modern Gdynia over a century ago has retained its power and universal significance.” Gdynia’s central district of Śródmieście was built largely between 1926 and 1939. Its rapid development at the time drew international attention, with a National Geographic reporter writing that “Poland dreams of building her New York”. Unlike Warsaw and nearby Gdańsk, it escaped extensive destruction during World War Two, preserving much of its original street layout and interwar architecture. According to the city authorities, UNESCO experts have recognised the Gdynia’s centre as one of the world’s most outstanding examples of early modernism in urban planning. The nomination also highlighted Gdynia’s distinctive model of modernist urban planning, setting it apart from contemporaneous developments such as Germany’s Bauhaus, Berlin’s housing estates, Kaunas in Lithuania and Tel Aviv. Gdynia’s modernist architecture is characterised by white façades and maritime-inspired details, including round windows and building forms resembling ship hulls. Gdańsk in Poland has been named a global City of Literature by @UNESCO. It is now one of only 63 such cities in the world, and the third in Poland to obtain the distinction https://t.co/QdMxlT65V4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2025 Notable examples include the so-called “bank building”, a modernist tenement block, and the Museum of Emigration, housed in the former Maritime Station, which from the 1930s until 1979 was a transit building from which thousands of Polish emigrants left for their new homelands. According to the city, the road to recognition took over 20 years, beginning in 2007, when the historic urban layout was entered into the regional register of monuments. It was designated a Monument of History in 2015, and Poland submitted the site to UNESCO’s Tentative List in 2019. Two sites in Poland were included in the inaugural World Heritage List in 1978: the Historic Centre of Kraków and the nearby Wieliczka and Bochnia Royal Salt Mines. Gdynia’s inscription is the 18th for Poland overall and the first for a Polish modernist urban complex. The most recent Polish additions before Gdynia were the Krzemionki Prehistoric Striped Flint Mining Region in 2019 and, in 2021, the beech forests in the Bieszczady Mountains. World.title: From Old Town to Main Station: Tourist Charged €150 for Short Taxi Ride
World.content:
A tourist has reported an alleged taxi scam in Prague, claiming that a journey from Old Town Square to Prague Main Railway Station ended with an unexpectedly high fare and a disputed payment.

The incident reportedly took place on July 25 at around 16:15. According to the complaint, the driver charged CZK 980 for the ride, an amount the passenger said was far higher than the expected price for such a short distance.

The tourist claims that the driver refused to accept payment by card and requested cash instead.



“I paid him 100 Euros for the fare. He just took the note, swapped it and lied to me saying what I gave was 100 in Czech currency, and demanded me to pay the remaining 50 euro taxi fare,” the tourist said in his complaint.

“So I paid the initial 100 euro that was swapped, plus the 50 euro taxi fare.”

According to the passenger, the total amount paid for the ride was therefore €150 (over 3,600 CZK). He said he was rushing to catch a train to Bratislava and was unable to resolve the dispute at the scene.

The tourist also claimed that no receipt was provided after the payment. According to his account, the driver said an invoice would be sent by email, but it was never received.

The case has been reported to the relevant authorities, while details of the incident have also been shared online to raise awareness among other visitors.

Travellers are also encouraged to use established taxi applications or services recommended by hotels, restaurants, and official tourist information centres. Paying by card and confirming the expected price in advance can help avoid disputes.

World.content:
The Czech prime minister also said Brussels is likely to permit a larger budget deficit as Prague seeks funding for hospitals, highways, and other domestic investment.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has expressed alarm over the country’s rapidly increasing payments to the European Union, warning that the Czech Republic could become a net contributor to the bloc as early as 2029.

Following talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerová, Babiš said Czech payments into the EU budget had risen by 22 billion crowns (€911 million) this year alone.

“I was shocked by how much we are paying into the European Union,” he said, as cited by Echo24. “If in one year we are told that we will pay 22 billion more, that is a lot.”



Officials currently expect the Czech Republic to become a net contributor to the EU budget for the first time in its history in either 2029 or 2030.

Babiš was also asked about next year’s state budget deficit. When asked whether it would exceed this year’s planned shortfall of 310 billion crowns (€12.8 billion), he replied, “Don’t test me. I don’t know what the deficit will be.”

Schillerová said a reliable estimate would only be possible after the Finance Ministry publishes its updated economic forecast next month.

The government has informed the European Commission that it expects next year’s structural deficit to reach as much as 2.9 percent of GDP, compared with 2.4 percent this year. According to Schillerová, Brussels has provisionally accepted the higher ceiling.

“We have to invest in hospitals, highways and bypasses,” he said, justifying the overspend but maintaining that the deficit should remain significantly below 400 billion crowns (€16.6 billion).

Planned spending includes psychiatric hospitals, surgical facilities, oncology centers, highways and city bypasses. The government also intends to maintain defense expenditure at 2 percent of GDP.

World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
Six hundred years ago, an angry crowd stormed Prague’s New Town Hall and threw several royal councillors from its windows.

The attack, known as the First Defenestration of Prague, took place on July 30, 1419, and is widely regarded as the event that ignited the Hussite Wars—a conflict that transformed medieval Bohemia and left a lasting mark on Czech history.

Yet the violence that unfolded that summer day had been years in the making.

Its roots lay in the teachings of Jan Hus, a Czech theologian, university lecturer, and religious reformer who became one of the most influential figures of the late Middle Ages. Hus openly criticized corruption within the Catholic Church, particularly the sale of indulgences and the growing power of the church hierarchy. Rather than viewing the Church as an institution led by the pope and bishops, he argued that the true Church was the community of faithful believers.

Summoned before the Council of Constance in 1415 to defend his beliefs, Hus was arrested despite receiving a promise of safe conduct. After refusing to renounce his teachings, he was convicted of heresy and burned at the stake.



His execution outraged many across Bohemia. While members of the nobility saw it as the unjust killing of one of the kingdom’s own, Hus’s followers spread his ideas far beyond Prague through a network of priests and former university students. The capital, home to Charles University and the Bethlehem Chapel where Hus had preached, became the center of a rapidly growing reform movement.

Bohemia’s political circumstances also allowed the movement to flourish. Neither King Wenceslas IV nor the Archbishop of Prague took decisive action to suppress it, allowing religious tensions to deepen over the following years.

By the summer of 1419, the situation had reached a breaking point.

On July 30, radical Hussite preacher Jan Želivský led a religious procession through Prague after delivering an impassioned sermon. Although the march may have appeared spontaneous, historians believe the confrontation had been carefully prepared. Some participants reportedly arrived carrying concealed weapons, expecting violence.

The procession made its way to Prague’s New Town Hall, demanding the release of Hussite supporters imprisoned there. When the councillors refused, the crowd forced its way inside.

The assault was led by Jan Žižka, a military commander who would later become one of medieval Europe’s greatest generals. Several councillors were seized and thrown from the building’s windows. Although the fall itself was not fatal for everyone, those who survived were beaten to death by the waiting crowd below.

For medieval society, the act carried a powerful symbolic meaning. Publicly casting powerful officials from an elevated position represented the dramatic downfall of those who had abused their authority.

The defenestration did not, by itself, begin the Hussite Wars, but it made peaceful reconciliation increasingly unlikely. Just weeks later, King Wenceslas IV died, leaving the throne to his brother Sigismund, whom many Bohemians blamed for failing to protect Jan Hus at Constance. Relations between the Hussites and the crown rapidly collapsed, and in 1420 the first crusade against Bohemia was launched.

The wars that followed lasted more than a decade. They devastated much of the kingdom but also produced extraordinary military victories under Jan Žižka and established the Hussites as one of medieval Europe’s most formidable fighting forces.

The First Defenestration of Prague remains one of the defining moments in Czech history—a single act of violence that turned years of religious unrest into a revolution whose legacy can still be seen throughout the country today.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Inside IAM Prague: How a Travelling Exhibition Laid the Foundation for One of the City’s Top-Rated Museums
World.content:
Just off Old Town Square, past the cafes and the crowds waiting for the Astronomical Clock, sits a museum that started almost by accident.

Today, IAM Prague has welcomed well over 1 million visitors from around the world and has held TripAdvisor’s Travelers’ Choice Award for five straight years.

From Shopping Malls to Old Town Square

The museum wasn’t originally supposed to be a… museum. Co-founder Jakub Bechyně and his partner Patrik Proško had been running a traveling illusion exhibit that moved between shopping malls, renting space for a month at a time before packing up and relocating. It worked, but it wasn’t permanent.

Then, in 2017, the owner of a building on Old Town Square approached them with an idea: turn part of it into a museum. The catch was the timeline. They wanted it open in two months.

Rather than build something from scratch, the team pulled from what they already had on the shelf, opening with one floor and sixteen exhibits in 2018. The collection has grown to more than 60 pieces since.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Illusion Art Museum Prague (@iamprague)

The museum moved to its current location in 2022 after the original building was sold. The new space, ideally located between Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, needed walls removed and floors rebuilt to accommodate the art. The costs were substantial, but it turned out to be a good problem to have as the location dramatically increased the exhibition’s visibility to passersby on one of Prague’s busiest tourist thoroughfares.

Choosing Technique Over Fame

IAM Prague doesn’t chase famous names. It chases techniques. The team looks for a specific kind of illusion craft, one with real artistic quality, a genuine optical trick, and ideally a story behind it worth telling.

That approach led them to reverse-perspective specialist Patrick Hughes, and to artists whose work they discovered secondhand and eventually acquired outright rather than simply displaying on loan. In several cases, the museum ended up owning the pieces after renting them for years and deciding they belonged permanently in the collection.

About 80 percent of the exhibition has changed since opening. Early pieces built quickly to fill the space have gradually been replaced as the museum brought in stronger, more polished work from local and international artists.

The exhibition’s evolution continues, with four new pieces from international artists like Jonty Hurwitz and Andrej Boleslavsky, ranging from traditional mirror anamorphoses to digital art, recently unveiled in June.

History Hidden in Plain Sight

Much of what makes IAM Prague distinct is how it uses illusion as a delivery method for history. A glass-art piece featuring four endangered animals turns out to double as an environmental message.

A defenestration scene lets visitors reenact one of Prague’s most repeated historical events, tied to the 1618 uprising that helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War. Even the museum’s own opening date, a century after Czechoslovak independence in 1918, was picked on purpose.

One exhibit nods to Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who coined the word “robot,” a term that entered global use even though it comes from a Slavic word for forced labor.

Another traces the story of Tomáš Baťa, the industrialist who pioneered mass shoe manufacturing and built factories across multiple continents, including a Pakistani city that still carries his name today.

AI’s Impact on Art & Travel

Though much has been made on artificial intelligence’s impact on the world of art, the team’s biggest current concern isn’t AI-generated art replacing the exhibition’s themselves. It’s the shift in how travelers plan their trips.

For years, visibility depended on traditional guidebooks, online travel agencies, physical advertising, and street presence. Increasingly, travelers are relying on AI chat tools to create itineraries, shifting the importance of more “traditional” visibility mechanisms, which is forcing venues like Illusion Art Museum Prague to adapt.

Despite the changing landscape, the plan going forward leans further into digital and kinetic art, including new motion-based installations recently brought in from Berlin by artists like Florian Goerlitz.

For a museum that started as a temporary mall exhibit, the goal has stayed consistent since day one: make people stop, look twice, and leave with a story they didn’t expect to learn.

World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Not an Official Visit: Petr Pavel Attends Hungarian GP as F1 Photographer
World.content:
The president of the Czech Republic, Petr Pavel, has made his way to the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday – but was not an official visit.

Ever wondered what world leaders do in their free time? For Czech Republic president Petr Pavel, the answer is sports photography – and he’s particularly passionate about motorsport.

This weekend, he was attending the Hungarian GP with a full photography kit – and an official FIA accreditation. He arrived at the Hungaroring for Saturday’s sessions and was already taking pictures, accompanied by Czech F1 photographer Jiri Krenek.



This wasn’t the first time he was seen at a major motorsport event as a hobby photographer. Most recently, Pavel travelled to France in June to attend the Le Mans 24 Hours, once again equipped with full camera gear.

In fact, the former NATO Military Chairman has attended several races on both two and four wheels over the years.

Within the Czech Republic, Pavel covered the MotoGP and World Superbike events at Brno, while he has travelled as far as the US and Saudi Arabia to photograph NASCAR and the Dakar Rally respectively.

Last year, he also raised nearly 30,000 euros for a charity dedicated to children, single parents and the elderly by auctioning a photo album.

While it is unusual for politicians to attend races purely for leisure, several leaders regularly appear at major motorsport events in their own countries.

Last year, then British Prime Minister Keir Starmer hosted F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, drivers and senior team figures at a reception in 10 Downing Street ahead of the British GP.

World.title: Hungarian fake Jesus arrested in Italy after fleeing prison sentence for fraud
World.content:
A 73-year-old Hungarian man known in the media as the “Zala county fake Jesus” has been arrested in Italy after fleeing Hungary to avoid serving a prison sentence for defrauding his followers of HUF millions.

The man was detained by Italian police in Macerata on 7 July, a spokesperson for the Zala County Police Headquarters confirmed. Hungarian and Italian authorities have since begun extradition proceedings, although no date has yet been set for fake Jesus’ return to Hungary. His status on the Hungarian police’s wanted persons database has also been updated to “captured”.

Fake Jesus sentenced to four and a half years in prison

The man was the subject of a nationwide arrest warrant after failing to report to prison to begin serving a four-and-a-half-year sentence. According to the Zalaegerszeg Regional Court, he could not be located at his registered address, prompting the court to issue a warrant for his arrest.

He had originally been sentenced in October 2024 to six years’ imprisonment for 23 counts of fraud and one count of disorderly conduct. The court also ordered him to pay a HUF 300,000 fine and nearly HUF 19 million, plus interest, in compensation to his victims. On appeal, the sentence was reduced to four years and six months in November 2025, taking into account his advanced age and previous clean criminal record.

Followers allegedly manipulated for decades

According to the courts, the man claiming to be Jesus’ reincarnation spent decades presenting himself as a spiritual healer, energy therapist and saviour of souls. He organised group sessions and private consultations in several Hungarian cities, including Zalaegerszeg, Nagykanizsa, Pécs, Budapest and Böhönye.

During these gatherings, he reportedly preached about unconditional love, God, the Saviour, modesty, self-sacrifice and rejecting material wealth, while claiming he had little understanding of financial matters.

Investigators found that he portrayed himself as the reincarnation of Jesus, gradually gaining the trust of people seeking healing or spiritual guidance. Prosecutors said he created emotional dependence among his followers and increasingly influenced their personal relationships, career choices and financial decisions.

Millions collected for charitable causes apparently funded luxury lifestyle

The court found that the man persuaded followers to donate money for what he described as charitable or noble causes, including buying homes, supporting people in need and funding children’s camps. Instead, prosecutors said the money was spent financing his own luxurious lifestyle.

The victims were defrauded of nearly HUF 20 million (EUR 55,200) in total. Some followers reportedly continued to believe in his spiritual mission throughout the investigation, while others questioned his activities but felt unable to break free from his influence. According to the court, he warned followers that anyone who “betrayed” him would become seriously ill.

Throughout the legal proceedings, the man denied criminal wrongdoing. While acknowledging that he was not Jesus, he maintained that he nevertheless possessed exceptional spiritual knowledge.

World.title: Hungarian parliamentary committee backs lifting Tisza MP’s immunity over drink-driving case
World.content:
Hungary’s parliamentary Immunity Committee has recommended lifting the parliamentary immunity of Tisza Party MP Lőrinc Varga in connection with a drink-driving offence committed in 2024, before he became a member of parliament.

Committee chair Edit Sasi-Nagy, also a Tisza Party MP, told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) after Wednesday’s meeting that the proposal will be submitted to Parliament for a vote next Monday.

According to Sasi-Nagy, the offence took place in 2024, when Varga was neither an MP nor a parliamentary candidate. However, because the court proceedings were still ongoing when he was elected to Parliament, the case was suspended, and the court requested that his parliamentary immunity be lifted so the trial could continue.

Committee unanimously supports lifting immunity

Sasi-Nagy explained that the committee follows a long-established practice: in public prosecution cases, it generally recommends suspending parliamentary immunity, while in private prosecution cases, it recommends maintaining it.

On that basis, the committee unanimously voted to recommend lifting Varga’s immunity. Varga, one of the youngest MPs in the Tisza Party parliamentary group, publicly addressed the incident in May.

In a social media post, he acknowledged responsibility, writing that during a routine police check following a gathering with friends, alcohol had been detected in his system the following morning.

“I made a mistake, and I fully accept responsibility,” he said at the time.

Magyar, Toroczkai and Takács retain immunity in defamation cases

The committee also considered several private prosecution cases involving other MPs. It unanimously recommended maintaining the parliamentary immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar in a defamation case initiated by a politician.

Similarly, the committee proposed maintaining the immunity of László Toroczkai, leader of the Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) party, in four separate court proceedings relating to the same alleged act involving defamation and insult.

The committee also unanimously recommended preserving the immunity of Fidesz MP Péter Takács, who is likewise facing private defamation and insult proceedings.

Committee: immunity protects political work, not criminal offences

Summing up the decisions, Sasi-Nagy said the private prosecution cases illustrate the original purpose of parliamentary immunity: ensuring that elected representatives can carry out their political duties without being hindered by private legal disputes.

By contrast, she noted that public prosecution cases—such as Varga’s alleged drink-driving offence—are generally treated differently, which is why the committee recommended allowing the criminal proceedings to continue.

World.title: Report: Orbán government sent EUR 705,000 overseas in 10 months, funding New York office, cemetery restoration
World.content:
The Orbán government’s Bethlen Gábor Fund (BGA) distributed HUF 255.9 million (approximately EUR 705,000) in discretionary grants to Hungarian diaspora organisations outside Europe between July 2025 and the end of April 2026, according to documents obtained through a freedom of information request.

The documents, first reported by Hungarian news outlet 444, show that the Orbán government’s funding reached organisations in the United States, Canada, Uruguay, Argentina, Chile and Japan, supporting both cultural programmes and day-to-day operating costs. Unlike standard grant schemes, the funding was awarded through individual applications rather than open public calls.

Two organisations received around two-thirds of the Orbán government’s funding

According to the documents, 19 individual funding decisions were made by the Orbán government during the ten-month period, with roughly two-thirds of the total allocated to just two organisations. The Hungarian Scout Association in Exteris, based in Morris Plains, New Jersey, received HUF 119 million (EUR 328,000) to operate the Hungarian House and support its Diaspora School Camp programme.

Meanwhile, the Hungarian Human Rights Foundation in New York was awarded HUF 70 million (EUR 193,000) for its Reconnect Hungary initiative, which brings young people of Hungarian descent born in the United States to Hungary to strengthen their ties with the country.

The Orbán government’s funding covered a wide range of expenses, including staff salaries, project management, flights to Hungary, accommodation, meals, admission fees and the operating costs of the organisation’s New York office. According to the report, HUF 35 million (EUR 96,500) of this funding was approved on 9 and 10 April, just days before Hungary’s parliamentary election.

Funding also supported church, cultural and heritage projects

Other grants included HUF 14 million (EUR 38,500) for the Independent Hungarian Reformed Church of Ontario in Canada, HUF 13 million (EUR 35,800) for the Duna Hungarian Arts and Folklore Association in Chile, HUF 10 million for the Pannonia Hungarian Bookstore in Ontario.

One of the more unusual projects was supported in Uruguay, where the Federation of Hungarian Organisations in Latin America received HUF 11.4 million (EUR 31,400) for operational costs and development projects, including the creation of a Hungarian diaspora museum and the renovation of the Hungarian Pantheon, a Hungarian mausoleum located in the Tucumán Cemetery.

Stay up-to-date: Scandal, if true — PM Orbán’s former deputy and opposition KDNP party head Zsolt Semjén accused of raping a minor by victim

Discretionary funding process has drawn criticism

According to the documents, organisations seeking support were required to submit detailed applications explaining their projects, budgets and how the proposed activities would serve the interests of Hungarian communities abroad. Following a professional assessment by the Bethlen Gábor Fund, the final decisions were made by the Prime Minister’s Office, under the supervision of the State Secretary responsible for national policy.

While discretionary grants are a recognised form of public funding in Hungary, the system has faced criticism from transparency advocates because awards are made without open competition and can involve substantial public funds. The latest disclosures follow earlier reports that the Bethlen Gábor Fund allocated HUF billions to Hungarian football academies and organisations outside Hungary during the same period.

World.title: Paks nuclear reactor unit shut down as Danube reaches record-low water levels
World.content:
Hungary has begun shutting down one of the four reactor units at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant after the Danube reached exceptionally low water levels, highlighting the growing impact of the country’s prolonged heatwave and severe drought.

The operator, MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant Ltd., announced on Wednesday afternoon that the shutdown of Unit 3 began at 3 PM as the Danube continued to fall to record-low levels along several sections of the river.

According to the company, the water level at Paks had dropped to -118 centimetres, prompting the decision to take the reactor offline in line with operational and environmental safety requirements.

Plant operators said they are continuously monitoring river flow and water temperature and will make further operational decisions based on changing conditions. The company stressed that maintaining the plant’s safe operation while complying with environmental regulations remains its top priority.

Emergency measures in place to secure cooling water

Earlier on Wednesday, Environment Minister László Gajdos announced that Hungary’s water management authority had entered a state of heightened readiness to ensure a continuous cooling water supply for the nuclear power station despite the extreme drought.

In a Facebook post, the minister said authorities have already deployed four floating pumping units and two floating cranes on the Danube near Paks. Although pumping is not yet necessary, 55 specialists are working around the clock on standby to respond if conditions deteriorate.

“The protective measures are ongoing. We are safeguarding Hungary’s water resources and national security,” Gajdos wrote.

Output had already been reduced

The shutdown follows several days of gradually reducing the plant’s electricity output as the Danube’s water level continued to decline.

Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány previously described the power reductions as a planned precautionary measure rather than a technical fault, emphasising that they are carried out under pre-established operational rules.

He also warned that another heatwave is expected to sweep across Europe in the coming days, likely increasing electricity demand while causing the Danube’s water level to fall even further.

Extreme heat and drought continue to affect Hungary

According to MVM, the combination of persistent drought and extreme summer temperatures has significantly reduced the Danube’s flow this year.

Environmental regulations limit the temperature of the cooling water discharged back into the river after passing through the reactors. To remain within these limits, the plant has already had to reduce the output of its reactor units on several occasions during June and July.

Meanwhile, the Danube has reached historic lows in Budapest as well. On Tuesday morning, the river gauge measured just 30 centimetres, before falling even further later in the day, according to Telex.

World.title: Bombs emerge from the Danube: record-low water levels expose suspected WWII explosives near Budapest
World.content:
Several suspected Second World War bombs have emerged from the bed of the River Danube near Érd, south of Budapest, after the prolonged drought caused water levels to fall to record lows.

In a Facebook post published on Wednesday, Érd Mayor László Csőzik urged residents to avoid the section of the Danube riverbank at the end of Molnár Street, where one of the suspected explosive devices is protruding around 20–30 centimetres above the water.

Area secured after discovery

According to the mayor, the suspicious objects were discovered by a local field warden. Municipal wardens, assisted by volunteer civil guards, immediately secured the area before police officers also arrived at the scene. The Hungarian Defence Forces’ bomb disposal unit was subsequently notified.

Csőzik noted that the exceptionally low water level has exposed suspected wartime explosives at several locations across Hungary, placing bomb disposal teams under considerable pressure.

Bomb disposal experts identifying the devices

Sándor Hadházi, press officer for the Hungarian Defence Forces’ 1st Explosive Ordnance Disposal and River Guard Regiment, told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) that the site has been secured and specialists are currently working to identify the object that surfaced from the riverbed.

At present, no public protection measures or movement restrictions have been introduced for local residents, he added.

World.title: Watch out: Budapest taxi fares to increase from Saturday
World.content:
Travelling by taxi in Budapest will become more expensive from Saturday, when the latest amendment to the city’s taxi fare regulation takes effect.

Higher base fare, distance and time charges approved by the city

Under the new pricing, the base fare will increase from HUF 1,100 to HUF 1,300, while the per-kilometre rate will rise from HUF 440 to HUF 521. The per-minute waiting charge will also increase from HUF 110 to HUF 130. (1 EUR = 362 HUF)

The fare adjustment was approved by the Budapest Metropolitan Assembly at its meeting on 26 June, marking the first increase in official taxi tariffs since 2023.

New airport surcharge introduced

Passengers travelling to or from Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport will also face a new HUF 800 airport surcharge. As a result, the effective starting fare for airport journeys will rise to HUF 2,100, combining the new base fare with the additional airport fee.

The airport surcharge is being introduced alongside changes affecting taxi operators using the airport. From 3 August, taxis picking up passengers at the departures level and on the outer lane of the arrivals area will be required to pay an HUF 800 access fee.

Following negotiations between the National Taxi Association and Budapest Airport Plc., non-contracted taxi drivers will be able to collect passengers at a more distant designated meeting point for a reduced fee of HUF 600, while passenger pick-ups at the City Break car park will cost HUF 450.

In case you missed it: New 2,500-ton railway bridge installed in major Budapest rail upgrade! – Photos

First fare rise in three years

The increase follows lengthy discussions between the city authorities and taxi industry representatives. Taxi organisations had been calling for higher fares, although there was initially no consensus within the sector on the scale of the increase.

The Budapest Metropolitan Assembly eventually approved the revised tariff structure at its final meeting before the summer recess, after previous attempts to reach an agreement had failed.

From Saturday, both residents and visitors using Budapest’s regulated taxi services should expect higher fares, particularly for journeys to and from the capital’s international airport.

World.title: Research institute warns PM Péter Magyar risks ‘wearing himself out’
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has dismissed criticism from political think tank Political Capital after it argued that his greatest political risk is his own constant public presence and communication style.

The debate follows the publication of Political Capital’s latest analysis, which argues that despite the government’s strong position, Magyar could gradually “wear himself out” by dominating Hungary’s political agenda.

Think tank sees risks despite government’s strong position

According to Political Capital, many Hungarian voters remain highly engaged in politics even during the summer months, meaning the governing Tisza Party cannot afford to become complacent despite the opposition’s current weakness.

The analysis points to the latest Medián opinion poll, which found that support for the governing party fell by 3–5 percentage points compared with the previous month. The researchers suggest the decline may have been linked to the government’s handling of its presidential nomination, although they stress that no direct causal relationship has been established.

Political Capital argues that the government’s first significant setback came not from the opposition but from its own communication mistakes, including the abandonment of a previously promised public consultation over the presidential nomination.

The think tank also notes that the Tisza government faces high public expectations regarding both economic performance and governance. While Hungarians remain optimistic about their own finances and the country’s economic outlook, the report says these expectations could become difficult to meet given the challenging fiscal situation inherited from the previous administration.

“Péter Magyar’s biggest political opponent is Péter Magyar”

One of the report’s central conclusions is that the prime minister currently faces little direct political competition. Instead, Political Capital argues that Magyar has become the dominant figure in Hungarian politics, with government communication largely revolving around his personal appearances and messaging.

According to the analysis, this strategy carries risks.

“For the time being, Péter Magyar’s biggest political opponent is Péter Magyar,” the report states, arguing that his constant visibility, occasional mistakes and highly active communication could eventually reduce his political appeal.

The report also notes that, unlike in previous years, Magyar did not schedule a competing political event during Viktor Orbán’s annual speech in Băile Tușnad (Tusnádfürdő), suggesting he allowed the former prime minister’s appearance to stand on its own rather than attempting to overshadow it.

PM responds: “There is plenty to wear away”

Magyar reacted directly to the analysis on Facebook after Telex shared an article summarising the report. “There is plenty to wear away,” the prime minister wrote, before adding in another comment that “polishing is not aimless wearing away.”

In a separate Facebook comment beneath another Telex post, Magyar also criticised the outlet for not highlighting one of the government’s latest policy decisions.

World.title: Elderly German man went missing near Lake Balaton
World.content:
Hungarian police have launched an extensive search for an 81-year-old German national who disappeared from his home near Tapolca on Tuesday afternoon.

According to the Veszprém County Police Headquarters, Martin Hofer left his home in the outskirts of Lesenceistvánd, near Tapolca, shortly after 3:00 PM on Tuesday, 28 July, and has not been seen since.

German man struggles with orientation and does not speak Hungarian

Police say the missing man has difficulty orienting himself in both time and place, raising concerns for his safety. He also does not speak Hungarian, which could make it more difficult for him to ask for assistance.

At the time of his disappearance, Martin Hofer was wearing:

a dark blue jacket,

light blue jeans,

and brown slippers.

Authorities have not released further details about the circumstances of his disappearance but are urging the public to remain vigilant.

Police appeal for public assistance

The Tapolca Police Department is asking anyone who may have seen the German man or has information about his whereabouts to come forward immediately.

Anyone with relevant information can report it in person at the Tapolca Police Department (2 Ady Endre Street, Tapolca) or by calling +36 30 227 3744.

Anonymous reports can also be made 24 hours a day via Hungary’s Telefontanú (Witness Hotline) on +36 80 555 111, or through the emergency number 112.

Police stress that even seemingly minor information could help locate the missing man safely.

Read also: Hungarian doctor performs mid-air CPR on Ryanair flight as passenger collapses

World.title: Romanian Parliament passes SAFE, PNRR-related bills during extraordinary session
World.content:
The two houses of the Romanian Parliament reunited on Wednesday, July 29, for an extraordinary plenary session and passed several projects related to the EU-funded Recovery and Resilience Plan, or PNRR, as well as the approval of the SAFE loan agreement.

The session comes amid heated disagreements between the centrist parties that formed the former governing coalition, namely the Social Democrats (PSD), the National Liberal Party (PNL), Save Romania Union (USR), and the Hungarian minority party UDMR.

During the session on July 29, the Chamber of Deputies adopted the draft law establishing the legal framework through which the authorities may intervene in crises on the fuel market, through temporary measures intended to limit the impact on the economy and consumers. Among the provisions are the temporary reduction of the excise duty on diesel, the reduction of VAT on gasoline and diesel to 19% in certain market segments, the establishment of a solidarity contribution, and restrictions on diesel exports.

The bill, which also includes measures for economic operators and oil refiners, was adopted with 293 votes in favor and 2 abstentions. As the decision-making body, the Chamber sent the bill to president Nicusor Dan for promulgation.

Deputies also adopted the project introducing annual bonuses for ANAF and Customs employees, depending on performance. The project was adopted with 208 votes in favor, 20 against and 65 abstentions.

The project regarding the decarbonization of the heating and cooling sector, another PNRR milestone, was passed the same day, with 210 votes in favor, 67 against and 11 abstentions. The project, which will go to the Senate before being sent to the president, includes measures for the modernization of heating and cooling systems and increasing the use of energy from renewable sources, according to Mediafax.

The Territorial Planning, Urbanism and Construction Code passed with 236 votes, with four votes against and 51 abstentions. The project is a milestone in the PNRR.

The Chamber of Deputies also passed a highly contested bill amending the laws regarding integrity and the functioning of the National Integrity Agency (or ANI), and a project allowing the filling of vacant and temporarily vacant positions in healthcare units, by exempting them from hiring restrictions. The law also amends the regime of sanctions for threats and assaults committed against medical, auxiliary and non-medical personnel in healthcare units.

The lower chamber also greenlit the granting of the teaching career bonus for teachers and auxiliary teaching staff, as well as the professional career bonus for administrative staff in state education, and extended the deadline for purchasing homes with 9% VAT until October 1.

Importantly, the Chamber of Deputies adopted the legislative proposal regarding the approval of the SAFE loan agreement worth EUR 16.68 billion between Romania and the European Union. However, the Senate is the decision-making chamber in this case.

The latter bill triggered disagreements between representatives of the center-right camp, made up of PNL and USR, and far-right parliamentarians from the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and smaller parties. While the former said that the agreement finances the Romanian defense sector, the latter criticized the lack of transparency, the cost of the loan and the procedure through which the document reached the vote.

PSD, in turn, supported the necessity of the program, but accused the government of using an incorrect legal procedure.

World.title: Bomb alert at Romania’s Black Sea Port of Constanța amid heightened security concerns
World.content:
Romania’s major point of access to the Black Sea, the Port of Constanța, was subjected to a bomb alert on Wednesday, July 29. The caller reportedly encouraged port employees to flee the scene.

“There are several bombs placed in the Port building and in the passenger terminal. They are disguised as various objects, so you will not have time to find them before they explode. If you do not want to get injured, the best thing is to leave,” sources among the investigators told Euronews Romania.

The interim defence minister, Radu Miruță, stated that the threat was reported from two phone numbers outside Romania, one number with a Ukrainian prefix and the other with a Polish prefix.

“Investigations are being carried out regarding these phone numbers. It is a standard procedure that takes place in such situations. An audio message in Romanian was sent through these phones, which our specialists assess was generated with artificial intelligence,” Radu Miruță explained to Digi24.

The interim defence minister added that all checks are being carried out by the institutions at the scene. “The port was not closed. Instead, people were evacuated from some buildings, those designated by the Romanian Intelligence Service,” the official said.

The prefect of Constanța County, Adrian Picoiu, stated that the bomb threat was received by the Romanian Naval Authority.

“At 11:26, a 112 emergency call was registered, through which an ANR employee informed that on the institution’s telephone network they had received a recorded audio message, in Romanian, regarding the existence of bombs in the Passenger Terminal area of the Port of Constanța,” the prefect of Constanța declared.

In other news, the same day, the Ministry of National Defence announced that aerial targets had been detected at the river border with Ukraine, and two F-16 aircraft were scrambled from Borcea Air Base.

“The radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defence detected on Wednesday, July 29, around 10:30, a group of aerial targets in the vicinity of the river border with Ukraine. Two F-16 aircraft from the 86th Air Base Borcea were scrambled at 10:57 to monitor the situation,” representatives of the Ministry of Defence announced.

Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the ambassador of the Russian Federation on Monday, July 27, following a series of incidents involving Russian drones shot down after entering the country’s territory. In exchange, the Russian government denied any involvement and promised retaliation.
