World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.title: China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018818/China’s Study Abroad Boom Finds a New Generation: Retirees
World.content:
After decades spent working, raising families, and putting personal ambitions on hold, two Chinese women in their 50s returned to school thousands of kilometers from home.

In Athens, 58-year-old Ella Wang found a new sense of purpose at university, studying Greek archaeology, history, and literature. While in New Zealand, 54-year-old Zhao found herself overwhelmed by an English program that was far beyond her level.

Both studied alongside classmates young enough to be their children, but their experiences could hardly have been more different. Yet both are part of a growing number of Chinese retirees looking overseas for education.

Having spent their working lives during China’s reform era, many now have greater financial security, more control over their time, and familiarity with overseas education after sending their own children abroad.

China already has about 105,000 universities for older adults, but overseas programs that combine learning with international travel have a particular appeal for retirees seeking cultural experiences beyond the classroom. EF Education First, one of the world’s largest international education providers, estimates that China’s broader overseas education market for older adults will reach 1.2 trillion yuan ($167 billion) by 2030.

Yet for those entering education systems designed around younger students, the challenge is finding a classroom that fits.

Lesson learned

Zhao discovered that within days of arriving in New Zealand.

She had enrolled in what she believed was a beginner English program. EF had assessed her at A1, the lowest level, and shown her an A1 textbook before she left China. But when lessons began, every available course was beyond her level, and teachers spoke only English.

“It was completely incomprehensible,” Zhao told Sixth Tone.

After one lesson, she returned to the same room for the next class, only to find it empty. The class had moved, but she had not understood the instructions. On another occasion, a teacher called on her, and she did not understand the question.

Zhao had paid about 160,000 yuan for tuition and an eight-month homestay. After retiring from Shanghai’s flower industry, she hoped the program would teach her enough English to travel while she was still healthy. EF’s promotional videos had shown students studying, immersing themselves in local culture, and traveling around New Zealand.

She soon considered quitting. The experience, she felt, had been “overly romanticized” by overseas education providers. “I completely broke down and burst into tears,” Zhao said. “I couldn’t tell my family how miserable it was. I only said I missed them.”

Zhang, 56, had enrolled in a six-week program at the same school and found the pace equally punishing. “It was like I hadn’t even learned to stand, and they were already asking me to run,” she said.

Both had hoped to learn practical English: how to read a menu, take a bus, ask for directions, and order food. Instead, their classes focused on subjects such as history, biology, and mathematics. Another Chinese retiree in the same course quit after three days.

Zhang began to question what she was struggling for. “Do I really need to learn history, biology, and math at this age?”

That mismatch has led some Chinese education providers to design programs specifically for retirees. Yao Xiaoqiong, head of private education provider New Oriental’s Global Campus Center, told Sixth Tone that one- to three-year courses remain difficult for many older students. Instead, the company offers two- to four-week overseas programs, including art courses in the UK and culinary courses in France.

The programs require no prior language skills and include 10 hours of preparation before departure, as well as interpreters and coordinators during the trip. Yao said older clients generally seek cultural immersion and hands-on learning rather than degrees.

Zhang encountered some of that outside the classroom. When she got lost or struggled to understand bus announcements, strangers stepped in to help.

But keeping up with the course consumed her. Zhang studied until 11 p.m. and woke at 4 a.m. to prepare. In class, she relied on a translation app but still “couldn’t keep pace with everyone else.” Younger students often avoided partnering with her for group work.

By the end of the program, she was physically and mentally exhausted. She still hoped to return to New Zealand one day as a tourist. “But this time, I just don’t have the mood to travel,” she said.

Zhang said the program did not match how it was promoted, and planned to file a complaint with EF. The company did not respond to Sixth Tone’s requests for comment.

Zhao’s longer course gave her more time to adjust. Gradually, she learned to manage the classes, grew more confident, found time to hike, and made local friends through a church.

“Now I’ve made it through,” Zhao said. “I’m mentally much stronger.”

Second chance

At the University of Athens, 58-year-old Wang found her way back to an undergraduate thesis she had never considered complete.

Titled “God, Humanity, and Their Destiny,” the thesis at the time fell short of the university’s highest assessment. At her defense, a professor told her she would need “at least another 30 years of life experience” before she could fully develop its argument.

In 2023, while staying at her family’s holiday home in Athens, Wang came across an English-taught undergraduate program in Greek archaeology, history, and literature. More than 30 years had passed since her professor’s remark. “If I finish the archaeology and literature courses here,” she recalled thinking, “maybe I can write the essay better.”

Born in northwestern China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Wang had worked as a Chinese teacher, an advertising executive, and later in publishing before retiring. With one child in college and the other already working, she was free to spend part of the year in Athens.

Most of her classmates were born around 2006. “The last students I taught were born in 1983 and 1984,” she said. “Now, their children are my classmates.”

Keeping up with them meant learning more than history. Wang typed with two index fingers and struggled to navigate the university’s online systems.

During her first semester, Wang’s daughter arranged to work remotely from Athens, helping her practice English and navigate campus life. Reading textbooks on a screen made Wang “dizzy,” so she ordered printed copies and asked her husband to bring them to Greece.

The effort showed. While many students skipped lectures, Wang rarely missed one. She sat in the front row, stayed after class to ask questions even when she could not fully follow the answers, and spent weekends catching up on coursework. Before long, she was using AI to review her exams and identify mistakes.

She even won over classmates by showing them photos of her cats. “No one can resist kittens,” she said. She also discovered that gray hair was no obstacle to using her student ID for a 10% discount at KFC.

Studying the Peloponnesian War changed how Wang thought about conflict. She began to see the same struggle playing out beyond ancient Greece. “One side wants to preserve the existing order, while the other wants to change it,” she said. “That’s how many conflicts in the world work.”

She came to see traditional expectations around family and marriage as part of that same order. She wanted to break away from them, while her husband, who benefited from the arrangement, was more comfortable preserving it.

“My life used to be a multiple-choice question with only one correct answer,” Wang said. “Work, love, marriage. There was always something I was supposed to do at each stage, and I was carried along by society. People were always defining me: whose daughter I was, whose student I was, whose wife I was, whose mother I was.”

“Now my definition comes from myself,” she said. “I no longer care about those labels. I even have a new name: Ella. I’m Ella.”

Wang has thought about becoming a museum guide or writing a memoir after graduation. But she said those plans matter less than what she has already discovered. “The biggest thing I’ve gained over the past two years is realizing that learning itself is the goal, not a means to something else. I just enjoy learning.”

Sometimes, Wang still thinks of her hometown’s long winters in Xinjiang. As the eldest of four daughters, she helped her parents prepare vegetables for the cold months ahead. Surrounded by piles of produce, she longed to play with other children but could not leave.

“My body was confined by labor, but my thoughts were free. They had already traveled thousands of miles around the world,” she said.

Decades later, Wang feels she has finally caught up with those childhood dreams.

“Now I am standing in the open field of life,” Wang said. “I am lonely, but I am free. It is the solitude of freedom.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Ella Wang in Athens. Courtesy of Wang)

World.title: BTS boycotts Grammys over new Asian pop award category
World.content:
K-pop group BTS says they will not submit any music for consideration at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards in February 2027.

The decision marks the first time the South Korean group, one of the biggest names in K-pop, have opted out of the awards ceremony

LOS ANGELES, USA – K-pop group BTS said on Wednesday, July 29, they will not submit any music for consideration at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards in February 2027, citing dissatisfaction with the academy’s new category for best Asian pop music performance.

The decision marks the first time the South Korean group, one of the biggest names in K-pop, have opted out of the awards ceremony. Each member of the group shared the news in a post on Instagram.

“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year. I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” they wrote.

The Recording Academy announced the new category on June 16 for music from South Korea, Japan, China, and elsewhere in the region.

“This category recognizes artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including but not limited to K-pop, J-pop and C-pop, with meaningful use of one or more Asian languages,” the Grammy website says.

The Recording Academy said in a statement that BTS’ decision was disappointing.

“I am saddened to hear that BTS has chosen not to participate in the Grammy Awards process this year, but as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision,” Harvey Mason Jr., CEO of the Grammys, said.

However, Mason said he wanted to clarify what he believes has been lost in the conversation surrounding the K-pop group’s boycott.

“The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters,” he added.

Mason also emphasized that submitting music to any category, including Asian Pop, does not prevent an artist or group from being considered for the general field categories, including record of the year, album of the year and song of the year.

“Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre. Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both,” Mason said.

The statement concluded with the CEO stressing the Recording Academy serves the global music community regardless of geography or language.

“I want to emphasize that we will continue to listen to the global music community and work to honor and celebrate all the artists whose music moves the world,” he said.

BTS released the comeback album ARIRANG on March 20 after a hiatus for their members to complete military service. A global success, it topped the Billboard 200 chart for two consecutive weeks, setting a new record for a K-pop act.

Tickets for BTS concerts in South Korea sold out rapidly during January’s presale, driven by demand from the band’s devoted fanbase, known as ARMY. The North American and European legs of the tour also sold out within hours, according to Hybe, the agency that manages BTS.

At the 52nd American Music Awards in May, BTS beat Taylor Swift and other major artists to win artist of the year, in addition to taking home two other awards.

BTS consists of seven members: RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V and Jungkook. They are managed by Big Hit Music, an independent label under Hybe. – Rappler.com

World.title: Opening a bank account is now easier for National ID holders
World.content:
As more banks connect to the National ID database, opening a bank account may soon be as easy as entering your name, birthday, and taking a live selfie

MANILA, Philippines – Opening a bank account is beginning to require little more than a live selfie for millions of Filipinos, as banks increasingly connect their onboarding systems to the government’s National ID database.

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) customers who are already registered with the National ID system can now open a BPI account through the bank’s mobile app without photographing or uploading a physical identification card. Instead, the customer enters basic information and takes a live selfie, which is matched against the facial image and other details stored in the Philippine Identification System (PhilSys).

“You take a selfie, you put your name and your birthday, and then it goes, pulls up your record from the National ID, and that’s how we verify you,” BPI president and chief executive officer Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco said, explaining that customers do not need to possess the physical National ID card.

BPI said the simpler process is already translating into more completed applications. Fitzgerald Chee, BPI’s head of consumer platforms, said account openings increased by about 50% after the bank introduced National ID-based verification. Around 85% of BPI’s account openings now use the National ID, according to consumer banking head Maria Cristina Go.

Aside from convenience, BPI executives said matching customers against government-held biometric records could help banks detect fabricated identities, fraudulent account applications, and so-called money mules whose accounts are used to receive or move proceeds from scams.

“This is not only good for BPI. This is really good for the whole banking system,” Limcaoco said during a signing ceremony on Thursday, July 30. “I foresee one day this is the only way it’s going to be.”

More banks, institutions connecting to PhilSys

BPI is only the latest major financial institution to connect its customer verification process to the National ID Authentication Services (NIDAS). Asia United Bank, GoTyme Bank, Philippine National Bank, and GCash have all worked with the PSA on National-ID based services.

PSA Deputy National Statistician Rosalinda Bautista said the agency ultimately wants all financial institutions to adopt the system.

The PSA is also pushing the National ID beyond banking and payments, positioning it as a common identity verification layer for healthcare, education, social protection, and other government services.

PhilHealth has integrated NIDAS into its PhilHealth Check Utility, allowing it to verify members through real-time facial recognition, identify duplicate records, and reduce fraudulent benefit claims.

Baguio General Hospital and Medical Center became the first government hospital to integrate National ID authentication into its patient registration system. Don Mariano Marcos Memorial State University has also connected to the system, becoming the first state university to use National ID authentication.

The PSA is also exploring possible applications with the Commission on Elections, as both agencies require the collection of fingerprints from ID applicants.

The technology removes a documentation barrier, particularly for people who have no passport, driver’s license, or other traditional ID. As of June 30, a total of 92,988,897 people had been issued Philippine Standard Numbers with verifiable National ID credentials. Of these, 91,893,866 could access their Digital National ID through the eGovPH app.

A physical plastic card is not required for authentication. PSA officials said about 55 million physical cards had been issued before card printing was halted, but registered Filipinos may use their Digital National ID or request a free paper National ID which carries the same functionality.

The PSA recorded more than 124 million successful National ID authentications as of June 30, including over 44 million transactions conducted by financial and other private institutions. By July 28, officials said the cumulative number across all sectors had risen to about 145 million. – Rappler.com

Here are some of the images in the aftermath of the powerful tremor

MANILA, Philippines — A magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Japan‘s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, July 28, leading to at least 17 deaths.

Rescue operations continued, with several people pulled from the rubble of the partially collapsed Aeon shopping mall near the city of Kumamoto that was torn apart by an explosion just over an hour after the earthquake.

The earthquake caused significant damage to infrastructure, including roads and buildings, and disrupted power supply to thousands of homes. It also raised concerns about disrupted supply chains and logistics.

World.title: China releases draft cyberbullying law covering AI-enabled abuse
World.content:
China's draft law aims to curb cyberbullying, including AI-enabled abuse. The regulator is canvassing public opinion on the draft law until August 28.

BEIJING, China – China’s cyberspace regulator on Wednesday, July 29, released a draft law aimed at curbing cyberbullying, including AI-enabled abuse, as Beijing tightens oversight of online bullying in the world’s largest internet community.

Here are some key details of the draft law published by the Cyberspace Administration of China:

The law would apply to cyberbullying activities carried out within China, as well as to organisations and individuals overseas that target the country.

Online platforms would be required to verify the real identities of users before allowing them to post information or use instant messaging services.

The proposed rules ask platforms to trace and report the risk of cyberbullying content generated or spread using AI technology, remove and block such content, and report it to authorities.

Schools are required to incorporate anti-cyberbullying material into their curricula.

Online service providers that violate the rules could face fines of up to 10 million yuan ($1.5 million), the shutdown of their websites or applications, or the revocation of business licenses, according to the draft.

The regulator is canvassing public opinion on the draft law until August 28. – Rappler.com

World.title: Arrest warrant out vs ex-Sultan Kudarat lawmaker Arnulfo Go in malversation case
World.content:
Former Sultan Kudarat representative Arnulfo Go and two others are also facing separate charges linked to the alleged misuse of the Priority Development Assistance Fund when he served as a congressman

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan has issued an arrest warrant against former Sultan Kudarat representative Arnulfo Go and three others in a malversation case involving over P8.8 million in public funds, with another warrant expected to be issued in a separate but related case.

The court’s 3rd Division issued the warrant on July 27 against Go, former Lebak, Sultan Kudarat mayor Dionesio Besana, municipal accountant Allan Bayani, and municipal treasurer Mario Labrador.

The Office of the Ombudsman filed the malversation charges earlier in July, and the prosecution had recommended that no bail be granted for the four accused, according to Sandiganbayan 3rd Division clerk of court Dennis Pulma.

Such are non-bailable because the amount allegedly involved exceeds the threshold that carries a penalty of reclusion perpetua upon conviction.

A hold departure order has been issued to prevent them from leaving the country. Pulma said the four remain at large.

They are also facing separate charges under the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act linked to the alleged misuse of the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) of Go when he served as a member of the House of Representatives from 2007 to 2016.

A 2014 special audit by the Commission on Audit (COA) identified Go among lawmakers whose PDAF allocations were allegedly coursed through questionable non-governmental organizations, with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) serving as an intermediary.

State auditors said P15 million from Go’s PDAF was released to the NCMF, which later transferred the funds to Rich Islas de Filipinas Foundation Incorporated (RIDFFI).

RIDFFI had also been identified as a recipient of PDAF allocations linked to former Misamis Occidental representative Loreto Leo Campos.

Campos, who also once served as governor of Misamis Occidental, was convicted by the Sandiganbayan 2nd Division in 2025 on one count each of graft, malversation of public funds, and falsification of public documents, along with NGO executives Josefina Candole and Jamie Ann Llinsangan. They were slapped with a 10- to 20-year imprisonment sentence and barred from holding public office for life.

The Sandiganbayan’s 4th Division is expected to act on another non-bailable malversation charge against Go and his co-accused, with an arrest warrant expected by Friday, July 31. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Bring the prisons closer to home
World.content:
The Bureau of Corrections has publicly announced that the New Bilibid Prison will be closed by 2028. The government has already begun transferring thousands of persons deprived of liberty from Muntinlupa to penal farms and regional facilities throughout the country.

Since 2022, more than 15,000 PDLs have reportedly been transferred as part of this massive decentralization program. They have been moved to facilities in Sablayan, Occidental Mindoro; Iwahig, Palawan; Abuyog, Leyte; San Ramon, Zamboanga City; and Panabo, Davao del Norte.

The prison population is being dispersed, but the human consequences of that dispersal remain largely unseen.

There is sound reasoning behind the regionalization of the prison system. New Bilibid Prison has long symbolized congestion, neglect, violence, corruption, and the institutional failures of Philippine corrections. Its enormous population has made effective classification, individualized programming, case management, and rehabilitation extremely difficult.

Smaller regional facilities can become safer, more manageable, and more responsive to the different risks and needs of incarcerated individuals. Regionalization, when properly implemented, can move the country away from the warehouse model of imprisonment.

There is also merit in the government’s plan to transform the vast New Bilibid Prison reservation into a commercial and income-generating area. Properly developed and transparently managed, portions of the property could generate resources to help sustain correctional operations, improve facilities, professionalize personnel, and expand rehabilitation programs.

BuCor has already explored proposals to develop or lease portions of its properties in preparation for the prison’s closure. The land should not remain idle while correctional institutions throughout the country struggle with inadequate resources.

Regionalized abandonment

But property development must never become more important than the people displaced by that development.

The problem is that many PDLs from Metro Manila and Northern Luzon are now being transferred hundreds, sometimes thousands, of kilometers away from their families. A person from Cagayan, Isabela, Ilocos Norte, Pangasinan, Baguio, or Metro Manila may find himself confined in Leyte, Palawan, Zamboanga, or Davao.

For government officials, this may appear to be a simple matter of population redistribution. For poor families, however, it can mean an impossible journey involving airplane fares, boat tickets, bus rides, meals, lodging, and several days away from work. Regionalization may ease congestion, but it can also regionalize abandonment.

Family visitation is not a mere privilege that prison administrators may casually disregard. It is an essential component of rehabilitation, mental health, institutional stability, and successful reintegration. Families provide emotional support, food, medicine, legal information, and a continuing connection to ordinary community life. They remind the incarcerated person that there is still a home to return to and a life that can still be rebuilt. When families cannot visit, the punishment extends beyond the person convicted and reaches spouses, parents, and children who committed no crime.

Distance also creates serious difficulties in following up legal cases and securing early-release opportunities. Families often coordinate with lawyers, courts, parole officers, prison records personnel, and government agencies. They help obtain documents, certificates, clearances, and records needed for parole, executive clemency, good-conduct time allowances, and other lawful release mechanisms. When the PDL is detained in a distant island or region, communication becomes slower and bureaucratic errors become harder to correct. A missing document can become another year in prison, while a delayed signature can become another season away from home.

The Bureau of Corrections has therefore correctly requested national support for the establishment of additional regional prisons in Luzon. Facilities are urgently needed in the Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, the Cordillera Administrative Region, Central Luzon, and Calabarzon. Metro Manila will likewise require accessible correctional facilities as New Bilibid Prison is gradually emptied and closed.

These should not be gigantic prisons that merely reproduce the problems of Bilibid elsewhere. They should be smaller, professionally managed, adequately staffed, and designed around classification, education, treatment, livelihood, mental health, family contact, and reintegration.

Humane prison system

The national government must allocate the land, resources, and institutional support required to construct these facilities. It should begin planning before the last prisoners are transferred and before families are completely separated by geography and poverty.

Prison reform cannot simply mean moving bodies from one overcrowded institution into several distant institutions. It must mean creating correctional environments where security, accountability, rehabilitation, and human dignity can exist together. A humane prison system does not merely ask where a person can be securely confined; it also asks how that person can remain connected to the family and community to which he will eventually return.

Regional prisons in Luzon are therefore not merely construction projects. They are investments in public safety, rehabilitation, family unity, and successful reintegration. They would reduce the enormous financial burden imposed on poor families while making case monitoring and release preparation more efficient. They would allow BuCor to build institutions that are smaller, safer, and more manageable than New Bilibid Prison.

Most importantly, they would affirm a basic principle of humane correctional management: imprisonment may restrict liberty, but it should not unnecessarily destroy the human relationships that make rehabilitation possible. – Rappler.com

Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
