World.title: Russian lawmaker makes another bid to enter South Ossetian politics
World.content:
North Ossetia parliament member Dzambolat Tedeyev, who represents the A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth party and is a former head coach of Russia’s national freestyle wrestling team, is officially returning to South Ossetian politics. What role he intends to play, however, remains unclear. His previous attempts to establish himself in the region’s political scene have all ended in failure.

A native of South Ossetia, Tedeyev once even sought to become the region’s president.

At the recent third congress of the Patriots of Alania party, which was already under Tedeyev’s influence, he was elected its chairman. The high-profile move in Tskhinvali coincided with the party’s nomination of Murat Valiyev — a serving officer in the State Protection Service and former KGB officer — as its presidential candidate.

Tedeyev said the party’s main goal would be to ensure that the views of South Ossetian citizens are heard by the republic’s leadership.

“Our position has never changed, but now we have our own platform from which we can defend the interests of our citizens and our country. Today, we see people leaving because they cannot find work. Despite an investment programme aimed at creating new businesses, unemployment remains a serious problem.

There are many issues to address. But today we have hope because, thanks to you, we now have a party where we can make our voices heard. We must unite and build the future of our republic together,” he told delegates at the party congress.

Commenting on the nomination of little-known State Protection Service officer Murat Valiyev as the party’s presidential candidate, Tedeyev appeared to acknowledge that Valiyev was being put forward as a “technical candidate.” He urged acting president and election frontrunner Marat Kambolov to “rely on” Valiyev and his allies.

Tedeyev also recalled his own failed presidential bid in 2011, when the Central Election Commission refused to register him as a candidate.

“There was a time when I wanted to run, but I wasn’t allowed to. Today, I see that Marat has greater potential, stronger connections, and is capable of achieving more. Why shouldn’t he rely on me? That’s why I decided that even if we nominate Murat Valiyev today, Marat should rely on him, on us, on all of us.

And let’s all put our ambitions aside a little. We all know what we’re capable of.”

Tedeyev’s remarks have prompted mixed reactions in South Ossetia. Local analysts say it remains unclear whether he genuinely intends to challenge for power or is instead demonstrating loyalty by putting forward his ally as a “technical candidate” in the hope of negotiating with Kambolov after the election.

The events of 2011, when Dzambolat Tedeyev unsuccessfully challenged the outgoing president, Eduard Kokoity, for power, remain fresh in South Ossetia’s collective memory.

After the Central Election Commission refused to register his presidential candidacy, Tedeyev threw his support behind former education minister Alla Dzhioyeva. Although the former official had been accused of corruption and placed under house arrest, her alliance with Tedeyev helped unite the protest vote and secure victory in the election.

The pair, however, were never allowed to take power. The Supreme Court annulled the election results, triggering days of street protests. The opposition, led by Dzhioyeva and Tedeyev, unsuccessfully sought to defend what they said was their electoral victory.

The standoff ended in a compromise that ultimately fell short of Tedeyev’s ambitions. Kokoity announced his resignation, even though his second and final term was already nearing its end, while the opposition agreed to end the protests. A repeat presidential election was scheduled for March 2012, but Dzhioyeva did not take part.

Since then, Tedeyev has periodically sought to influence political developments in South Ossetia, but without much success. Ahead of the 2024 parliamentary elections, for example, he formed an alliance with the parliamentary People’s Party, whose members were once supporters of former president Eduard Kokoity.

According to local analysts, in exchange for Tedeyev’s financial backing, the party agreed to include his allies on its electoral list. However, the alliance ultimately failed to secure a majority of seats in parliament.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Dzambolat Tedeyev takes over South Ossetia party

World.title: ‘Moscow will only push Armenia out of Russian-led blocs’: Reaction to Russia’s foreign intelligence claim
World.content:
SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

“Brussels understands that Armenia will face a severe economic crisis if Yerevan leaves the Eurasian Economic Union,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on the previous day.

The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a Russia-led economic bloc. Its members are Russia, Armenia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Kyrgyzstan.

“Brussels should not expect the EAEU countries to keep Yerevan’s political crew afloat or bankroll its marathon swim toward the European Union,” the SVR said.

In Armenia, observers noted that the statement followed a phone call between Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin on July 27. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said one of the main topics was a referendum in Armenia on European Union membership or continued participation in the EAEU.

“We stressed the need for Armenia to hold a referendum as soon as possible so Armenians can decide which direction they want to take,” Peskov said.

The Kremlin’s readout of the call did not mention Pashinyan’s response. However, the Armenian prime minister’s office said he told Putin:

“Holding such a referendum would only become possible after Armenia submits an official application to join the European Union and the issue takes on practical significance.”

The Armenian authorities have given Russia the same response on several previous occasions.

Local analysts viewed the Kremlin’s remarks and the SVR statement as another attempt to pressure Armenia.

In their view, the crisis in bilateral relations continues, and “there is still no solution in sight”. They also questioned why Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, rather than the EAEU itself, had spoken on the bloc’s behalf.

The Armenian prime minister’s office said that, during the call, “Pashinyan stressed that restrictions on exports of Armenian-made goods to the Russian market violate the legal framework governing Armenia-Russia relations and Eurasian Economic Union regulations. He asked Russia to take steps to resolve the issue.” Pashinyan appears to have called Putin primarily over Russia’s ban on imports of numerous Armenian food products and other goods. Russia introduced the restrictions at the end of May.

Statement by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service

The SVR titled its statement, “The EU Lures Armenia but Cannot Help It.” The statement argues that Armenia would face a severe economic crisis if it left the EAEU.

“Armenia will lose the income it currently receives from Eurasian integration. The remaining EAEU members will not bankroll the Armenian authorities as they row toward the European Union. EU institutions acknowledge that the bloc’s worsening economic problems, driven by anti-Russian sanctions and what they describe as Brussels’ obsession with supporting the war in Ukraine, will leave the EU unable to offset Armenia’s multi-billion-dollar losses. Several European countries have already told EU leaders they are unwilling to open their markets to Armenian goods at the expense of domestic producers.”

Russia’s foreign intelligence service also claims the EU will continue to assure Yerevan of its unwavering support.

“The EU plans to explain the lack of tangible assistance by arguing that accession depends entirely on Yerevan and on its own ‘progress’ toward European integration.”

According to the SVR, the EU has already presented Pashinyan’s government with the following demands:

reduce the presence of Russian businesses in strategic sectors;

sever humanitarian ties with Russia;

suppress domestic opponents who resist those policies.

The statement adds that the EU will encourage Armenia by “holding out the prospect of visa liberalisation for Armenian citizens and promising that, at some distant point in the future, Armenia will become a ‘prosperous crossroads of peace.’

How Armenians View European Integration: Poll Results

Against the backdrop of Russia’s call for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether to remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership, local broadcaster Factor TV conducted an online poll. Participants answered the following question: “If a referendum on choosing between the EAEU and the EU were held this Sunday, which would you vote for?”

According to the broadcaster, more than 3,300 people have already taken part in the poll. The results are as follows:

74% said they would vote for EU membership;

said they would vote for EU membership; 21% said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU;

said they would prefer Armenia to remain in the EAEU; 5% said they were undecided.

Reactions

Political analyst Samvel Melkisetian said:

“Statements like these from Moscow are nothing new. They fit a long-established Russian pattern. The aim is to show both domestic and international audiences that Russia remains actively involved in regional developments. They also seek to expose what they portray as the EU’s and the West’s ‘hidden mechanisms’ of harmful influence across the post-Soviet region.”

He also noted that Moscow’s rhetoric often portrays Armenia not as a sovereign state making its own decisions, but as an object of external influence.

Political analyst Hovsep Khurshudyan said:

“What does Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service have to do with the EAEU that allows it to speak on behalf of the bloc’s member states? Has the SVR become the press office for the EAEU or its members?”

Khurshudyan also questioned Russia’s intelligence service:

“How can Brussels be accused of driving Armenia’s economy into crisis when it is Brussels that is compensating for the losses caused by the sanctions Russia has imposed?”

He was referring to EU support programmes launched after Russia restricted imports of Armenian goods.

Khurshudyan argues that, in the end, Russia’s actions will only accelerate:

Armenia’s withdrawal from Russian-led integration structures, including the EAEU and the Collective Security Treaty Organization;

the withdrawal of Russian border guards from Armenia’s borders with Iran and Turkey;

the termination of the concession agreement under which a Russian company operates Armenia’s railways.

Khurshudyan believes Armenia still has room to take further steps, while Russia has already exhausted most of its leverage.

SVR warns of economic crisis in Armenia as Yerevan pushes back

World.title: Imam of Georgia’s Akhaltsikhe mosque and family members brutally beaten
World.content:
Georgia‘s Interior Ministry has launched an investigation into an attack on the family of a Meskhetian Muslim in the city of Akhaltsikhe. According to the victims, more than 10 people assaulted the imam of the local mosque, Shevket Dvalidze, and members of his family during the incident on 18 July.

The attack was first reported by the news outlet Batumelebi. According to the publication, the assault began after the imam’s son and an underage relative visiting from Turkey were heard speaking Turkish to each other.

Meskhetian Muslims, also known as Meskhetian Turks or Ahiska Turks, are a Turkic ethnic group originating from the historical region of Meskheti in southwestern Georgia.

Shevket Dvalidze, imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque

According to the imam’s family, the group initially confronted them verbally, hurling insults over their use of the Turkish language, before the argument escalated into a physical assault.

The victims said the attackers followed them to their home and brutally beat them in the courtyard. Shevket Dvalidze, the imam of the Akhaltsikhe mosque, sustained the most serious injuries and was later taken to hospital.

Batumelebi reported that Dvalidze was also urged to withdraw his police complaint.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it had opened an investigation under Article 126 of the Criminal Code, which covers physical violence.

The Georgian-based Social Justice Center responded to the incident by calling on the authorities to conduct a prompt and effective investigation and to properly assess whether the attack was motivated by discrimination.

According to the organisation, the victims said that between 10 and 12 people took part in the assault, and that most of them had been identified. However, only two suspects were arrested and were later released on bail by a court.

The Social Justice Center said the circumstances suggested the case could constitute not only an act of violence but also a hate crime, as the attack may have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation said investigators should examine whether the assault was motivated by the victims’ ethnic, religious or linguistic identity and ensure those circumstances are properly reflected in the legal classification of the case.

According to the Social Justice Center, correctly classifying the attack as a hate crime is important not only because of its legal consequences, but also because it acknowledges the true nature of the offence and helps prevent similar incidents.

The organisation called on the Interior Ministry and the Prosecutor’s Office to identify all those involved in the attack, rather than limiting the investigation to the two detained suspects. It also urged investigators to examine allegations that pressure had been put on the imam to withdraw his police complaint.

The Social Justice Center also called on the government and the Office of the State Minister for Reconciliation and Civic Equality to publicly condemn the violence against the Meskhetian Muslim family, which it said appeared to have been motivated by linguistic and religious intolerance.

The organisation further urged the authorities to strengthen policies promoting equality, rebuilding trust and supporting cultural diversity in Akhaltsikhe’s Meskhetian Muslim communities, while reviewing barriers related to the repatriation and citizenship of Meskhetian Muslims.

Imam beaten in Georgia after speaking Turkish

World.title: Nauru cuts diplomatic ties with occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The Pacific island nation of Nauru has cut diplomatic ties with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

According to the ministry, Nauru’s cabinet decided on 21 July 2026 to terminate diplomatic relations “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of South Ossetia, also known as the State of Alania,” and “between the Republic of Nauru and the Republic of Abkhazia.”

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation based on shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions to be independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to back the Moscow-backed move.

Nauru is a small island nation in the Pacific Ocean, in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 square kilometres, the country is smaller than several districts of Tbilisi, while its population is estimated at around 12,000 to 13,000 people.

Nauru ends ties with Abkhazia and South Ossetia

World.title: Five fined and four jailed in Tbilisi activists’ case
World.content:
A court in Georgia has concluded hearings in the cases of 10 activists detained outside Tbilisi City Hall on 26 July. Four were sentenced to administrative detention, while five were fined. Proceedings against one remaining activist have been postponed until 31 July.

What happened

The incident began when activist Tornike Toshkhua staged a solo protest outside Tbilisi City Hall holding a banner reading: “Bidzina d*ck? Yes – No.” The slogan referred to Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Police detained Toshkhua at the scene.

Tornike Toshkhua

In response, a group of activists gathered outside Tbilisi City Hall carrying banners with the same slogan to express solidarity with Toshkhua. Within minutes, police began detaining them as well. In total, nine more people were arrested alongside Toshkhua.

They have been charged with using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders.

Fines and detentions

The activists began appearing in court from the afternoon of 28 July, before the 48-hour detention period had expired.

The first ruling was delivered in the case of Vaso Beridze. The judge fined him 5,000 lari ($1,850), rejecting the Interior Ministry’s request to place him under administrative detention.

In the case of Ia Melitauri, the Interior Ministry sought the maximum administrative detention, but the judge sentenced her to five days in custody instead. Police accused Melitauri of using abusive language in a public place and disobeying lawful police orders. The judge found no evidence that she had disobeyed police and convicted her only of petty hooliganism.

Melitauri had previously been found guilty twice of administrative offences involving disobeying police and insulting a police officer. A third offence under the same provision carries criminal liability.

According to people present at the hearing, Melitauri told the court she had been mistreated by police following her arrest and showed the judge injuries she said she had sustained during her detention.

The hearing in the case of the third detainee, Tornike Tikaradze, was postponed until 31 July. Tikaradze did not attend the hearing in protest.

Another judge heard the cases of seven other activists and, after several hours of witness testimony and reviewing video evidence, delivered the following verdicts:

Tornike Toshkhua was fined 3,000 lari ($1,110);

Mariam Mekantsishvili was fined 6,000 lari ($2,220);

Nato Bolkvadze was sentenced to five days of administrative detention;

Shako Bagdoshvili was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Lasha Dgebuadze was sentenced to 10 days of administrative detention;

Marine Nanava was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850);

Sandro Sekhniashvili was fined 5,000 lari ($1,850).

Scuffle outside the courthouse

Several reports of scuffles between members of the public and court bailiffs emerged throughout the day as the hearings were under way.

Videos circulating on social media showed bailiffs forcibly removing people from the courthouse.

During the final hearing, activist Ruska Mchedlidze and lawyer Marika Arevadze said court bailiffs used force against them.

Ruska Mchedlidze

“Zonder bailiff Davit Matiashvili and other zonder bailiffs physically assaulted me in the courtyard of this unjust court. Yes, I spat at them, and yes, I spat at them again after the assault, once I was outside the gates.

These bruises will heal, but everyone will remember his disgrace forever. His, and that of the other zonder bailiffs carrying out unlawful orders. There were around 20 police officers standing there, watching as these aggressive men assaulted me, and not one of them intervened,” Mchedlidze wrote on social media.

Activist Lado Jakhua also shared footage showing several court bailiffs dragging Ruska Mchedlidze out of the courthouse courtyard.

Tbilisi activists sentenced over protest

World.title: Opposition grows in Abkhazia over monument to citizens killed in Ukraine war
World.content:
A group of Abkhaz politicians and public figures has spoken out against plans to erect a monument in Sukhum to citizens of Abkhazia who were killed while fighting in the war in Ukraine.

They appealed to the republic’s president, Badra Gunba, and the city authorities to cancel or postpone the decision, which was approved by the Sukhum City Assembly at the initiative of the city administration.

The appeal was signed by former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia, People’s Artist Batal Jopua, historian Guram Gumba, former education minister Adgur Kakoba, Akhyatsa civic organisation head Akhra Bzhania, and former leader of the Aruaa veterans’ movement Ilya Guniya.

The signatories argue that any memorial erected in the Abkhaz capital should commemorate historical events only after they have stood the test of time.

“Fighting is still under way, people are dying, yet the local authorities in Abkhazia have taken the unprecedented decision to erect a monument to a war that has not yet ended.

“No one knows how, when or on what terms these two closely related peoples will first reach understanding and then reconciliation. But that will inevitably happen. Only then, years later, will we be able to return to the question of creating a memorial to this historical event,” the appeal says.

The authors also point out that Sukhum still has no monuments to Abkhazia’s first president, Vladislav Ardzinba, or to volunteers from the North Caucasus republics who fought alongside Abkhazia during the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war.

“If we intend to begin preserving our historical memory, we should start with them. Otherwise, not only the people of Abkhazia but also our friends in the North Caucasus and the parents of the fallen volunteers will not understand us,” the appeal says.

The signatories also argue that the issue has an important foreign policy dimension. Despite its strategic partnership with Russia, they say, Abkhazia is not at war with Ukraine.

“Our state has never carried out any mobilisation or organisational measures in connection with what Russia calls its ‘special military operation’. The relevant authorities have no information about either the total number of our citizens in the conflict zone or the terms under which they entered military service,” the appeal says.

They argue that officially recognising the participation of Abkhaz citizens in the fighting would provide diplomatic grounds for Ukraine and its regional allies, including Turkey, to regard Abkhazia as a party to the conflict. As a result, they say, “our citizens’ participation in the war would cease to be a matter of personal choice and instead become our collective choice.”

Although the appeal has been signed by only six people, its authors say they believe their views are widely shared across Abkhaz society.

“We are in contact with people from all walks of life and can say with confidence that thousands of residents of Sukhum and citizens of Abkhazia share our views and the arguments set out above.”

The signatories call on the president and the city authorities to act with prudence and wisdom.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Monument to Abkhazians who fought in Ukraine

World.title: Turkey takes practical steps to restore rail link with Armenia
World.content:
Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

Turkey has begun restoring the entire railway infrastructure along the Akyaka–Gyumri route, the section connecting it with Armenia. Preliminary estimates suggest the work will take two to three months to complete. Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas told this to a group of Armenian journalists visiting Turkey.

According to Toptas, the construction work now under way in Turkey signals preparations for reopening the Armenian-Turkish border. He said reopening the border would give Turkey another route to the Caucasus. It would also allow Armenia to establish transport links with Middle Eastern countries through Turkey.

Kadir Bozan, chairman of the Kars Chamber of Commerce and Industry, also told the Armenian journalists that freight traffic on the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway has increased by 400% in recent months. He did not specify whether Armenia uses the route for exports or imports.

However, on 24 May, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that “the Akhalkalaki–Kars railway is now open for exports from Armenia and imports into Armenia.” He described the development as extremely important for the country’s economy.

Armenian journalists’ impressions from their visit to Turkey

According to official information, a group of Armenian journalists travelled to Turkey as part of a journalist exchange programme. The purpose of the visit was to observe progress on the work to reopen the railway on the Turkish side.

The journalists also wanted to see how Turkey’s railway infrastructure operates more broadly. In particular, they travelled by train from Kars to Akyaka. The 57-kilometre journey took just 50 minutes.

After returning, they wrote that Akyaka station lies only 18–20 kilometres from the Armenian city of Gyumri. That means the journey would take just 30–40 minutes. However, the closed border currently makes it impossible to travel from Akyaka to Gyumri.

Tender announced for Akyaka–Gyumri highway

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas said Turkey plans to restore not only the railway but also the highway.

“The tender for the construction of the road from Akyaka to Gyumri has already been announced. We now expect work on that project to begin as well,” he said.

According to Toptas, these developments indicate that both governments are moving towards establishing good-neighbourly and friendly relations.

The mayor said reopening the Armenian-Turkish border and expanding bilateral economic cooperation would benefit both countries. He believes the two sides have opportunities to cooperate in both agriculture and industry.

The Armenian journalists also spoke with residents of Turkish settlements near the Armenian border. Most said they hope the border will reopen as soon as possible. They also believe it will create new economic opportunities for local communities on both sides of the border.

“We do not expect any obstacles to reopening the border”

Akyaka Mayor Erduger Toptas expressed optimism about the prospects for normalising relations between Armenia and Turkey. In his view, once Armenia and Azerbaijan normalise their relations, reopening the Armenian-Turkish border should not present any difficulties.

He said that, on the instructions of the Turkish president and under the coordination of the transport ministry, officials have begun preparatory work at the border crossing points ahead of the border’s reopening. Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Dictator wants to be liked by everyone. Those who don’t like him must be neutralised’
World.content:
Transparency International Georgia researcher Zviad Koridze believes that Georgia’s current system of governance is built on fostering civil confrontation and deepening divisions within society. In his view, authoritarian regimes rely on social polarisation and the portrayal of people with different opinions as enemies in order to maintain power.

Koridze said that Georgian society still retains the capacity to resist, and that, ultimately, it is civic engagement that will serve as the main force pushing back against these processes.

On 26 July, MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several supporters, announced the creation of a civic movement that will “respond immediately” to issues involving ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. According to Kartvelishvili, the movement will be “highly active, well-organised and constructive”, and any “patriotic Georgian” will be able to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

Zviad Koridze: “the system of governance that has taken hold in Georgia — Bidzina Ivanishvili’s dictatorship — regards civil confrontation as its natural state, just like any other dictatorship. Without it, those in power cannot consolidate their rule. They cannot persuade citizens that their continued grip on power and authoritarian governance serve the public interest. To do that, they need civil confrontation.

“All dictatorships are structured and develop in exactly this way. They need to identify groups and segments of society whose views differ from those of the autocrat. Then another social group must emerge to confront and suppress them. That is the language of civil confrontation.”

“When parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that we do not need to join the European Union because we should have the right to make our own decisions, that is clearly not his independent position but Bidzina Ivanishvili’s. Papuashvili’s role is to voice that position and to support the creation of precisely these kinds of vigilante groups. He is expected to welcome their emergence. He sees this as a form of sovereign governance, and that is exactly why he does not want Georgia to join the European Union.

“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: The Australian matches the Irish wake up at all hours to watch
World.content:
In the middle of the night in a house in Ballinamore, in the North West of Ireland, Sharon O'Dowd wakes up to put on an Australian broadcast.

Two years ago, her young sister Eilish, who she helped raise with 12 years between them, moved from County Leitrim to Sydney to play AFLW for GWS.

Sharon and Eilish ODowd at a Gaelic game. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

When one of two of Eilish's matches haven't been available to stream across the ocean, the mother of two — her kids three and six — has put the commentary on and sat and listened instead while the rest of her house sleeps.

"I don't mind getting up this early as I love to watch her and the Giants play," Sharon told ABC Sport.

"If it's a particularly early game I usually go back to bed after it."

Sharon is one of many families across Ireland who wake up at all hours to watch GAA-turned-AFLW stars.

There are 47 Irish players in the AFL women's competition, many of whom will be on show in this weekend's inaugural AFLW Australia v Ireland clash in Sydney.

Their feats regularly make headlines back home.

Eilish with the first touch of her ball for GWS scored the fastest opening goal in AFLW history. The clip — in which she won the tap in the ruck and bolted straight through the corridor to score within 15 seconds — made the national news.

Sharon and EIlish O'Dowd. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

As it was her first game, Sharon was still getting familiar with the stream and watched, stunned, from her phone.

"I was in shock when she scored because I just couldn't believe what had happened," Sharon said.

"Everyone else in my house was asleep so I couldn't even celebrate with them. I knew my parents were watching the game in their house so I texted them.

"But it had happened so quickly they didn't even see it because they hadn't got logged into their streaming account fast enough."

Luckily, they have since watched the video of the replay multiple times.

Vikki Wall is a two-time premiership player with North Melbourne. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Over in Dunboyne, a town of less than 10,000 people in County Meath, the Wall family regularly pack their house for North Melbourne games.

Tom and Caroline Wall's daughter, Vikki Wall, is a star sportswoman from the Eastern Coast.

She twice led County Meath to historic All-Ireland Senior Championship titles in 2021 and 2022 before being signed as an international rookie by North Melbourne and playing all 13 games of her 2022 debut season.

Vikki Wall is a star player in Ireland. (Supplied: Caroline Wall)

She missed the 2023 AFLW season to play rugby sevens for Ireland ahead of the Paris Olympics and returned to Arden Street to win premierships in 2024 and 2025.

"We've had events in our house where 30-plus people come and have breakfast and cheer on the teams," Tom told ABC Sport.

"We try to watch all of Vikki's matches but it can be difficult to access the games online sometimes, so we listen to the match commentaries on the radio, if necessary."

Like Sharon, this means getting up before the sun. "But it's worth it," said Tom.

Dublin, Ireland, August 15, 2021: Vikki Wall of Meath is congratulated by family following the TG4 All-Ireland Senior Ladies Football Championship Semi-Final match between Cork and Meath at Croke Park. (Getty: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

Vikki's younger sister Sarah was drafted to the Kangaroos last year. Thankfully for Tom and Caroline, this means still just the one early alarm.

Similarly, Collingwood's Sarah Rowe is a cross-code athlete, whose dad has followed her career across the globe.

Sarah represented County Mayo across all age groups from under-12 to the senior team before she moved to Australia.

There, she became a fan favourite for the Magpies after debuting in 2019 and won an A-League Women's championship with the Central Coast Mariners in 2025.

Her father Alan hasn't missed a game.

"My passion for the AFLW is total," Rowe told ABC Sport.

Sarah Rowe with her dad Alan after winning the A-League Women championship. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

"I originally had not a clue about the rules, regulations or how to play the game but over a period of time, I've got to understand everything about it, I've seen the great players grow and understood the game passionately and very deeply, to now [to be able to] say that's it's one of the great games that I love watching."

Rowe has made the trip over to Sydney for the first AFLW Australia v Ireland representative game, as he does for all her big games: her 50th, 75th and Collingwood's 2022 semi-final against Adelaide.

"It's a great honour to represent the country at the highest level and I will be there with great pride and for the family and for the town of Ballina," Rowe said.

Alan Rowe hasn't missed a single game of his daughter's, Collingwood star Sarah Rowe. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

Back in Ballina, Sarah's mother Grainne will be watching the match with "everybody within our family," Rowe said, including aunties, uncles and cousins.

"It's one of the big days of sporting life within the Irish calendar.

" And it'll be one that everyone will be so much looking forward to watching and very proud to be a part of. "

Sharon said it gets hard being away from Eilish, but she's happy players like her sister can give their all to the game overseas.

"When she has had a great game I would just love to be there to be able to tell her how amazing she is, and also when she is having a hard time or she gets injured I would love to be able to make sure she is ok. We do video calls all the time though so that helps," Sharon said.

The AFLW Australia v Ireland Cup and Best on Ground medal ahead of the inaugural clash. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

She's hoping it'll be a very happy FaceTime after Saturday's game against Australia at North Sydney Oval.

"It is an incredibly proud moment for all our family to see Eilish wear an Irish jersey and represent her country. There is no higher honour in sport in my opinion," she said.

"I'd imagine for this game the whole family will get up early to see her. We will have our Irish flags out and cheer the whole team on."

World.title: Storm coach responds to Munster's PNG ultimatum
World.content:
A part of Craig Bellamy would love it if he and Cameron Munster could bow out of Melbourne together.

But as the pair consider their NRL futures, Bellamy remains committed to supporting Munster whether or not he signs with expansion franchise PNG.

Storm veteran Munster turned the heat on Bellamy on Wednesday by claiming he would reject interest from the Chiefs for 2028 if Bellamy remained Melbourne's coach for that season.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Bellamy re-signed with the Storm through 2028 in February, but the master mentor's diagnosis with a neurodegenerative condition has since cast doubt over his future.

On Thursday, Bellamy reiterated "the next year or two I'll be finishing up" but did not say whether his health would permit coaching on as late as 2028.

Bellamy handed Munster his NRL debut in 2014 and coached him in two premiership triumphs, with the 31-year-old now the Storm's longest-serving active player.

For Bellamy, the chance to bow out together would be fitting, but Munster indicated on Wednesday he may not be able to wait for the coach to make his own decision.

"I'd love to go right through my coaching career with him, ending about the same time," Bellamy said.

"[But] he's got a decision to make. He'll make the right decision for what's right for his family. He's got the right to do that.

"I'll back 'Mun' up, whatever he wants to do."

Munster remains sidelined with a knee injury for Friday's clash with resurgent Canterbury and is now joined on the pine by captain and hooker Harry Grant.

In a season of injury carnage, Bellamy said Grant's hamstring problem was another big blow for the 12th-placed Storm.

"Any team losing their captain, that's a big loss, but Harry especially," Bellamy said.

"He's always in the middle of the play whether it be with the ball or without the ball."

Injuries, roster turnover and a seven-game losing streak early in the season have all left the Storm's finals hopes hanging by a thread ahead of round 22.

A loss to the Bulldogs would ensure they miss the top eight for only the second time under Bellamy, and first since mass salary cap breaches consigned them to the wooden spoon in 2010.

It would also mark a 12th loss of the year — the most the Storm would have suffered in any of their 24 seasons under Bellamy.

"We know it's going to be a tough ask tomorrow night, but we've had a good week's preparation with the guys we've had," Bellamy said.

AAP

World.title: US strikes 'dozens of targets' in Iran as war threatens to engulf Middle East
World.content:
The United States has carried out fresh strikes on Iran, according to the US Central Command (CENTCOM), further intensifying a five-month-old war that was already expanding beyond its main fronts to embroil additional countries in the region.

The attack began at 3:30am in Iran on Thursday and lasted for two hours, according to statements from CENTCOM posted on X.

"The strikes are a powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East," the command said, later adding that it had struck dozens of "military command centres, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defence sites, and maritime capabilities" belonging to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

"More than 50,000 US service members are currently deployed to the Middle East and remain highly vigilant, focused, lethal, and ready," the command said.

US President Donald Trump had earlier promised to hit Iran "very hard", telling reporters in the Oval Office it was "our turn" after a series of escalating exchanges between Washington and Tehran, following a two-day pause in hostilities earlier this week.

He also reportedly told conservative US outlet Fox news he planned to "beat the f***ing s***" out of Iran, in a phone interview which was not broadcast.

The outburst was prompted by news on Wednesday that Iran had fired missiles at three ships in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as launching a surprise attack aimed at American troops in Jordan on Tuesday.

Smoke rises from a tanker after a suspected drone strike on an Egyptian port. (Supplied via Reuters)

While CENTCOM said all of Iran's missiles were intercepted in Tuesday's attack, Jordan's US bases have recently become primary Iranian targets, with ​three US service members dying so far this month, the worst US losses since March.

On Wednesday, US and Saudi forces launched strikes against Iran-aligned groups in eastern Iraq in retaliation for drone attacks on Saudi oil targets, while two ships, including a US-owned gas storage tanker, caught fire after an explosion at Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta.

Maritime security firm Ambrey said the explosion appeared to be the result of a drone attack, though it could not identify the source of the attack.

The strikes in Iraq and Egypt are now threatening to draw more Middle Eastern countries into the conflict, after the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen last week declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.

A temporary ceasefire agreement between Washington and Tehran in June collapsed amid renewed fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran says it now controls.

'Death to America' shouted in Iraq

The joint US-Saudi attacks in Iraq marked the first time Riyadh has publicly joined strikes alongside Washington.

Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces, powerful Iran-backed paramilitary groups incorporated into the ​Iraqi ‌security forces, said at least 20 members were killed and 32 wounded in the US-Saudi strikes, which targeted several bases across Iraq.

Iraqi men shouted "Death to America!" as they carried the bodies of dead fighters in coffins and body bags.

Mourners carry coffins draped in the Iranian and Iraqi flags through Mosul following US and Saudi strikes. (AP Photo: Hadi Mizban)

After the joint attacks, Saudi Arabia's defence minister met with US Vice-President JD Vance to urge the Trump administration not to escalate the conflict further by attacking Yemen's Houthis or by carrying out additional ‌strikes in Iraq, two sources told the Reuters news agency.

One of ‌the sources added that such escalation would open the door to "major unknown risks". The White House and the Saudi embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

US officials have privately cautioned that resuming major combat operations against Iran would ‌carry significant risk, given America's dwindling stocks of munitions.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, estimated this week that the US military has fewer than 1,000 Patriot interceptor missiles and fewer than 250 THAAD interceptors, two key air defence systems.

Though Iran denies its forces have directed strikes from Iraqi territory, Iranian newspaper Hamshahri reported that four Iranian Revolutionary Guards advisers had ‌been killed in the strikes ​on Iraq.

Four IRGC advisers were reportedly killed in US and Saudi strikes on Mosul. (AP Photo: Farid Abdulwahed)

Iraq's Shia-led government is one of the few in the world to balance close military and diplomatic ties with both Tehran and Washington, but those divided loyalties are a constant source of tension and frequent domestic unrest.

The office of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who took power just two months ago, urged the parties involved to avoid escalation and said he wanted to keep the country out of regional conflicts.

The Iraqi presidency denounced the strikes on the paramilitaries as "an unacceptable attack and a flagrant violation of Iraq's sovereignty", while also calling for a halt to attacks by armed ⁠groups against Iraq's neighbours.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Alleged knife-wielding attacker was shot before stabbing officer, police say
World.content:
A man was allegedly shot in the leg by police before continuing to charge forward and stab a female officer in the neck in Adelaide's north yesterday, South Australia's Police Commissioner says.

The incident unfolded at about 11am on Wednesday, when police responded to reports of a male armed with a large knife running onto Main North Road at Elizabeth East.

Police Commissioner Grant Stevens revealed more details about the "highly volatile and highly dangerous" incident on 891 ABC Adelaide this morning.

He said the 27-year-old man allegedly "rushed at police with a large knife" and "as a result of that he was shot" by a male officer.

"But he [the alleged attacker] continued, moved past one police officer and managed to stab a senior constable in the neck," Commissioner Stevens said.

"As unlucky as Jessie is having being stabbed, she's incredibly fortunate there's no serious injury or ongoing concerns in relation to that wound, and we're hopeful she'll be released from hospital today."

Emergency services at the scene of the incident at Elizabeth East on Wednesday. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The commissioner praised Jessie and her police partner for showing "significant courage and professionalism" during yesterday's incident.

"It's always very confronting when those situations actually unfold in front of you and you have to make split second decisions, that you go to protecting members of the public as well as the people you're working alongside as a police officer," he said.

The alleged attacker from Woodville Gardens was also taken to hospital but police said his injuries were not considered life-threatening.

Commissioner Stevens said they were expected to charge the man "in the near future".

Grant Stevens says the two officers showed courage in yesterday's incident. (ABC News)

He said the matter was now the subject of a Police Commissioner's Inquiry and a senior officer would be allocated to examine the circumstances of the incident.

The commissioner said Major Crime Investigation Branch would also investigate the incident.

"Obviously we'll reveal all of our practices and procedures to make sure — not to suggest anything has been done incorrectly — but these are the opportunities we have to verify training and our protocols are right and that we're doing everything we can to ensure police officers can do their job safely," he said.

World.title: Closure of major industrial companies risks hit to Tasmanians' power bills
World.content:
Household energy bills could be forced up by the closure of major Tasmanian industrial companies, a leading energy analyst has warned, while pointing to the potential need for costly transmission upgrades.

The Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter announced its closure earlier this month, following a period of voluntary administration.

Meanwhile, negotiations for a power deal at Bell Bay Aluminium, the state's biggest energy consumer, are continuing, with a risk it may close.

It is understood owner Rio Tinto has set an end-of-August deadline to reach a new deal with state-owned electricity generation company Hydro Tasmania, before it considers shutting the factory.

However, it could also provide a windfall gain for Hydro Tasmania, which would be able to sell the spare energy for two to three times as much as the major industrials pay.

Energy analyst Marc White said TasNetworks had been set a maximum figure it could charge its customers by the Australian Energy Regulator, including that paid by Liberty Bell Bay.

"TasNetworks are potentially allowed under the regulatory model to recover that money from the remaining users," Mr White said.

Marc White says the closure of Tasmania's major businesses could affect the amount households pay for power. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The exact figures charged to major industrials are kept commercial in confidence, though Mr White estimated Liberty Bell Bay had paid about $8 million per year in network costs.

Spread among other power customers, it would be equivalent to a 0.6 per cent rise on the average power bill.

Mr White also estimated Bell Bay Aluminium paid $25 million per year in network charges, which, he said, could lead to another 2 per cent rise to bills if that facility closed.

TasNetworks interim chief executive Renee Anderson said the figure paid by Liberty Bell Bay was "more modest" than Mr White's estimate, but did not give an exact amount.

" They had a fairly significant reduction in their load over 12 months ago, which we supported them from a cost impact. "

She said that TasNetworks had absorbed the loss this financial year and the company did not yet have a position on whether it would do so in future years.

Balance of power grid a priority

Along with paying the lion's share of costs related to the state's transmission network, all the major industrials play an important role in keeping the grid in balance.

The two Bell Bay facilities, along with the Boyer Paper Mill and Nyrstar Zinc Smelter, are contractually obligated to reduce or increase their energy usage when asked, to keep the network in balance, known as the System Protection Scheme (SPS).

Mr White questioned whether major upgrades to the George Town substation might also be required as a result of smelter closures.

"TasNetworks might actually trigger another $120 million investment in the George Town substation because they no longer have that System Protection Scheme load available from Bell Bay Aluminium," he said.

Ms Anderson said the SPS would not be affected by the closure of Liberty Bell Bay, but said the situation would be reviewed if Bell Bay Aluminium were to shut.

"There are a lot of things that could trigger changes or investment in our infrastructure, including at George Town, so we would just follow our regulatory processes depending on what that trigger was," she said.

Spare energy presents 'significant opportunity'

Bell Bay Aluminium uses approximately 355 megawatts, or 25 per cent of the state's total energy.

Meanwhile, Liberty Bell Bay used approximately 90 megawatts, or about 7 per cent of the state's total energy.

Tasmania's major industrials receive significantly cheaper power.

This week, Industry Minister Felix Ellis said the facilities paid a quarter of the price for energy that households did, and half of what was offered to smelters on the mainland.

When it was operational, Liberty Bell Bay used approximately 7 per cent of Tasmania's total energy. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Mr White estimated Liberty Bell Bay had been paying about $40 million per year for its energy, and that Bell Bay Aluminium was paying about $100 million per year.

He said Hydro Tasmania could sell that energy for two to three times as much elsewhere, through a mix of new contracts and selling when prices were high.

"It would contract some to have stable cash flows, but it would also probably seek to play some on the arbitrage or the spot market," he said.

When built, the $5 billion Marinus Link undersea connector between Tasmania and Victoria will more than double Hydro Tasmania's capacity to trade energy with the mainland.

The completed Marinus Link is expected to bolster energy trading between Tasmania and the mainland. (Supplied: Prysmian Group)

Data centres, which use significant amounts of energy, have been floated as potential replacement buyers for the energy used by major industrials.

Firmus Technologies, which is building a 100MW centre at St Leonards and has two more facilities planned, says it receives no discount on its power.

Public 'ought' to know smelter discounts

Following the closure of Liberty Bell Bay, and the upcoming closure of Boag's Brewery, there have been concerns about the impact of another hit to northern Tasmania's economy.

Bell Bay Aluminium employs more than 500 people, plus 120 contractors, and is estimated to indirectly support nearly 1,000 other jobs.

The state government counts the smelter's total economic contribution at more than $500 million.

Rio Tinto and Hydro Tasmania were unable to reach a deal for a new power agreement last year, instead signing a one-year extension, which ends in December.

It is estimated Bell Bay Aluminium supports more than 1,600 jobs, either directly or indirectly. (Supplied: Bell Bay Aluminium)

Rio Tinto has said it is working in good faith with Hydro Tasmania, while the state-owned power company has said it is offering a price that is as low as it can go without it becoming "uncommercial".

The state government has so far refused to intervene in the negotiations and has instead called on the federal government to make its Green Aluminium Production Credit scheme available to the smelter.

Trickier bargaining position

Economist Saul Eslake said the power prices that major industrials paid should be made publicly available.

"The public ought to be able to make an informed judgement as to whether the cost in terms of revenue foregone, of delivering electricity at below market prices to big users, is worth it," Mr Eslake said.

Saul Eslake says the prices major industrials pay for power should be made available to the public. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Eslake was a board member of Hydro Tasmania between 2008 and 2018.

He said Rio Tinto had always played a "tough hand" in power price negotiations.

"This is one of the downside risks for any government that seeks to attract a major employer by offering financial inducements," he said.

World.title: Residents at homeless shelter plead for help to save their homes
World.content:
Hundreds of residents living at a Darwin's largest homeless shelter are pleading for help to save their homes as the process of closing the facility begins, with many fearing they will have have nowhere to go.

More than 220 adults and 130 children currently living at short-stay accommodation centre YiSSA have been told they must vacate by October 11.

Despite organisations on the frontline warning the Northern Territory is in a housing crisis, the NT government earlier this month announced the facility would be shut down after lease negotiations with the owner of the buildings — Ausco Modular — collapsed.

YiSSA has around 220 adults and 130 children on site. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The NT government said it offered Ausco $3 million for the infrastructure — a price it described as fair market value — and the option to waive contractual property restoration costs, but received counter offers between $8 million and $12 million.

Ausco is owned by the Modulaire Group, which is owned by global asset manager Brookfield Corporation.

The NT government this week ordered YiSSA to stop accepting new residents, meaning more than 300 people who were on the waitlist for homelessness support — including 89 children — will now have to go elsewhere.

The NT government said it is assessing alternative accommodation options for current residents and insisted "nobody will be left on the streets", but many have told the ABC they are growing increasingly uncertain about their future.

Silipa Fangaake, who moved to YiSSA almost three years ago after she became sick and was facing homelessness, said she is currently on dialysis and doesn't know where she will go.

"I'll probably end up at the park on that side where people go and camp — that's where most will probably go," she said.

Leonardo DeSantis says he's worried about where he will live when YiSSA closes. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

Resident Leonardo DeSantis is also worried about the impending closure.

"I've been here about 12 months now and I was on the street before that recovering from stomach cancer, which is in remission now," he said.

" It's really nice here and it's really like a family and I'm just disappointed that we all have to move out all of a sudden and we don't even have anywhere to stay. "

Rose Laynba said she and other residents were desperately hoping someone would step in and save the facility from closure.

Rose Laynba says she has lived at YiSSA for more than three years. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald)

"Many of us here are on waiting lists for [public] housing," she said.

"Most of our people have been waiting for 10 years [but] they're dead and gone, we buried them.

"So we are really worried what exactly is going to happen during the time when they close the YiSSA.

"I'm asking out there if someone, any government, would be able to help us."

Yvette Park, chief executive of Yilli Housing Aboriginal Corporation, which runs YiSSA, said she was working with the NT government to explore options.

However, she warned the uncertainty hanging over residents' homes was taking a heavy toll and resolving the situation would require significant funding.

"We welcome the commitment from the government that nobody will be left on the street … but in order for that to be met, we need to do a lot of work to either set up an alternative site, or multiple sites, that meet the 200 bed capacity at YiSSA," Ms Park said.

Yvette Park says significant funding is needed to resolve the problem. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"Or if negotiations with Ausco can be resolved, we look forward to staying on site."

A spokesperson for Ausco said in a statement that recent public comments regarding negotiations were disappointing.

"We are committed to meeting all of our contractual obligations and are working hard to reach a commercial outcome that is fair to all parties, and one which delivers the best value for the Territory," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Victorian premier apologises to victim-survivors of child sexual abuse in schools
World.content:
Victim-survivors of child sexual abuse in state government schools have attended Parliament House to listen to the Victorian government apologise.

Premier Ben Carroll delivered the formal apology to victim-survivors and their families this morning, recognising abuse prior to 2000.

The apology was informed by victim-survivors' experiences shared through the Forum for Truth and Recognition, the Beaumaris Board of Inquiry, and the Systemic Review into historical child sexual abuse in Victorian public schools.

The reports found that perpetrators exploited weak regulations in the education system.

Since 2000, Victoria has implemented several reforms to prevent abuse of children in schools and to change the way those in authority respond to allegations, including Working with Children Checks, mandatory Child Safe Standards, the Reportable Conduct Scheme and strengthening teacher registration requirements.

'A terrible reality'

Mr Carroll described the "terrible reality" of systemic failures that allowed abuse to occur.

"Children and young people who should have been safe in Victorian government schools were sexually abused by people entrusted with their care," Mr Carroll said.

"Students were not believed and their abusers were not held to account."

"I want to say today's apology is not an ending. It is a start. It is a start for meaningful change, meaningful action and reform."

Ben Carroll says the students should have been safe with people entrusted with their care. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said policymakers must push to bring transparency and accountability.

"An organisational culture of looking the other way, of avoiding the hard questions, of failing to be adequately self-reflective or self-critical must never be allowed to take place again," Ms Wilson said.

'Inherent failures'

Lawyers Arnold Thomas & Becker are investigating abuse allegations on behalf of more than 730 former students from over 460 Australian schools.

The list names 357 schools being investigated in Victoria.

Kim Price, the head of Arnold Thomas & Becker's institutional abuse practice, said the firm continued to receive a significant number of enquiries every month, including allegations as recent as 2024.

"The staggering number of people coming forward demonstrates the inherent failures of our education systems to implement effective policies and procedures to prevent, identify and respond to sexual and physical abuse within schools," he said.

"We have identified numerous schools where complaints of abuse had allegedly been made but were not properly addressed, and where alleged offenders remained in contact with students.

"In some matters, our investigations indicate that alleged offenders were transferred between schools, where further abuse was subsequently alleged."

Kim Price says the growing number of survivors coming forward highlights failures to adequately protect children within Australia's education system. (Supplied: Arnold Thomas & Becker )

Mr Price said the Victorian government's parliamentary apology to survivors was an "important step" but it did not address the lifelong impact of trauma.

"An apology alone is not enough," Mr Price said.

"Survivors also need access to fair financial compensation, psychological treatment and ongoing medical support."

World.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the return of the mid-tier Marvel movie
World.content:
It's a bold move to subtitle your Spider-Man movie Brand New Day, then spend most of the run time fixated on the previous films.

Fast facts about Spider-Man: Brand New Day What: The fourth/eleventh/fourteenth Spider-Man film (depending how you count) Starring: Tom Holland, Zendaya, Sadie Sink, Jacob Batalon Directed by: Destin Daniel Cretton When: In cinemas now Likely to make you feel: As if you've seen it all before

A quick recap for those who missed No Way Home: Peter Parker (Tom Holland) has erased himself from collective memory to protect his friends MJ (Zendaya) and Ned (Jacob Batalon), leaving behind no trace of Peter and committing to being full-time Spider-Man.

He is beloved by New York City, but completely anonymous beneath his mask. Without Parker's billionaire benefactor or Avengers connections, Spider-Man's remit is now "small potatoes", according to a New Avenger in her requisite cameo.

But after an opening montage jam-packed with recreations of classic Spider-Man comic covers, the film quickly falls into Peter reconnecting with MJ and battling a telepathic villain who presents an existential threat to humanity, while undergoing his own transformation into a literal Spider-Man. It's not small potatoes, and that means the film lacks the grounded reality that was once Spider-Man's biggest strength.

MJ (Zendaya) doesn't remember Peter Parker or their relationship in Brand New Day. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

There's plenty to like about Brand New Day — Jon Bernthal reprises his role as a machine-gun toting Frank Castle/The Punisher from Marvel's TV universe, providing an absurdly hard-edged foil to Spider-Man.

A handful of beloved TV actors like Stranger Things' Sadie Sink, Severance's Tramell Tillman and The Bear's Liza Colón-Zayas round out the cast.

Holland continues to be a likeable Spider-Man and sympathetic Peter, and he has undeniable chemistry with MJ (played by his real-life wife), but it all coasts on the previous films while veering dangerously close to a soap opera's amnesia subplot.

Tom Holland and Jon Bernthal team up again in Brand New Day after co-starring in The Odyssey. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

There are hints of real drama: one scene where the villain takes control of MJ gives a glimpse of the kind of performance Zendaya is capable of, and the film's big finish is a rare Bechdel test-passing finale.

But there's simply too much going on; the disparate plot lines dilute each other and never allow the film to focus on one core story. Arguably, the most interesting narrative aspect passes by in the opening montage, with Spider-Man thriving while Peter scrapes by in an asbestos-riddled loft.

The Spider-Man in Brand New Day develops organic webbing in a throwback to Sam Raimi's early 2000s trilogy. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

Visually, Brand New Day is deeply disappointing: the Spider-Man films have a history of big swings (if you'll pardon the pun), but the swoop and sweep of Spider-Man web-slinging his way across New York has lost its sparkle.

The telepathic villain's ability to hack into other super-powered bodies means the film has Spider-Man taking on The Hulk and a handful of his other classic characters, but it leaves the fights feeling distant and rote; a box checking activity rather than compelling combat. (Marvel and Sony have scrupulously tried to keep the villain's identity secret — the reveal got a gasp in the cinema, but it won't surprise any comic fans who know their lore).

The identity of Sadie Sink's Brand New Day character was kept under lock and key.

The new film looks particularly dull when compared to its animated Spider-Verse counterpart, in which every frame jumps off the screen and grabs you by the throat in a riot of colour and sound that pushes the very limit of technology. Brand New Day looks like yet another Marvel movie, shot mostly on green screens.

Spider-Man: No Way Home refreshes the franchise by returning all the villains — and letting loose Tom Holland’s trilogy ventures into the multiverse, with a little help from Benedict Cumberbatch’s Doctor Strange, offering fans the opportunity to see Spidey fight baddies from former franchises.

Holland's Spider-Man movies have suffered from serious green-screen creep on both a visual and narrative level. In Homecoming, Peter knows the name of his local bodega cat and rescues it from a burning building, but the New York of Brand New Day feels like a background rather than somewhere Peter actually lives.

Brand New Day is better than director Destin Daniel Cretton's previous superhero film, Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, but it doesn't hold up to Cretton's more recent Marvel TV show Wonder Man, which brought life back to the tired genre.

Wonder Man covers much of the same ground as Brand New Day — a likeable but isolated superhero loses control of his powers, an odd-couple friendship with a fan favourite character, the bureaucratically evil Department of Damage Control — but Wonder Man felt fresh where Brand New Day treads the same ground as the multitude of Spider-Man films that came before it.

Peter Parker seeks out Bruce Banner (Mark Ruffalo) for help with his evolving superpowers. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

More than anything else, Brand New Day feels overstuffed and under-done. Even at almost two and a half hours long, there's still a grab-bag of characters and plot lines that go under-explored. Many elements of the film feel like they were borrowed from other comics — Peter's struggle with his new, animalistic Spider side looks and concludes like a Venom arc, while Sink's mind-controlling villain belongs in an X-Men film.

Ultimately, Brand New Day has more in common with a filler episode of TV than the highs of Spider-Man 2 or Into the Spider-Verse. It's a film for fans who want to spend a couple of hours with Peter, MJ and Ned, but even they will be disappointed by the lack of focus. It's the return of the mid-tier Marvel movie, perfectly watchable but bland and forgettable, the cinematic equivalent of fast-food fries made from small potatoes.

Spiderman: Brand New Day is in cinemas now.

World.title: Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged over alleged assault
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCrime Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged over alleged assault Rob Harris Updated July 30, 2026 — 2:04pm ,first published 10:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been charged with two counts of assault on Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly at a community festival in Darwin this month. Northern Territory police said the federal member for Solomon, 54, was arrested on Thursday morning over an incident allegedly involving the administrator at a public event on July 18. Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling. Alex Ellinghausen Gosling has strenuously denied the charges, which carry a maximum penalty of up to 14 years behind bars. In a statement, police said Gosling was taken into custody at Palmerston police station before he was charged after investigations began last week. He was bailed to appear before Darwin Local Court on September 1.



His barrister Marty Aust expressed reservations about the handling of the matter, warning there was a risk of “politicisation” surrounding the case. “There’s a real concern that there’s a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter’s being handled already,” Aust told reporters outside the police station, according to the NT News. “What I can say is that the charge is completely and utterly denied and will be contested.” The alleged incident was previously reported to have occurred during the NT Thailand Grand Festival in Darwin, where both men took part in official proceedings. Gosling posted photos from the event on his social media that day. The administrator is the King’s representative in the Northern Territory, performing a role equivalent to a state governor. In a statement released before he was charged, Gosling said: “The Northern Territory Police have released a statement on this matter. I am co-operating fully with their inquiries.”



Gosling, who has held the Darwin-based seat since 2016, has previously rejected the allegations, describing them as “ridiculous” and saying he had “no dealings” with Connolly beyond congratulating him on his appointment as administrator last year. After the allegations emerged, a spokesman for Connolly said that “an incident occurred during His Honour the Administrator’s official attendance at a community event”, but declined further comment while police investigated. Gosling reportedly ignored waiting reporters after his release, got into the passenger seat of a Toyota Prado waiting outside the station, and the car then drove away and entered a nearby McDonald’s drive-through. Under the Northern Territory Criminal Code, assaulting the administrator while carrying out official duties carries a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment.



Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP may be disqualified if convicted and under sentence, or subject to be sentenced, for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment - meaning a conviction would trigger a byelection. Labor holds the seat of Solomon, which takes in largely the Darwin metropolitan area and Palmerston, with margin of 7.09 per cent. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Australia news LIVE: NT federal Labor MP arrested over alleged assault; KPMG says no decision made on job cuts following whistleblower scandal Connolly’s appointment last year was marked by the emergence of controversial comments he’d previously posted on social media about women’s sport, the prime minister and race. This prompted condemnation from Territory Labor figures, including Gosling, who described the comments at the time as “reprehensible and offensive”. Gosling was appointed as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia following last year’s election. He served for 13 years in the Australian Defence Force’s parachute infantry, commandos and defence cooperation programs.



Shadow defence spokesman James Paterson said the allegations were “incredibly serious”. “While everyone is entitled to the presumption of innocence, an arrest for assault requires him to immediately stand down from his duties,” he posted on X. “The PM must act today.” A spokesman for Albanese declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process.
