World.title: Dragons axe five-eighth Atkinson for Dolphins clash
World.content:
Daniel Atkinson has been dumped from St George Illawarra’s starting side with Lyhkan King-Togia the new five-eighth for Friday’s showdown with the Dolphins. Atkinson, who was brought to the Dragons from Cronulla as their big off-season recruit, faces a challenge to win back his halves spot – not just this season but next year, too, after the Red V’s signing Kodi Nikorima and Luke Metcalf for 2027. Daniel Atkinson will make way for Lyhkan King-Togia against the Dolphins on Friday. Getty Images King-Togia, 21, spent most of Thursday’s session training in the halves alongside Kyle Flanagan. Moses Suli, who was named in the No.18 jersey, also appears ready to start in the centres at the expense of Mat Feagai.



Roosters veteran prepared to entertain Super League move Winger Daniel Tupou is leaning towards playing one more year with the Sydney Roosters, but should the Bondi club not accommodate him, he is prepared to pursue a two-year deal in the Super League. Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson on Tuesday confirmed Tupou would return for the NRL finals after dislocating his shoulder last Friday night against the Knights – but no call had been made about next year. Daniel Tupou is eyeing a Super League swansong. Getty Images Tupou’s preference would be to play a 16th season in the red, white and blue. But the 35-year-old met his manager Sam Ayoub on Monday who informed him several English Super League clubs had expressed interest in him.



The chance to sign a two-year deal has appeal, while Tupou also knows the Super League would be less physically demanding. Tupou remains one of the best aerial threats in the game, and bagged a hat-trick in his 300th milestone match against the Eels earlier this month. The Super League is known for its attacking brand of football, which would suit the Tongan international. Daniel Tupou receives his 300-game ball from recently departed NRL boss Andrew Abdo. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase will leave the Roosters at the end of the season to return to rugby, and should Tupou also try his luck abroad, the Roosters have plenty of depth, including Cody Ramsey, Tommy Talau, Billy Smith, Manly recruit Reuben Garrick, and Tom Rodwell. They also have Rex Bassingthwaighte who is being groomed to be James Tedesco’s No. 1 successor, with the club happy to give their future fullbacks time on the wing at the start of their careers. Tupou has never wanted any fuss made about his achievements, and played down the extent of his injury early in the second half in Newcastle last week.



Tedesco said on Sunday: “The other night he laid on the floor and said, with no emotion, ‘My shoulder’s out’. That was it. “We all went up to him, but he was his usual calm self. They popped it back in, he was still out there, and I started to think he was going to keep playing, but they took him off. “Players get older and you expect a bit of a dip [in form], but that’s not the case with ‘Toops’ – he goes about his business with no fuss and we have so much confidence and belief when he’s out there.” The setback means Tupou, who has played 302 matches for the club, is no chance to overtake Jared Waerea-Hargreaves as the most-capped Rooster should this year be his last.



Waerea-Hargreaves played 310 games, and with the Roosters to play six regular season games, and potentially up to three finals, Tupou could have moved to 311. Robinson confirmed Tupou would return for the finals, and the shoulder injury would sideline him between four and six weeks. As for his future, Robinson said: “I’d say it’d be in the next two to three weeks, we’ll know where ‘Toops’ is at and where we’re at.” Young weighs up Raiders’ deal Dan Walsh Canberra have offered Hudson Young a multimillion-dollar, three-year extension as his Raiders teammate Morgan Smithies will join Perth next season.



The Raiders have progressed negotiations with Young after he was sidelined with a season-ending Achilles injury last weekend, and are gunning to keep their star NSW back-rower off the open market on November 1. Loading A three-year deal would keep Young in the nation’s capital until the end of 2030. With the NRL’s salary cap forecast to rise to at least $15 million from 2028, Young’s total extension is expected to be worth around $3 million and make him one of the game’s best-paid back-rowers. Along with Penrith enforcer and Blues teammate Liam Martin, Young is the most accomplished edge forward coming off-contract in 2027. Young’s Achilles rupture came as a cruel blow to Canberra’s late-season finals charge given the 28-year-old’s superb Origin campaign and status as a nailed-on World Cup starter for the Kangaroos.



Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24), Wests Tigers’ Samuela Fainu (22) and the Dolphins’ recent Queensland Origin debutant Kuikefu Finefeuiaki (22) represent the next crop of back-rowers yet to be tied down long-term, though the Tigers’ plans to present Fainu with an upgraded deal were a significant factor in Jarome Luai being released early to join Parramatta next year. Hudson Young in action for Canberra. Getty Images Martin’s agent will meet with the Panthers this week as the club works through its star-studded off-contract list, with co-captains Nathan Cleary and Isaah Yeo the club’s retention priorities. Martin and Brian To’o have both been linked to the incoming PNG Chiefs franchise, and while Penrith will be given first and last rights on Martin’s future, a request for permission to negotiate early with rival clubs hasn’t been ruled out, either. Teammate Moses Leota was granted a brief window to talk to rivals by the Panthers last month to get an idea of his market value.



Related Article NRL 2026 The Tigers said Doueihi talks were ‘positive’. What happens next will tell the real story Melbourne have also given five-eighth Cameron Munster permission to negotiate specifically with PNG after undergoing minor knee surgery, though the Storm have tabled a two-year extension for 2028-29 at a reduced rate from his estimated $1.25 million salary. The Chiefs are unlikely to present their own offer until November 1, or when there is clarity around Cleary’s future given he is their preferred playmaking target. Smithies, meanwhile, has agreed to terms on a three-year offer from Perth. The 25-year-old had been deep in negotiations with Canberra earlier this year before the club was told his preference was to move back to the UK and resume his English Super League career. Perth’s offer proved too good for Smithies to refuse, but the English international will leave the Raiders on good terms despite the change of plans.



The Bears have also targeted Eels co-captain Junior Paulo as a potential captaincy option for inaugural coach Mal Meninga next season, with a two-year offer expected to be taken up by the veteran prop this week. Perth have slowly but surely built a robust pack with Penrith’s Liam Henry and Scott Sorensen, Cronulla utility Siosifa Talakai and Bulldogs back-rower Josh Curran their most notable signings up front. The Bears have ample salary cap space to add a marquee spine player given Storm utility Tyran Wishart headlines their playmaking options for 2027.

World.title: We were already weird about the afterlife. AI just made us more so
World.content:
Life’s greatest mystery has occupied filmmakers for years. Just like them, I’m still looking for answers.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When nine-year-old Cole Sear whispers his famous line about seeing dead people in that flat, petrified voice, it’s supposed to be one of the scariest moments in The Sixth Sense, one of the highest-grossing films of 1999. It worked on me, too, before I did the thing psychologists do to every good scary thing: explain why it works, and thereby ruin it. At the time, I was just starting my PhD in developmental psychology. My thesis project? How children think about the afterlife. For whatever reason — an overactive imagination, or growing up near a spooky old pioneer graveyard in Virginia — I’d been obsessed with ghosts since childhood. By the time I was Cole’s age, I’d binged the Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark series and haunted the ghosts and hauntings aisle of my local library. For as long as I can remember, I’ve had one obsessive foot in the ethereal otherworld. Basically, it all scares the bejesus out of me. But I still can’t get enough of it. What actually unsettled audiences in The Sixth Sense wasn’t the ghosts, per se – it was making them so palpable. The rest of us perceive the dead around us, too, just less literally. We keep putting ourselves into the shoes of people who no longer have shoes, or feet, or brains for that matter. We ask what they’d think of us now. We apologise to them, sometimes out loud, alone, in cars. Haley Joel Osment as Cole Sear, the boy who sees dead people, including Bruce Willis’ Dr Malcolm Crowe, in The Sixth Sense. M. Night Shyamalan built a career-making twist on a premise that’s more or less true, minus the full-bodied apparitions, in the theatre of your own skull. The dead don’t simply disappear in a puff of smoke, even when cremated. They linger, often despite themselves. We don’t have to believe in ghosts to be haunted.



At the University of Otago in New Zealand, my colleagues and I study exactly how this all works at our afterlife beliefs lab. I should say upfront that we are not setting out to prove or disprove heaven, hell, or whether you’ll “survive” death. We specialise in how the living think about the minds of the dead, not whether the dead actually have minds. Whether your great-aunt is presently enjoying a cocktail on a pink cloud is something else entirely, for parapsychologists to investigate. What interests us, arguably, is stranger still. Your brain does not care whether your great-aunt still exists. It just keeps running her as if she does. Ghosts are just like us (and that’s the problem) Let’s start with the most basic move your mind makes around death: it keeps guessing what the dead person is thinking, in the present tense. Cognitively, this is no different from guessing what your spouse is thinking when they sigh loudly at dinner, except the person doing the thinking no longer has a brain. Fiction has always understood this attributional compulsion better than science has. Hamlet’s father shows up specifically to complain about being murdered, as though death had rudely upended his bucket list. Patrick Swayze’s ghost in Ghost spends the entire film trying to get one message to the woman he loves, unbothered by having no body but very bothered by the risk of being misunderstood. Patrick Swayze and Demi Moore in Ghost. Paramount Pictures Such stories are built on the basic premise that the dead remain mentally active. Consider a “simple” question we ask participants in our studies: can your dead loved ones still see? We mostly get the same answer from believers: yes, obviously. But it’s unclear why they are so certain of ongoing perceptual experiences after death. Pushed into an uncomfortable corner – what exactly are they seeing with, now that their eyes have decomposed and their visual cortex is gone – people tend to short-circuit, or invoke discarnate eyes, which just begs more questions. Michael Keaton in Beetlejuice. Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures



Most of us agree, if pressed, that a functioning brain is required for every twinge and ripple of subjective experience. Yet fiction can’t stop giving ghosts working minds anyway. The ghosts in Beetlejuice eat and argue and get furious about home décor; Robin Williams’ character in What Dreams May Come explores a lush, sensory afterlife. This isn’t just sloppy screenwriting – it’s the same glitch researchers find in ordinary people. In one of my early studies, even non-believers occasionally reasoned that a dead person “knew” he was dead. Because, obviously. In a more recent experiment, Jamin Halberstadt and I found that, when told a ghost is in the room, then left alone with the lights flicking on and off unexpectedly, even participants who said ghosts are make-believe showed a greater physiological stress response than those who heard nothing about a ghost. Psychologist and author Jesse Bering: “For as long as I can remember, I’ve had one obsessive foot in the ethereal otherworld.″⁣ Where ghosts come from Pixar has been running informal afterlife-information campaigns targeting children for a decade. Coco is structured around grief counsellors’ favourite takeaway: our loved ones survive death because we keep thinking of them. The movie’s Land of the Dead – where you exist in cheerful skeletal form until nobody living remembers your name, at which point you suffer the alarmingly named “Final Death” – dramatises this exactly. Coco, says Jesse Bering, “is structured around grief counsellors’ favourite takeaway: our loved ones survive death because we keep thinking of them.” AP



In Soul, the unborn soul (Tina Fey) tells the dead soul (Jamie Foxx) that in this liminal state one cannot taste or smell – “things the body does” – while seeing, hearing and thinking presumably aren’t. That sentiment – abstract thoughts and feelings as immortal, psychobiological states as mortal – echoed what kids (and adults) told me in my own studies, where we used a puppet show in which a mouse gets killed by an alligator. Can he still taste the grass he ate, remember what he learnt that day, or love his Mum? Even children privileged the loftier, “nonbodily” states as surviving death – even though it’s all bodily, really. These films betray how constrained the human imagination is when picturing the afterlife without a built-in commonsense dualism, as developmental psychologists call this penchant for belief in souls. What’s genuinely unresolved is whether three- and four-year-olds reach for an afterlife on their own, the way infants reach for language, or pick it up from Coco, from church, from grandma. Untangling nature from Pixar is harder than it sounds. An evolutionary alibi for ghosts Afterlife belief shows up in nearly every culture ever studied. The specific nature of the belief is largely irrelevant; it makes no difference whether the soul ascends, descends, recycles or slumbers. The point is that it’s likened to personal consciousness, some mindful part of the individual, and is almost always moralistic. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on HBO Max right now One explanation is what Dominic Johnson and I termed the “supernatural punishment hypothesis.” It’s dramatised in A Christmas Carol. Marley’s ghost shows up not to comfort Scrooge but in chains, forged out of his own selfishness, to frighten him straight.



The Good Place runs the same logic through a spreadsheet: every rude or selfish thing you do gets tallied against you for eternity. In my own studies, telling participants a ghost had been seen in their testing room made them less likely to cheat on an unrelated money task. A similar effect showed up in children told about a friendly invisible presence (“Princess Alice”). The idea is that believing the watchful dead were keeping score nudged our ancestors towards co-operation. Nobody needs an actual ghost filing the paperwork for the belief to have done real work. Natural selection doesn’t reward an organism’s grip on reality; it rewards genetic fitness. What looks superstitious may be a baked-in adaptive illusion, or what the late Daniel Dennett called an “evolved misbelief”. Dead house rules There’s an unspoken rule against badmouthing someone at their own funeral. When the rule is violated, that gets people’s attention. Across five seasons of Six Feet Under, the writers mined this discomfort around death etiquette. Six Feet Under mines our discomfort around death etiquette. The Lovely Bones dug even deeper, letting its murdered narrator watch her family and silently grade how well they’re grieving her. And don’t get me started on 13 Reasons Why, in which vulnerable teens probably couldn’t help but picture mourners weeping at their funerals, bullies getting their comeuppance, or friends and family finally appreciating them. Katherine Langford in 13 Reasons Why. Netflix

World.title: McLaren hits thick titanium-rich sands from surface in WA Eucla project
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears McLaren hits thick titanium-rich sands from surface in WA Eucla project Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 30, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

McLaren Minerals has kept the heavy mineral (HM) hits rolling at its namesake titanium project in Western Australia’s Eucla Basin, with a fresh 68-hole assay batch confirming broad and consistent mineralisation from surface across its growing titanium play. The latest results cover 1432 metres of sampled intervals from the 2026 drilling campaign and returned a length-weighted average of 3.76 per cent HM across an average 21m thickness. Importantly, the company says no heavy mineral cut-off was applied, meaning the numbers reflect the complete sampled intervals rather than cherry-picked higher-grade zones. McLaren Minerals’ titanium metal could find application in human prosthetic joint implants. All 68 holes averaged at least 2 per cent HM, while 59 holes, or 87 per cent of the batch, averaged at least 3 per cent. A further 24 holes, or 35 per cent, ran at 4 per cent HM or better, giving McLaren another solid slab of data to feed into its updated geological model, mineral resource estimate and bankable feasibility study work. Additionally, 58 drill holes, or 85 per cent of the batch, delivered sampled intervals of at least 18m, including 48 holes, or 71 per cent, with intervals of 21m or more.



‘The focus of this program has always been on increasing confidence in the Resource and continuity of mineralisation.’ McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis Standout intercepts – notably all from surface - include 24m at 5.44 per cent HM with a maximum grade of 10 per cent HM from 8m to 9m; 24m at 5.08 per cent; 22m at 5.16 per cent; and 12m at 5.95 per cent, the highest average grade encountered in the results. Thicker runs included 29m at 4.07 per cent HM in one hole, almost mirrored by another hole returning 27m at 4.17 per cent HM. McLaren says the repeatability of both grade and thickness across successive drill traverses is the real prize. Also, the consistent occurrence of grade from surface is another key merit in the dataset. Both characteristics are valuable development attributes, smoothing out geological modelling and potentially providing a more uniform basis for mine design, production scheduling and process-feed planning. McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis said: “I’m going to sound repetitive, but that’s because these results continue to tell the same story. We’re consistently intersecting broad mineralised intervals from surface with repeatable grades and thicknesses across the deposit. That’s exactly what we wanted this drilling program to demonstrate.”



The latest assays build on a busy few weeks for McLaren. In June, the company reported bonanza grades of up to 34.6 per cent HM from its resource upgrade and expansion drilling, including encouraging early results from a southeastern extension area outside the present indicated resource footprint. Earlier this month, the company confirmed it had completed its 2026 drilling program, with all of its planned 663 holes drilled for 11,568m, just 86 per cent of its planned drilling metreage. That campaign was the first major stage of McLaren’s bankable feasibility study work and is expected to support a resource upgrade, follow-on mine reserves estimation and the broader development studies now gathering pace. McLaren’s project sits in the western Eucla Basin and already hosts a 529-million-tonne JORC-compliant resource grading 4.5 per cent HM for an estimated 23.7Mt of contained HM. The company has its eye principally on the titanium mineralisation, with titanium recognised globally as a critical mineral. Demand for the metal continues to rise, driven by its importance in aerospace, defence, medical and energy technologies.



Titanium possesses the highest strength-to-weight ratio of any metallic element, closely matching the strength of low-grade steels. It is also resistant to corrosion forming a tight, self-healing oxide film on its surface when exposed to air and moisture, making it highly resistant to seawater and chlorine. Titanium is also biocompatible, being non-toxic and completely non-reactive to human body tissues and bone, making it safe for use in medical applications such as strong, light, weight-bearing replacement implants in skeletal joints. With final assays still to be validated and folded into the model, metallurgical test work moving ahead and the feasibility study pathway well under way, McLaren appears to have achieved what every aspiring developer desires; transforming a drilling program into a bigger, tidier and more bankable-looking dataset. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Emotional portrait of strength and sorrow gets people’s vote in Archibald Prize
World.content:
CultureArt & designArchibald Prize Emotional portrait of strength and sorrow gets people’s vote in Archibald Prize Nick Galvin July 30, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The winner of this year’s $5000 Archibald People’s Choice Award is seven-time finalist Michael Zavros with his portrait of Jewish community leader Alex Ryvchin. Ryvchin, co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, rose to prominence in the aftermath of the December 2025 Bondi Beach terror attacks. Zavros’ portrait, Alex with his tefillin in the sea, depicts Ryvchin walking barefoot in the shallows of a harbour beach. Wrapped around his arm is his tefillin, a small leather box containing verses from the Torah. Michael Zavros (left) with the subject of his portrait, Alex Ryvchin. James Brickwood Zavros made reference photos with Ryvchin just weeks after the Bondi massacre in which 16 people died, including one attacker. In an emotional acceptance speech at the Art Gallery of NSW, Zavros said he was humbled his work had received the most votes of the nearly 46,000 visitors who cast a ballot at this year’s exhibition.



“I’m deeply grateful for that this portrait has connected with so many people,” he said. “Overwhelmingly, I don’t believe Australians are racist. I don’t believe we are homophobic. And I don’t believe we are antisemitic. Those things have no place in the country we aspire to be. “It’s worth reminding ourselves how fortunate we are to live in this great Western liberal democracy that welcomed my family from Cyprus in the 1950s, and welcomed Alex who arrived from the Ukraine as a four-year-old refugee in the 1980s. What unites us is so much more powerful than what divides us.” Gallery director Maud Page called Michael Zavros the nation’s “foremost realist painter”. Oscar Colman Zavros’ connection with Ryvchin goes back years to when he first became aware of the uncanny physical resemblance between the two. He followed Ryvchin’s career from afar and then, after Bondi, decided he wanted to him to be the subject of his 2026 Archibald entry. “I had this serendipitous connection with Alex because we look alike,” he said. “And to that end, I just started to connect with him and watch him over the years. And then, following Bondi, he led the country in a way that I think our leaders failed to do. And I thought I really want to honour him somehow. I want to capture everything that I admire about him, all of his strength and dignity and all of the pain that he so beautifully articulates.”



Zavros believes his work resonated with visitors because of the deeply emotional subject matter. “I think people are just really moved by it,” he said. “I painted something I believed in. I found common ground with this man. I was moved by something and I painted it. And sometimes I think that’s the best thing you can do as an artist, is paint the thing you can’t explain.” Michael Zavros’ winning portrait. Art Gallery of New South Wales Announcing the award, gallery director Maud Page called Zavros the nation’s “foremost realist painter”. “His immaculate brushstrokes are perfection,” she said. “He works with assuredness, able to not only render a subject in his total likeness but also position him within an evocative narrative setting where the very ripples of water on the sand convey as much as the twist of Alex’s body.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: You’re probably ignoring this part of your CV. It could cost you
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceJobs Opinion You’re probably ignoring this part of your CV. It could cost you Tim Duggan Work columnist July 30, 2026 — 1:11pm

July 30, 2026 — 1:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every few years, you pull up an old file on your computer, add a few new headers and bullet points and save it as a new document. This ritual of updating your CV to get a new job has been performed for decades. But there’s one area of your resume that most people overlook, and it’s more important than you realise. I’m talking about the few simple words you write to describe your interests and hobbies, which say more about you than almost any other part of your resume. Using AI to craft your cover letter is a quick way to have your application ignored entirely. iStock Usually hidden right at the bottom of your page, it’s the last remaining part that you can truly personalise. As AI-generated resumes flood the inboxes of hiring teams, the way you summarise your life outside work has increased in importance and should get just as much attention as the rest of it. I’ve spoken to several different recruiters, who tell me that when they have the unenviable task of reviewing dozens of resumes in a single sitting – which all describe similar experiences at similar jobs – and their eyes are drawn immediately to the final few lines to read what interests might set them apart.



For most candidates, this is the last thing they hurriedly fill out before sending it off, but what you do outside the workplace says a lot about the type of worker you’d be inside it. To help you better understand this forgotten corner of your resume, here are some of the most commonly listed interests on a CV, and what they say about you. A love for travel in your interests signals curiosity and independence, and hints you can easily adapt to whatever’s thrown at you. Let’s begin with sport, as most people do. Anyone who writes that they play a team sport, like soccer or netball, signifies they are likely to be co-operative at work, and have no problem working towards shared goals with others. A solo sport, like running or swimming, says you’re self-motivated and resilient, and will persist at hard tasks with discipline even when things get uncomfortable. A history of volunteering shows reliability, empathy and gives a nod towards service-orientation to help other people, while listing games of any sort (from computer to board) implies that you’re a strategic and systems thinker who can remain calm in high-pressure situations.



A love for travel in your interests signals curiosity and independence, and hints that they can easily adapt to whatever’s thrown at them, like delayed flights and lost luggage teach you to. Editor's pick Opinion

AI The telltale signs you’re working for a ‘ChatGPT Boss’ Tim Duggan Work columnist Playing any kind of instrument demonstrates patience, scuba diving means good communication, writing implies reflection, and even gardening infers you have the patience required to not see immediate fruits of your labour for a very long time. Now, this is not an exact science, of course. Hobbies can give a general sense of what someone might be like, but it’s not a direct predictor of future employee performance. But when you next open up that computer file and start updating it before your first round of job interviews, don’t hurry past the small section that lists out your hobbies. Instead, think broadly about how they can sum you up as a human, and get specific around how you spend your time.



Know that these will be read and interpreted as a sign of your future temperament and judgement, and are a shortcut to standing out. As computer programs scan your resume for the right keywords, or a person from HR scrolls quickly through it, listing the right hobby alone is not going to land you the job. But it might just spark a good conversation, or help you to be memorable, and those are the small differences between being overlooked and landing your dream job. World.title: Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged over alleged assault
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCrime Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling charged over alleged assault Rob Harris Updated July 30, 2026 — 2:04pm ,first published 10:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has been charged with two counts of assault on Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly at a community festival in Darwin this month. Northern Territory police said the federal member for Solomon, 54, was arrested on Thursday morning over an incident allegedly involving the administrator at a public event on July 18. Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling. Alex Ellinghausen Gosling has strenuously denied the charges, which carry a maximum penalty of up to 14 years behind bars. In a statement, police said Gosling was taken into custody at Palmerston police station before he was charged after investigations began last week. He was bailed to appear before Darwin Local Court on September 1.



His barrister Marty Aust expressed reservations about the handling of the matter, warning there was a risk of “politicisation” surrounding the case. “There’s a real concern that there’s a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter’s being handled already,” Aust told reporters outside the police station, according to the NT News. “What I can say is that the charge is completely and utterly denied and will be contested.” The alleged incident was previously reported to have occurred during the NT Thailand Grand Festival in Darwin, where both men took part in official proceedings. Gosling posted photos from the event on his social media that day. The administrator is the King’s representative in the Northern Territory, performing a role equivalent to a state governor. In a statement released before he was charged, Gosling said: “The Northern Territory Police have released a statement on this matter. I am co-operating fully with their inquiries.”



Gosling, who has held the Darwin-based seat since 2016, has previously rejected the allegations, describing them as “ridiculous” and saying he had “no dealings” with Connolly beyond congratulating him on his appointment as administrator last year. After the allegations emerged, a spokesman for Connolly said that “an incident occurred during His Honour the Administrator’s official attendance at a community event”, but declined further comment while police investigated. Gosling reportedly ignored waiting reporters after his release, got into the passenger seat of a Toyota Prado waiting outside the station, and the car then drove away and entered a nearby McDonald’s drive-through. Under the Northern Territory Criminal Code, assaulting the administrator while carrying out official duties carries a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment.



Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP may be disqualified if convicted and under sentence, or subject to be sentenced, for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment - meaning a conviction would trigger a byelection. Labor holds the seat of Solomon, which takes in largely the Darwin metropolitan area and Palmerston, with margin of 7.09 per cent. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Australia news LIVE: NT federal Labor MP arrested over alleged assault; KPMG says no decision made on job cuts following whistleblower scandal Connolly’s appointment last year was marked by the emergence of controversial comments he’d previously posted on social media about women’s sport, the prime minister and race. This prompted condemnation from Territory Labor figures, including Gosling, who described the comments at the time as “reprehensible and offensive”. Gosling was appointed as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia following last year’s election. He served for 13 years in the Australian Defence Force’s parachute infantry, commandos and defence cooperation programs.



Shadow defence spokesman James Paterson said the allegations were “incredibly serious”. “While everyone is entitled to the presumption of innocence, an arrest for assault requires him to immediately stand down from his duties,” he posted on X. “The PM must act today.” A spokesman for Albanese declined to comment, citing an ongoing legal process. World.title: Dragons axe five-eighth Atkinson for Dolphins clash
World.content:
Daniel Atkinson has been dumped from St George Illawarra’s starting side with Lyhkan King-Togia the new five-eighth for Friday’s showdown with the Dolphins. Atkinson, who was brought to the Dragons from Cronulla as their big off-season recruit, faces a challenge to win back his halves spot – not just this season but next year, too, after the Red V’s signing Kodi Nikorima and Luke Metcalf for 2027. Daniel Atkinson will make way for Lyhkan King-Togia against the Dolphins on Friday. Getty Images King-Togia, 21, spent most of Thursday’s session training in the halves alongside Kyle Flanagan. Moses Suli, who was named in the No.18 jersey, also appears ready to start in the centres at the expense of Mat Feagai.



Roosters veteran prepared to entertain Super League move Winger Daniel Tupou is leaning towards playing one more year with the Sydney Roosters, but should the Bondi club not accommodate him, he is prepared to pursue a two-year deal in the Super League. Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson on Tuesday confirmed Tupou would return for the NRL finals after dislocating his shoulder last Friday night against the Knights – but no call had been made about next year. Daniel Tupou is eyeing a Super League swansong. Getty Images Tupou’s preference would be to play a 16th season in the red, white and blue. But the 35-year-old met his manager Sam Ayoub on Monday who informed him several English Super League clubs had expressed interest in him.



The chance to sign a two-year deal has appeal, while Tupou also knows the Super League would be less physically demanding. Tupou remains one of the best aerial threats in the game, and bagged a hat-trick in his 300th milestone match against the Eels earlier this month. The Super League is known for its attacking brand of football, which would suit the Tongan international. Daniel Tupou receives his 300-game ball from recently departed NRL boss Andrew Abdo. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase will leave the Roosters at the end of the season to return to rugby, and should Tupou also try his luck abroad, the Roosters have plenty of depth, including Cody Ramsey, Tommy Talau, Billy Smith, Manly recruit Reuben Garrick, and Tom Rodwell. They also have Rex Bassingthwaighte who is being groomed to be James Tedesco’s No. 1 successor, with the club happy to give their future fullbacks time on the wing at the start of their careers. Tupou has never wanted any fuss made about his achievements, and played down the extent of his injury early in the second half in Newcastle last week.



Tedesco said on Sunday: “The other night he laid on the floor and said, with no emotion, ‘My shoulder’s out’. That was it. “We all went up to him, but he was his usual calm self. They popped it back in, he was still out there, and I started to think he was going to keep playing, but they took him off. “Players get older and you expect a bit of a dip [in form], but that’s not the case with ‘Toops’ – he goes about his business with no fuss and we have so much confidence and belief when he’s out there.” The setback means Tupou, who has played 302 matches for the club, is no chance to overtake Jared Waerea-Hargreaves as the most-capped Rooster should this year be his last.



Waerea-Hargreaves played 310 games, and with the Roosters to play six regular season games, and potentially up to three finals, Tupou could have moved to 311. Robinson confirmed Tupou would return for the finals, and the shoulder injury would sideline him between four and six weeks. As for his future, Robinson said: “I’d say it’d be in the next two to three weeks, we’ll know where ‘Toops’ is at and where we’re at.” Young weighs up Raiders’ deal Dan Walsh Canberra have offered Hudson Young a multimillion-dollar, three-year extension as his Raiders teammate Morgan Smithies will join Perth next season.



The Raiders have progressed negotiations with Young after he was sidelined with a season-ending Achilles injury last weekend, and are gunning to keep their star NSW back-rower off the open market on November 1. Loading A three-year deal would keep Young in the nation’s capital until the end of 2030. With the NRL’s salary cap forecast to rise to at least $15 million from 2028, Young’s total extension is expected to be worth around $3 million and make him one of the game’s best-paid back-rowers. Along with Penrith enforcer and Blues teammate Liam Martin, Young is the most accomplished edge forward coming off-contract in 2027. Young’s Achilles rupture came as a cruel blow to Canberra’s late-season finals charge given the 28-year-old’s superb Origin campaign and status as a nailed-on World Cup starter for the Kangaroos.



Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24), Wests Tigers’ Samuela Fainu (22) and the Dolphins’ recent Queensland Origin debutant Kuikefu Finefeuiaki (22) represent the next crop of back-rowers yet to be tied down long-term, though the Tigers’ plans to present Fainu with an upgraded deal were a significant factor in Jarome Luai being released early to join Parramatta next year. Hudson Young in action for Canberra. Getty Images Martin’s agent will meet with the Panthers this week as the club works through its star-studded off-contract list, with co-captains Nathan Cleary and Isaah Yeo the club’s retention priorities. Martin and Brian To’o have both been linked to the incoming PNG Chiefs franchise, and while Penrith will be given first and last rights on Martin’s future, a request for permission to negotiate early with rival clubs hasn’t been ruled out, either. Teammate Moses Leota was granted a brief window to talk to rivals by the Panthers last month to get an idea of his market value.



Related Article NRL 2026 The Tigers said Doueihi talks were ‘positive’. What happens next will tell the real story Melbourne have also given five-eighth Cameron Munster permission to negotiate specifically with PNG after undergoing minor knee surgery, though the Storm have tabled a two-year extension for 2028-29 at a reduced rate from his estimated $1.25 million salary. The Chiefs are unlikely to present their own offer until November 1, or when there is clarity around Cleary’s future given he is their preferred playmaking target. Smithies, meanwhile, has agreed to terms on a three-year offer from Perth. The 25-year-old had been deep in negotiations with Canberra earlier this year before the club was told his preference was to move back to the UK and resume his English Super League career. Perth’s offer proved too good for Smithies to refuse, but the English international will leave the Raiders on good terms despite the change of plans.



The Bears have also targeted Eels co-captain Junior Paulo as a potential captaincy option for inaugural coach Mal Meninga next season, with a two-year offer expected to be taken up by the veteran prop this week. Perth have slowly but surely built a robust pack with Penrith’s Liam Henry and Scott Sorensen, Cronulla utility Siosifa Talakai and Bulldogs back-rower Josh Curran their most notable signings up front. The Bears have ample salary cap space to add a marquee spine player given Storm utility Tyran Wishart headlines their playmaking options for 2027.

World.title: We were already weird about the afterlife. AI just made us more so
World.content:
Life’s greatest mystery has occupied filmmakers for years. Just like them, I’m still looking for answers.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When nine-year-old Cole Sear whispers his famous line about seeing dead people in that flat, petrified voice, it’s supposed to be one of the scariest moments in The Sixth Sense, one of the highest-grossing films of 1999. It worked on me, too, before I did the thing psychologists do to every good scary thing: explain why it works, and thereby ruin it. At the time, I was just starting my PhD in developmental psychology. My thesis project? How children think about the afterlife. For whatever reason — an overactive imagination, or growing up near a spooky old pioneer graveyard in Virginia — I’d been obsessed with ghosts since childhood. By the time I was Cole’s age, I’d binged the Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark series and haunted the ghosts and hauntings aisle of my local library. For as long as I can remember, I’ve had one obsessive foot in the ethereal otherworld. Basically, it all scares the bejesus out of me. But I still can’t get enough of it. What actually unsettled audiences in The Sixth Sense wasn’t the ghosts, per se – it was making them so palpable. The rest of us perceive the dead around us, too, just less literally. We keep putting ourselves into the shoes of people who no longer have shoes, or feet, or brains for that matter. We ask what they’d think of us now. We apologise to them, sometimes out loud, alone, in cars. Haley Joel Osment as Cole Sear, the boy who sees dead people, including Bruce Willis’ Dr Malcolm Crowe, in The Sixth Sense. M. Night Shyamalan built a career-making twist on a premise that’s more or less true, minus the full-bodied apparitions, in the theatre of your own skull. The dead don’t simply disappear in a puff of smoke, even when cremated. They linger, often despite themselves. We don’t have to believe in ghosts to be haunted.



At the University of Otago in New Zealand, my colleagues and I study exactly how this all works at our afterlife beliefs lab. I should say upfront that we are not setting out to prove or disprove heaven, hell, or whether you’ll “survive” death. We specialise in how the living think about the minds of the dead, not whether the dead actually have minds. Whether your great-aunt is presently enjoying a cocktail on a pink cloud is something else entirely, for parapsychologists to investigate. What interests us, arguably, is stranger still. Your brain does not care whether your great-aunt still exists. It just keeps running her as if she does. Ghosts are just like us (and that’s the problem) Let’s start with the most basic move your mind makes around death: it keeps guessing what the dead person is thinking, in the present tense. Cognitively, this is no different from guessing what your spouse is thinking when they sigh loudly at dinner, except the person doing the thinking no longer has a brain. Fiction has always understood this attributional compulsion better than science has. Hamlet’s father shows up specifically to complain about being murdered, as though death had rudely upended his bucket list. Patrick Swayze’s ghost in Ghost spends the entire film trying to get one message to the woman he loves, unbothered by having no body but very bothered by the risk of being misunderstood. Patrick Swayze and Demi Moore in Ghost. Paramount Pictures Such stories are built on the basic premise that the dead remain mentally active. Consider a “simple” question we ask participants in our studies: can your dead loved ones still see? We mostly get the same answer from believers: yes, obviously. But it’s unclear why they are so certain of ongoing perceptual experiences after death. Pushed into an uncomfortable corner – what exactly are they seeing with, now that their eyes have decomposed and their visual cortex is gone – people tend to short-circuit, or invoke discarnate eyes, which just begs more questions. Michael Keaton in Beetlejuice. Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures



Most of us agree, if pressed, that a functioning brain is required for every twinge and ripple of subjective experience. Yet fiction can’t stop giving ghosts working minds anyway. The ghosts in Beetlejuice eat and argue and get furious about home décor; Robin Williams’ character in What Dreams May Come explores a lush, sensory afterlife. This isn’t just sloppy screenwriting – it’s the same glitch researchers find in ordinary people. In one of my early studies, even non-believers occasionally reasoned that a dead person “knew” he was dead. Because, obviously. In a more recent experiment, Jamin Halberstadt and I found that, when told a ghost is in the room, then left alone with the lights flicking on and off unexpectedly, even participants who said ghosts are make-believe showed a greater physiological stress response than those who heard nothing about a ghost. Psychologist and author Jesse Bering: “For as long as I can remember, I’ve had one obsessive foot in the ethereal otherworld.″⁣ Where ghosts come from Pixar has been running informal afterlife-information campaigns targeting children for a decade. Coco is structured around grief counsellors’ favourite takeaway: our loved ones survive death because we keep thinking of them. The movie’s Land of the Dead – where you exist in cheerful skeletal form until nobody living remembers your name, at which point you suffer the alarmingly named “Final Death” – dramatises this exactly. Coco, says Jesse Bering, “is structured around grief counsellors’ favourite takeaway: our loved ones survive death because we keep thinking of them.” AP



In Soul, the unborn soul (Tina Fey) tells the dead soul (Jamie Foxx) that in this liminal state one cannot taste or smell – “things the body does” – while seeing, hearing and thinking presumably aren’t. That sentiment – abstract thoughts and feelings as immortal, psychobiological states as mortal – echoed what kids (and adults) told me in my own studies, where we used a puppet show in which a mouse gets killed by an alligator. Can he still taste the grass he ate, remember what he learnt that day, or love his Mum? Even children privileged the loftier, “nonbodily” states as surviving death – even though it’s all bodily, really. These films betray how constrained the human imagination is when picturing the afterlife without a built-in commonsense dualism, as developmental psychologists call this penchant for belief in souls. What’s genuinely unresolved is whether three- and four-year-olds reach for an afterlife on their own, the way infants reach for language, or pick it up from Coco, from church, from grandma. Untangling nature from Pixar is harder than it sounds. An evolutionary alibi for ghosts Afterlife belief shows up in nearly every culture ever studied. The specific nature of the belief is largely irrelevant; it makes no difference whether the soul ascends, descends, recycles or slumbers. The point is that it’s likened to personal consciousness, some mindful part of the individual, and is almost always moralistic. Related Article Streaming The 30 best movies to stream on HBO Max right now One explanation is what Dominic Johnson and I termed the “supernatural punishment hypothesis.” It’s dramatised in A Christmas Carol. Marley’s ghost shows up not to comfort Scrooge but in chains, forged out of his own selfishness, to frighten him straight.



The Good Place runs the same logic through a spreadsheet: every rude or selfish thing you do gets tallied against you for eternity. In my own studies, telling participants a ghost had been seen in their testing room made them less likely to cheat on an unrelated money task. A similar effect showed up in children told about a friendly invisible presence (“Princess Alice”). The idea is that believing the watchful dead were keeping score nudged our ancestors towards co-operation. Nobody needs an actual ghost filing the paperwork for the belief to have done real work. Natural selection doesn’t reward an organism’s grip on reality; it rewards genetic fitness. What looks superstitious may be a baked-in adaptive illusion, or what the late Daniel Dennett called an “evolved misbelief”. Dead house rules There’s an unspoken rule against badmouthing someone at their own funeral. When the rule is violated, that gets people’s attention. Across five seasons of Six Feet Under, the writers mined this discomfort around death etiquette. Six Feet Under mines our discomfort around death etiquette. The Lovely Bones dug even deeper, letting its murdered narrator watch her family and silently grade how well they’re grieving her. And don’t get me started on 13 Reasons Why, in which vulnerable teens probably couldn’t help but picture mourners weeping at their funerals, bullies getting their comeuppance, or friends and family finally appreciating them. Katherine Langford in 13 Reasons Why. Netflix

World.title: McLaren hits thick titanium-rich sands from surface in WA Eucla project
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears McLaren hits thick titanium-rich sands from surface in WA Eucla project Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 30, 2026 — 1:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

McLaren Minerals has kept the heavy mineral (HM) hits rolling at its namesake titanium project in Western Australia’s Eucla Basin, with a fresh 68-hole assay batch confirming broad and consistent mineralisation from surface across its growing titanium play. The latest results cover 1432 metres of sampled intervals from the 2026 drilling campaign and returned a length-weighted average of 3.76 per cent HM across an average 21m thickness. Importantly, the company says no heavy mineral cut-off was applied, meaning the numbers reflect the complete sampled intervals rather than cherry-picked higher-grade zones. McLaren Minerals’ titanium metal could find application in human prosthetic joint implants. All 68 holes averaged at least 2 per cent HM, while 59 holes, or 87 per cent of the batch, averaged at least 3 per cent. A further 24 holes, or 35 per cent, ran at 4 per cent HM or better, giving McLaren another solid slab of data to feed into its updated geological model, mineral resource estimate and bankable feasibility study work. Additionally, 58 drill holes, or 85 per cent of the batch, delivered sampled intervals of at least 18m, including 48 holes, or 71 per cent, with intervals of 21m or more.



‘The focus of this program has always been on increasing confidence in the Resource and continuity of mineralisation.’ McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis Standout intercepts – notably all from surface - include 24m at 5.44 per cent HM with a maximum grade of 10 per cent HM from 8m to 9m; 24m at 5.08 per cent; 22m at 5.16 per cent; and 12m at 5.95 per cent, the highest average grade encountered in the results. Thicker runs included 29m at 4.07 per cent HM in one hole, almost mirrored by another hole returning 27m at 4.17 per cent HM. McLaren says the repeatability of both grade and thickness across successive drill traverses is the real prize. Also, the consistent occurrence of grade from surface is another key merit in the dataset. Both characteristics are valuable development attributes, smoothing out geological modelling and potentially providing a more uniform basis for mine design, production scheduling and process-feed planning. McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis said: “I’m going to sound repetitive, but that’s because these results continue to tell the same story. We’re consistently intersecting broad mineralised intervals from surface with repeatable grades and thicknesses across the deposit. That’s exactly what we wanted this drilling program to demonstrate.”



The latest assays build on a busy few weeks for McLaren. In June, the company reported bonanza grades of up to 34.6 per cent HM from its resource upgrade and expansion drilling, including encouraging early results from a southeastern extension area outside the present indicated resource footprint. Earlier this month, the company confirmed it had completed its 2026 drilling program, with all of its planned 663 holes drilled for 11,568m, just 86 per cent of its planned drilling metreage. That campaign was the first major stage of McLaren’s bankable feasibility study work and is expected to support a resource upgrade, follow-on mine reserves estimation and the broader development studies now gathering pace. McLaren’s project sits in the western Eucla Basin and already hosts a 529-million-tonne JORC-compliant resource grading 4.5 per cent HM for an estimated 23.7Mt of contained HM. The company has its eye principally on the titanium mineralisation, with titanium recognised globally as a critical mineral. Demand for the metal continues to rise, driven by its importance in aerospace, defence, medical and energy technologies.



Titanium possesses the highest strength-to-weight ratio of any metallic element, closely matching the strength of low-grade steels. It is also resistant to corrosion forming a tight, self-healing oxide film on its surface when exposed to air and moisture, making it highly resistant to seawater and chlorine. Titanium is also biocompatible, being non-toxic and completely non-reactive to human body tissues and bone, making it safe for use in medical applications such as strong, light, weight-bearing replacement implants in skeletal joints. With final assays still to be validated and folded into the model, metallurgical test work moving ahead and the feasibility study pathway well under way, McLaren appears to have achieved what every aspiring developer desires; transforming a drilling program into a bigger, tidier and more bankable-looking dataset. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Emotional portrait of strength and sorrow gets people’s vote in Archibald Prize
World.content:
CultureArt & designArchibald Prize Emotional portrait of strength and sorrow gets people’s vote in Archibald Prize Nick Galvin July 30, 2026 — 1:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The winner of this year’s $5000 Archibald People’s Choice Award is seven-time finalist Michael Zavros with his portrait of Jewish community leader Alex Ryvchin. Ryvchin, co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, rose to prominence in the aftermath of the December 2025 Bondi Beach terror attacks. Zavros’ portrait, Alex with his tefillin in the sea, depicts Ryvchin walking barefoot in the shallows of a harbour beach. Wrapped around his arm is his tefillin, a small leather box containing verses from the Torah. Michael Zavros (left) with the subject of his portrait, Alex Ryvchin. James Brickwood Zavros made reference photos with Ryvchin just weeks after the Bondi massacre in which 16 people died, including one attacker. In an emotional acceptance speech at the Art Gallery of NSW, Zavros said he was humbled his work had received the most votes of the nearly 46,000 visitors who cast a ballot at this year’s exhibition.



“I’m deeply grateful for that this portrait has connected with so many people,” he said. “Overwhelmingly, I don’t believe Australians are racist. I don’t believe we are homophobic. And I don’t believe we are antisemitic. Those things have no place in the country we aspire to be. “It’s worth reminding ourselves how fortunate we are to live in this great Western liberal democracy that welcomed my family from Cyprus in the 1950s, and welcomed Alex who arrived from the Ukraine as a four-year-old refugee in the 1980s. What unites us is so much more powerful than what divides us.” Gallery director Maud Page called Michael Zavros the nation’s “foremost realist painter”. Oscar Colman Zavros’ connection with Ryvchin goes back years to when he first became aware of the uncanny physical resemblance between the two. He followed Ryvchin’s career from afar and then, after Bondi, decided he wanted to him to be the subject of his 2026 Archibald entry. “I had this serendipitous connection with Alex because we look alike,” he said. “And to that end, I just started to connect with him and watch him over the years. And then, following Bondi, he led the country in a way that I think our leaders failed to do. And I thought I really want to honour him somehow. I want to capture everything that I admire about him, all of his strength and dignity and all of the pain that he so beautifully articulates.”



Zavros believes his work resonated with visitors because of the deeply emotional subject matter. “I think people are just really moved by it,” he said. “I painted something I believed in. I found common ground with this man. I was moved by something and I painted it. And sometimes I think that’s the best thing you can do as an artist, is paint the thing you can’t explain.” Michael Zavros’ winning portrait. Art Gallery of New South Wales Announcing the award, gallery director Maud Page called Zavros the nation’s “foremost realist painter”. “His immaculate brushstrokes are perfection,” she said. “He works with assuredness, able to not only render a subject in his total likeness but also position him within an evocative narrative setting where the very ripples of water on the sand convey as much as the twist of Alex’s body.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: You’re probably ignoring this part of your CV. It could cost you
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceJobs Opinion You’re probably ignoring this part of your CV. It could cost you Tim Duggan Work columnist July 30, 2026 — 1:11pm

July 30, 2026 — 1:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every few years, you pull up an old file on your computer, add a few new headers and bullet points and save it as a new document. This ritual of updating your CV to get a new job has been performed for decades. But there’s one area of your resume that most people overlook, and it’s more important than you realise. I’m talking about the few simple words you write to describe your interests and hobbies, which say more about you than almost any other part of your resume. Using AI to craft your cover letter is a quick way to have your application ignored entirely. iStock Usually hidden right at the bottom of your page, it’s the last remaining part that you can truly personalise. As AI-generated resumes flood the inboxes of hiring teams, the way you summarise your life outside work has increased in importance and should get just as much attention as the rest of it. I’ve spoken to several different recruiters, who tell me that when they have the unenviable task of reviewing dozens of resumes in a single sitting – which all describe similar experiences at similar jobs – and their eyes are drawn immediately to the final few lines to read what interests might set them apart.



For most candidates, this is the last thing they hurriedly fill out before sending it off, but what you do outside the workplace says a lot about the type of worker you’d be inside it. To help you better understand this forgotten corner of your resume, here are some of the most commonly listed interests on a CV, and what they say about you. A love for travel in your interests signals curiosity and independence, and hints you can easily adapt to whatever’s thrown at you. Let’s begin with sport, as most people do. Anyone who writes that they play a team sport, like soccer or netball, signifies they are likely to be co-operative at work, and have no problem working towards shared goals with others. A solo sport, like running or swimming, says you’re self-motivated and resilient, and will persist at hard tasks with discipline even when things get uncomfortable. A history of volunteering shows reliability, empathy and gives a nod towards service-orientation to help other people, while listing games of any sort (from computer to board) implies that you’re a strategic and systems thinker who can remain calm in high-pressure situations.



A love for travel in your interests signals curiosity and independence, and hints that they can easily adapt to whatever’s thrown at them, like delayed flights and lost luggage teach you to. Editor's pick Opinion

AI The telltale signs you’re working for a ‘ChatGPT Boss’ Tim Duggan Work columnist Playing any kind of instrument demonstrates patience, scuba diving means good communication, writing implies reflection, and even gardening infers you have the patience required to not see immediate fruits of your labour for a very long time. Now, this is not an exact science, of course. Hobbies can give a general sense of what someone might be like, but it’s not a direct predictor of future employee performance. But when you next open up that computer file and start updating it before your first round of job interviews, don’t hurry past the small section that lists out your hobbies. Instead, think broadly about how they can sum you up as a human, and get specific around how you spend your time.



Know that these will be read and interpreted as a sign of your future temperament and judgement, and are a shortcut to standing out. As computer programs scan your resume for the right keywords, or a person from HR scrolls quickly through it, listing the right hobby alone is not going to land you the job. But it might just spark a good conversation, or help you to be memorable, and those are the small differences between being overlooked and landing your dream job.
