World.title: Teachers worried about critical thinking as AI becomes widespread in schools
World.content:
Listen live: St Patrick's College Head of science Doug Walker on combating AI

RNZ national

The Education Review Office says most schools are using artificial intelligence but fear it is damaging children's critical thinking.

In a report out on Thursday, the office said generative AI is becoming part of everyday school life and teachers and principals want more formal guidance from the Education Ministry.

The report Ready or not: How are schools responding to Artificial Intelligence recommended development of a national AI in education framework and national policies on teacher and student use of the technology.

It said the review office found 40 percent of secondary students had misused artificial intelligence for their schoolwork though less than half that figure admitted to using it to cheat in assessments.

The report said AI was emerging as a key issue in education and more than 90 percent of New Zealand school principals and more than 80 percent of teachers used it.

Principals generally used it to ease their admin workload for drafting messages and summarising information while teachers used the technology to tailor resources and develop lessons.

"Across the schools we visited, AI was most often described as a practical tool that can support efficiency, reduce workload, and assist learning. Leaders and teachers generally see AI as a tool that should support, rather than replace, professional judgement," it said.

Less than 20 percent of students admitted to using AI to cheat in assessments. 123RF

The report said half of teachers said AI made their job easier but they also worried that unplanned use of the technology was having a negative effect on students' critical thinking.

"More than half of teachers (57 percent) report that AI has had a negative effect on students' critical thinking," the report said, adding that the concern was highest among secondary teachers (72 percent).

ERO calls for national framework for AI use in schools Morning Report Download MP3 5m

It said students also recognised the risk.

"It gives you the answer, but you don't do any thinking for yourself," said one.

The report said some teachers refused to use the technology.

"We also heard from a small group of teachers who identify as 'conscientious objectors', choosing not to use AI on principled grounds. These teachers were particularly concerned about the example its use sets for students and its potential impact on creativity, independence, and development," it said.

Education Review Office (ERO) chief executive David Ferguson told RNZ he was surprised how widespread AI had become with most people in schools using it regularly.

"It's been one of the biggest game changers in the sector I think in the last few years... We're led to believe it changes quickly so we think it's really significant," he said.

Ferguson said schools' use of AI was positive.

"This is a big deal for schools in terms of keeping everybody safe, making sure they're maximising the potential in terms of using it. That's why we're suggesting that we think having a consistent deliberate, strategic framework for all schools, a centrally-provided one, would be a good idea," he said.

Ferguson said ERO's work had not revealed a digital divide based on schools socio-economic backgrounds.

"We didn't discern differences there in terms of equity or a digital divide. It was so widespread we thought, that it looks like it's being used far and wide," he said.

Education Review Office chief executive David Ferguson. RNZ/ Luka Forman

Westlake Girls' High School director of futures and AI strategy Susana Tomaz said data privacy was an issue she wanted more conversation around.

Generative AI is becoming part of everyday school life Nine To Noon Download MP3 11m

She said the report showed 90 percent of principals, 80 percent of teachers and 75 percent of students reported using AI.

"It's obvious that we've moved beyond the use of AI, it's officially being in schools... I think we need to move to a conversation more around implementation and safety."

However, she said only seven in 10 leaders having an AI privacy policy in place and three in four schools remaining in what has been described as an "unplanned category".

Tomaz said this was a concern for student safety and privacy.

"Heavily using AI without the governance and the AI literacy to support effective, responsible and ethical use is a big priority to focus on."

"They need to be coached to understand the pitfalls around offloading the cognition, the hard work onto AI," she said. "This is a big concern that is emerging."

"I think the biggest investment is going to be on building capability on our teachers which need to transfer into becoming metacognitive coaches in the age of AI and continue really enforcing the pedagogy around teaching and learning and ensuring that they're guiding the students in the understanding of the cognitive offloading risk and how they leverage on the AI to build the critical thinking."

"But for that you do need to build that capability amongst teachers."

She said students using AI should be given "the benefit of the doubt" if they are not being taught how to use it responsibly.

What students had to say about AI

Meanwhile, 75 percent of students reported using AI, mainly to find information and generate ideas.

The report said primary school teachers tended to manage student use of AI and it was more widespread in secondary schools.

"It's totally normalised, you don't really even think about using it," a secondary student told the report writers.

Another student described AI as a very good tool but said others over-used it.

"I use it to get inspiration for when I'm doing my work. But at the same time, I know students who use it as a crutch to do all their work for them," they said.

A primary school student said they used AI to correct their grammar and punctuation.

"I'll ask it to improve my spelling and paragraphs and my full stops, exclamation marks, and stuff like that. Sometimes, if I'm not sure how… I'll just go, 'could you improve this?'," they said.

The report said some students (38 percent of secondary students, 20 percent of primary and intermediate students) used AI in ways they knew they should not.

"Students told us they sometimes turn to AI to complete parts of tasks more quickly, particularly when work feels repetitive, when they believe they already understand the content, or when they are managing competing demands across subjects. The easy availability of AI tools, combined with lower levels of oversight than in assessment contexts, creates more opportunities for this type of use," it said.

"It's addictive, if you use it once then you just can't stop using it. I can think for myself, but if it's anything more in depth, then I have to use [AI] - I can't think that deep," a primary school pupil said.

Some students used AI in ways they knew they should not. Unsplash/ Taylor Flowe

However, fewer students reported using AI inappropriately for work that was assessed.

"Overall, relatively few students report knowingly using AI inappropriately for assessments, with 14 percent reporting that they have used AI in ways they know they should not for assessments or tests. Almost three quarters (72 percent) say they have never done so. However, a further 14 percent are unsure whether their use is inappropriate," the report said.

The rate was highest in secondary schools, where 19 percent of students reported inappropriate use in assessments and a further nine percent unsure.

Even fewer students said they had been caught using AI when they should not by a teacher - just five percent of secondary students and seven percent of primary students.

The report said the ministry provided high-level guidance on the use of generative AI but most teachers (73 percent) had not seen it.

It said many schools did not have formal policies for AI use and teachers' rulings on student use of AI varied.

"Despite this, one expectation is consistently understood: AI should not be used for assessment unless explicitly permitted. Students generally recognise this boundary, and schools use a range of approaches to reinforce it," the report said.

The report recommended integrating AI into learning rather than creating a standalone AI subject for senior secondary school students as the government was last year considering.

World.title: Ministry for Regulation recommends legalising plug-in solar
World.content:
The Ministry for Regulation has recommended legalising plug-in solar and allowing accredited installers to sign off on an installation without an inspection.

The ministry says its recommendations will speed up processing times and lower costs for solar uptake.

Plug-in solar is currently illegal in New Zealand, with the inverters required for plug-in solar banned due to concerns over electricity risks and starting house fires.

Those standards have been in place since 2012, but the ministry's review found those barriers could be removed if suitable safety standards and were developed.

"Plug-in systems can be used by renters and people living in apartments who can't access traditional rooftop solar. If they're good enough for Germany and the UK, they're good enough for us," Minister for Regulation David Seymour said.

The government is already in the early stages of developing plug-in standards, including looking at what safety requirements need to be met before it can be enabled.

In May, Seymour ordered a review into the solar installation process, saying he wanted to make New Zealand the easiest place in the world to switch to solar.

He said the ministry had spoken to installers, industry participants, regulators, and other stakeholders, and found in some cases installing a small-scale solar system could involve up to six different sign-offs and five site visits from four different entities before it could be switched on.

The review recommended a more proportionate, risk-based inspection model, without always requiring an electrical inspector to check every installation in-person. Accredited installers could be exempted from needing an in-person inspection for installations of up to 100kW.

It also suggested shortening processing times for lines companies processing requests to install solar from 10 working days to the next working day for standard residential requests, and exempting some types of installations from needing a resource consent.

The ministry expected all of its 15 recommendations could be implemented within 18 months.

Some, such as legalising plug-in solar and exempting accredited installers from inspections, could be implemented through secondary legislation.

Eight recommendations, such as proposals to make metering data more accessible, would involve amending the Electricity Industry Participation Code.

The ministry estimated its recommendations could deliver net benefits between $28 million and $50m over 10 years, through lower compliance costs, reduced delays, and the use of plug-in solar.

Energy minister Simeon Brown has been working on developing plug-in solar standards.

He said the Ministry for Regulation's proposals would help make solar uptake cheaper and faster.

"The government is focused on ensuring New Zealand has access to affordable and reliable power with these proposals building on what the government is already delivering, from fast-track consenting big renewable projects, to doubling the export limits for households exporting power back to the grid."

While the review focused on improvements to regulation, others have identified the upfront cost and access to finance as the biggest barriers.

Both National and Labour are campaigning on low-interest loans to help households invest in solar.

National would also remove some planning rules to make it easier for households to install solar without the need for council consent.

Labour would offer kickstart subsidies for renters and low and middle-income families to cover the installation costs.

World.title: Climber who survived 200m fall on Mount Aspiring should buy Lotto ticket, rescuers say
World.content:
A climber who survived a big fall down a steep, icy face on Mount Aspiring should buy a Lotto ticket, his rescuers say.

Emergency services launched a highly technical, high-altitude rescue on Tuesday night after the man's climbing companion hiked three hours to call for help, presuming his friend was dead.

The pair had summited Aspiring's south face and were descending via a steep snow and ice ridge known as The Ramp on Bonar Glacier.

Helicopters Otago chief executive Graeme Gale said climber fell just after dark at about 7pm.

"The message that I got was that he had fallen approximately 200 metres and his companion felt it was unsurvivable," he said.

The fallen climber had all of the pair's gear, including their locator beacon, Gale said.

With no way to signal for help, the second climber spent about three hours trekking back towards the summit in freezing conditions, searching for cellphone coverage.

Once the call for help came through, Gale said Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response.

"We had some pretty sketchy co-ordinates of where it was, taken from the cellphone by the police. Police did a great job co-ordinating it and then we started pulling our guys together," he said.

With the climbers at nearly 10,000 metres, wind building and poor weather pushing in from the west, the helicopter had to be stripped and made as light as possible.

Gale said crews used night vision goggles to track down the climber who had called for help.

"We could land on the edge of the ice shelf and pick him up and so we were able to hover load - with one skid on the edge - and got him in," he said.

The crew then decided to investigate a light source they had spotted "a couple of thousand feet below".

"They thought it was possibly other climbers on the mountain but it turned out to be this guy's companion and he was actually on his feet, although he'd had injuries," he said.

"Once again, we didn't need to winch, which was great. We were able to put a skid down, just hoverload again, and one of the alpine [cliff rescue team] guys got out and escorted him back into the helicopter."

Once the call for help came through, Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue teams met Helicopters Otago crews in Queenstown to co-ordinate a response. Supplied / Screenshot

Gale was not sure the climber would have survived the night in frigid conditions if rescuers had not reached him.

He said the rescue was "the best of the best outcome" crews could have hoped for.

"It could have been catastrophic for him," Gale said.

"He was standing on a high shelf, on a slope on the mountain itself, so pretty lucky that he had gone into a crevasse and pretty lucky he hadn't had other injuries that would have been life-threatening. He was in remarkably good shape for the fall that he'd had. I reckon he should go and buy a lottery ticket for Saturday night."

Second rescue from The Ramp in a month

Wakatipu Alpine Cliff Rescue Team co-ordinator Russ Tilsley said it followed another even more technical rescue on 30 June on the same section of Mount Aspiring.

That rescue also took place late at night and involved two climbers who had ascended the south face, he said.

"These guys had basically been out too long and I think they were very tired. They abseiled down into an area where they got stuck in and they couldn't get out," he said.

"They were frostbitten, tired and had run out of food."

While winter was typically a quiet time for the rescue team, there seemed to be more and more people undertaking winter climbing missions, Tilsley said.

Summitting Mount Aspiring from the nearest walk-in Department of Conservation hut, French Ridge Hut, was a "big thing to do in a day", he said.

"To go up, climb and come back again is probably a 24-hour mission."

Earlier Sergeant Darren Cranfield from Wānaka Police described Tuesday's rescue as a timely reminder of the risks of alpine areas.

"Conditions in the mountains can change rapidly and even experienced climbers can find themselves in dangerous situations," he said.

World.title: How much you'll be paying under Wellington's new water regime
World.content:
Wellington region residents react to new water bills Nine To Noon Download MP3 19m

There has been shock and confusion for some Wellington residents, as households received separate water bills totalling hundreds of dollars for the quarter.

Tiaki Wai, which took over from 1 July, sent the first quarterly bill to Wellington region residents yesterday - with a due date of payment of 1 September 2026.

RNZ has seen bills ranging between $400 and $900 due in just over a month. Property owners can pay by direct debit, online or phone banking, or over the counter at NZ Post stores offering the service.

New water entity Tiaki Wai has said Wellingtonians will face steep charges for water over the coming decade as it tries to fix old, failing infrastructure and decades of under-investment.

The average Wellington resident was previously paying about $2100 in water services as part of their rates bill. Water bills on average will increase by 13.3 percent in this financial year.

That has led to confusion over whether new council rates will be the same amount, and whether the increased cost for water comes on top of that.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little told Nine to Noon that it was not the case that people's total water and rates bills were soaring by 40 or 50 percent.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little. RNZ / Mark Papalii

The water component - which had previously been incorporated in the council rates bill - will be taken out of the next overall rates bill, which made up about 20 percent of council rates' bills. Council rates were increasing by 5.9 percent.

"It is a little bit confusing," Little said. "Water has come out [of the rates bill], it's been increased, rates have been increased by an average of 5.9 percent, that will be your total picture."

People should receive their Wellington city rates bills by email next week; posted copies will come the week after that.

In a social media post on Wednesday, Deputy Mayor Ben McNulty said combined increases from water and rates bills would come to about 9 percent for the average Wellingtonian.

People can check the amount of their new council rates on the council site here and the amount of their water bills here.

But residents have raised concerns about affordability.

"Hell of a shock when I opened that email - I'm a widow, living on my own in the family home and this is certainly not affordable for people on a benefit," one person posted on social media.

Little said there had been "a fair effort" in communicating the change - with regular messages from both the council and Tiaki Wai about different components.

"So preparing people for the idea there will be separate bills I think has been, I think a reasonable effort has been made to do that."

Another person said: "I just love that our whanau are going to be paying $3000 per year for water, yet the leak at the end of the driveway isn't getting fixed any time soon."

A leak in the Wellington CBD. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Asked about the affordability of the new water entity, Little said there had "been a wake-up call to water infrastructure and the quality of water supply".

But he said there was a "tension" in pricing arrangements between councils and Tiaki Wai, in that councils now had little control over the entity, which had been set up as a new company with the five Wellington councils only minority shareholders.

The five councils had some say in their membership on the partners committee.

"I have to say it's not rigorous control. There's no veto right that the partners committee has in terms of decisions Tiaki Wai makes. It is a point of influence, but that's as far as it goes.

"I think we do need to do, we need to have more. I think the Commerce Commission needs to be more actively involved. And I think the reality is that partners committee is going to just have to be sort of belligerent and courageous and assert the rights and interests of residents and ratepayers. That's the only way it's going to work."

World.title: Nine more people charged in relation to brawl outside Palmerston North court
World.content:
Police believe they have identified nine more people involved in a melee outside the Palmerston North District Court earlier this month.

An altercation involving rival gang members left one person in critical condition on 16 July at the entrance of the courthouse.

Police arrested and charged a 33-year-old man at the time, who is due to appear in Palmerston North District Court on 18 August on charges of fighting in a public place and theft from a person.

Using CCTV footage to identify and locate individuals, a further nine people have been arrested and charged in relation to the brawl.

Inspector Phil Ward praised the intervention of court security staff.

"They put themselves directly in harm's way to separate the group, and ultimately prevented this situation from escalating further."

He added that violence would not be tolerated and that the community's safety was his priority.

World.title: Greyhound trainers face up to future without racing
World.content:
A sense of the inevitable has shrouded the Hatrick Raceway this week as the Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club prepared for its last ever meeting on Friday evening.

The government is shutting down the industry over animal welfare concerns.

In April, Racing Minister Winston Peters announced the Racing Industry Amendment Bill passed its third and final reading with "overwhelming" cross-party support.

"This action wasn't taken lightly, but independent reviews in 2013, 2017 and 2021 provided clear evidence of serious animal welfare concerns."

Peters said while improvements were made, those gains plateaued and injury/death rates remained unacceptably high to the point the sport had lost its social licence.

Owners from around the country gathered at Hatrick Raceway earlier this week for the club's final straight-track meeting.

Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club president, John McArthur, said he'd been in the sport for 50 years.

It was part of his DNA.

Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club president John McArthur has tough decisions ahead about what to do with his dogs. RNZ / Robin Martin

"I just love the fact that the common man - don't forget that the common man - can afford to own a greyhound and take it to the races, look after it and care for it.

"It's not the landed gentry of racehorses. We are the common people and we know that. It's one of the reasons we are in the position we are."

McArthur didn't shy away from the fact dogs sometimes got injured.

He reckoned about nine dogs had been euthanised nationwide this season across hundreds of meetings.

That number climbed to 10 on Tuesday with the death of five-year-old Tiger Jane who fell at Addington Raceway fracturing her left humerus.

McArthur took RNZ through the Hatrick Raceway kennels where the dogs were prepared for racing.

Trainers retrieve their dogs after a race at the Hatrick Raceway in Whanganui. RNZ / Robin Martin

"The dogs come in and they go here where they are identified by the chip in the dog. They are then weighed and they then go up here on to the examination table where the vet examines them.

"He does a full examination of the dogs and if they've come through the veterinary inspection they are then kennelled in their own separate kennel."

When it comes time to race, the dogs were walked out to the straight-track - installed two years ago in the centre of the Whanganui Racecourse at a cost of $3 million - in response to welfare concerns.

The greyhounds are placed in start boxes and then they're off.

The race is over in a matter of seconds ... but Clevedon trainer Peter Heterick loves it nevertheless.

"Aw mate, it's just, yeah, my passion. I love it. You know, dogs they bring something to you that, you know, horses don't.

"They just love being around you, they're kind. They're just beautiful animals."

He was gutted racing was being shut down.

RNZ / Robin Martin

"Aw devastated, yeah, it's just crazy, honestly."

Heterick would be keeping his dogs.

"I'm gonna stay at home and look after them.

"A transition agency take over, but you've still got to look after your dogs, you've got to get up in the morning and take them for a walk, feed them and everything.

"You know, nothings going to change you're just not racing."

Heterick reckons retired greyhounds would make great pets.

"Oh, they will, they will, especially this one here, but she's coming with me."

Greyhounds racing on the Hatrick Raceway straight at Whanganui. RNZ / Robin Martin

In a statement, SPCA chief scientific officer Dr Arnja Dale said the greyhound racing ban was necessary after years of welfare concerns and repeated but unsuccessful attempts to improve safety.

"This is a historic day for animal welfare. It's the beginning of a new chapter where greyhounds can simply be loved as family pets."

Dale said the rehoming challenge for the remaining 1300 greyhounds was significant but achievable.

"The racing is ending, but the work certainly isn't. Our focus now is providing support to the Greyhound Transition Agency to help greyhounds find the loving homes they deserve."

Waikato owner Michael Schneider had come south for the Hatrick Raceway meet.

Waikato trainer Michael Schneider, whose dog, got a second placing on the straight-track this week, says his dogs will be retiring at home with him. RNZ / Robin Martin

He got into racing through adopting a retired greyhound.

"I would go there on Saturday mornings and help them train their dogs and slip them up their straight-track and took our old boy - well he wasn't that old at that time - and just let him run for exercise and just seeing how much they loved it.

"I love the whole idea of animals that have a job to do, but also really love their job."

He had plans for his dogs.

"They're all coming home with us. We've actually bought a property specifically for that. We're setting up a big track for them. Setting up kennels, but they'll probably all end up in the house anyway.

"So, we've got mum and one of the pups at home at the moment and we've got another three coming to retire with us."

Schneider said the prospect of no more racing was 'just gut-wrenching really".

Meanwhile, tough decisions lay ahead for McArthur who had 18 dogs.

"I've got a lot of dogs here that are too old to go into an adoption systems, so I guess I've got virtually no option.

"I'm a superannuitant, I don't have huge pockets loads of cash, so I suppose I will have to make the decision to do something with them, but that's down the track and I'll face that when I have to."

World.title: Magnitude 5.9 earthquake strikes Kermadec Islands region
World.content:
Earth Sciences New Zealand says a 5.9 magnitude earthquake has struck the Kermadec Islands region.

The islands are approximately 800-1000 kilometres northeast of the North Island.

The quake was recorded shortly before 10.30am on Thursday, about 200km away from Raoul Island, Geohazards duty officer Sheng Lin-Lin said.

There were no reports of damage and checks of GeoNet instruments have found all systems functioning as usual, Lin-Lin said.

There was no observed tsunami signal or unusual water levels.

Lin-Lin added that while the quake did not have a big impact it was a reminder that significant earthquakes can occur in this region and around Aotearoa.

No Earth Sciences staff were on the island at the time and it's not aware of anyone else being on the island. DOC also said it had no staff or contractors visiting the islands and no records of any other agencies, researchers or visitors being there.

World.title: Luxon criticises Winston Peters for 'inappropriate attention-seeking comments' towards Green MP
World.content:
Christopher Luxon has criticised Winston Peters for making "inappropriate attention-seeking comments" after the foreign minister told a Chinese-born New Zealand MP to "go back to your own country".

The prime minister and National Party leader used the occasion to urge voters to support the National Party and said he backs Chinese New Zealanders.

And National's campaign chair Simeon Brown described Peters' comments as "racist".

The condemnation came alongside pointed remarks from Chinese ambassador Wang Xiaolong in response to Peters' insult.

Peters launched his attack during Parliament's general debate on Wednesday after being heckled by Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan. In response, Peters told Xu-Nan to "go back to where you've come from, you loudmouth".

"This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to," he said. Peters also accused China of lying "like a flatfish".

Xu-Nan was born in China but moved to New Zealand as a child in 1994.

Approached for comment, a spokesperson for Luxon issued a statement in his role as National Party leader.

"Winston Peters has a long track record of inappropriate attention-seeking comments designed to get the media and other politicians to talk about him instead of the issues Kiwis are facing. This is another example of that," Luxon said.

"To our Kiwi-Chinese community, National and I back you, and to every New Zealander who wants representatives focused on the issues that matter to you, rather than attention-seeking for cheap headlines, Party Vote National."

Asked what he made of Peters' behaviour, Brown said: "I think those comments are racist."

"I represent an electorate with a huge number of Chinese New Zealanders, and they'll be looking at that and saying... that's someone who doesn't represent me."

Peters doubles-down, decries 'pearl clutching and faux outrage'

Luxon's comments were put to Peters on his way into the debating chamber on Thursday afternoon.

"Look, I'm defending New Zealand's democracy," Peters said. "I'm proud of it. It's only one of nine countries that have had that since 1854, and we're never going to change defending New Zealand's democracy."

Asked how his insult could be seen as a defence of democracy, Peters told the reporter: "if you don't understand it, go back to university."

NZ First deputy Shane Jones also stood by his leader, saying Xu-Nan should "know his place".

"It's not proper for him to provoke and insult my leader. We are historical foundation New Zealanders," Jones said. "We're not worried about these mummified Green people. The less we see of them, the better."

NZ First leader Winston Peters and Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan. RNZ

Peters has not resiled from his initial remarks, instead doubling-down and engaging in a back-and-forth with China's ambassador on Thursday.

Wang published a post on X on Thursday morning, writing: "We have absolutely no interest in being dragged into the domestic politics of other countries.

"Suffice it to say, sometimes, a statement says more about the person that makes it than anything or anybody else."

In a social media post in response, Peters decried the "pearl clutching and faux outrage" and said Wang's comment simply proved the point he had made in Parliament.

"We live in a democracy that includes free speech and rights - those two values that other certain countries not only limit, but do so with force.

"If you want to compare what our free democratic country has - in particular our parliament - then go back and see what it's like in those communist and dictatorship countries and look for yourself."

Peters concluded his message: "If that offends the pearl clutchers and the communist shills labelling it as 'dangerous' - welcome to New Zealand."

Former prime minister Helen Clark also weighed in on X late Wednesday, describing Peters' comments as a "dangerous way" to refer to New Zealand's largest trade partner.

MPs from across Parliament condemn Peters' remarks

Speaking at Parliament, Xu-Nan called on the prime minister to show some leadership and hold both Peters and Jones to account for their racism.

"It is extraordinary that you have a minister who is so careless and irresponsible with what he says."

Fellow Green MP Tamatha Paul said Peters' language risked encouraging racist behaviour in the community.

"Racism is unacceptable," she said. "It's not the 70s anymore, Winston Peters, you can't go around talking to people like that."

Labour deputy Carmel Sepuloni said Luxon should sack Peters as foreign minister for such "explicitly racist" language.

"Those comments are so incredibly racist and offensive, and you cannot make those types of comments as a Cabinet Minister, but particularly as the Minister for Foreign Affairs."

Trade Minister Todd McClay said Peters' comments were "not acceptable", but he did not think they would put New Zealand's relationship with China at risk.

"Each member of Parliament must be accountable for what they say themselves," McClay said. "The public will judge you on your words."

ACT leader David Seymour also described Peters as "attention-seeking".

World.title: Cricketer dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' suspended as stats show unusual trend
World.content:
The club at the centre of the "Clicky Ponting" scandal in English amateur cricket has suspended its player over the matter.

Saltburn Cricket Club said Brian Devine had been suspended for the rest of the season after several videos were posted online with claims Devine was clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat to mimic the sound of an edge.

The club has forfeited its next match in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the league's investigation," a statement read.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

Devine is yet to comment on the matter and an investigation into the claims has yet to be completed, with the allegations so far unproven.

However, an amateur data analyst on social media platform X said they had trawled all scorecards from Saltburn games, and found wicketkeeper catches dramatically increased when Devine was playing.

"Been requested to split it by the matches where Devine (the slip clicker) played, and it's even more stark," X account @maxtempers, which usually posts about British politics, wrote.

"39 keeper catches in 13 matches with Devine. 5 keeper catches in 7 without."

The post followed an original analysis that found wicketkeeper catches increased four-fold when the particular keeper standing alongside Devine in the alleged clicking footage was playing, including eight catches in one innings.

The record at Test level is seven catches in one innings, shared by five players.

"The League has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25 July, 2026," a league statement read when the controversy came to light

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete, no further comment will be made."

Australian cricket podcasters The Grade Cricketer have offered to provide financial support to Devine and Saltburn.

World.title: Broncos premiership prop announces medical retirement due to blood clots
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen has announced his medical retirement from the NRL after ongoing problems.

Jensen, who played 95 games for Brisbane including last year's grand final win over Melbourne Storm, also played 58 games in five seasons for North Queensland.

After becoming unwell during round seven, Jensen was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs).

"After receiving medical advice and speaking to specialists, it's clear that it's no longer safe for me to play rugby league," he told reporters.

Jensen said he had been told he would have to take blood thinners for the rest of his life.

Big Ben heading to NFL The Brisbane Broncos are releasing forward Ben Te Kura from the rest of his NRL contract to allow him to pursue his dream of playing in the NFL.

"Since [the diagnosis] I've been able to train properly again, it's been like a mini pre-season, and I can do everything other than the contact, which is the frustrating part.

"Overall, my health's pretty good, I can continue training in the future and it's not going to affect me in any way."

The Broncos had confirmed he had another incident with deep vein thrombosis in his calf a year earlier, with both incidents considered unprovoked, meaning there was no obvious trigger such as a long-haul flight or injury.

"I leave with absolutely no regrets," he said, thanking his teammates for being part of the premiership win with them.

"I never chased individual recognition, but being part of a team, seeing people grow and knowing that in some way I may have contributed."

Corey Jensen played 95 games for the Broncos after joining the Brisbane side for the 2022 season. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Jensen teared up, thanking his wife Shannen for all her support and the sacrifices she had made.

"People see the player, but they don't always see what partners give up behind the scenes," he said.

Jensen is a qualified sports scientist, having completed a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science at James Cook University, and will have a bright future in that space if he chooses to pursue it.

Jensen was not a star as a youth but, through hard work, turned himself into a weapon after debuting for the Cowboys in 2017 and playing in the grand final.

"The late Paul Green gave me my debut back then.

"I was a bit of a late bloomer, so I'm grateful they took a punt on me, and I have to acknowledge how much the Cowboys did for my career," Jensen said.

"Coming down here was kind of a kind of a new lease on life. The Broncos gave me the opportunity, and I'm eternally grateful for what this club's done for me both on and off the field."

ABC/AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Swimmer spurns Love Island offer, dictator's grandson's vow
World.content:
A Scottish swimmer rejects an approach to appear on a dating reality show, Idi Amin's grandson reveals his royal plans and an Australian weightlifter adds to his family's medal history.

Here are the quick hits from day six of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Swimmer gives up Love Island opportunity

Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan turned down an offer to appear on Love Island. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Last year, Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan had a choice to make.

Should she keep training with an eye on earning Commonwealth Games selection?

Or appear on reality dating program Love Island?

Shanahan spurned the chance to enter the villa and chose to focus on her swimming career and the decision is paying off.

The 22-year-old won silver in the women's 200m backstroke at the Glasgow Games.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season", Shanahan told BBC Scotland News.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

2. Idi Amin's grandson's vow

Aziz Abdul is disqualified during his bout on day six. (Reuters: Matthew Childs)

Carrying a family legacy into a sporting occasion can be a good thing.

In this instance, we're not sure it is.

Ugandan 90+kg boxer Aziz Abdul is the grandson of former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin.

Amin took charge in a coup in 1971 and ruled the country for eight years, during which an estimated half a million people were killed and the country's entire Asian population was expelled.

The Butcher of Uganda, as he was also known, had a bizarre fascination with Scotland, which was the subject of a film starring Forest Whitaker as Amin, The Last King Of Scotland.

It appears his grandson shares a similar love for the nation.

"In everything we do, God knows tomorrow," he told BBC Sport Scotland.

"It's God's plan. I might be the new king of Scotland. It's possible.

"When I arrived, I put up the flag, 'cause I like Scotland so much."

He fought England's Damar Thomas on day six in Glasgow but was disqualified for a headbutt during their quarterfinal.

3. Ollie's fall

Oliver Hoare falls during the mile heats. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Ollie Hoare suffered a major scare in the mile heats, falling half way through the race after appearing to be tripped.

"There was no-one in front of me and I fell down," Hoare later said in the mix zone.

"Tough to have that happen because obviously I wanted to compete on my own merit, and having something like that happen sucks.

"I got up and kept competing because that's what we do."

The Australian team immediately appealed to get Hoare into Saturday's final and were successful, meaning the worst of things for Hoare was a bit of track rash.

"I'm a bit scabbed up and feeling crap about it but we move on," he said.

He joins fellow Australians Adam Spencer and Cam Myer in the final.

4. Like father, like son

Oliver Saxton secured Commonwealth Games bronze in Scotland 40 years after his dad did the same. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

At the 1986 Edinburgh Commonwealth Games, English weightlifter Andrew Saxton claimed his first Commonwealth Games medal, a bronze in the 100kg sub-heavyweight division.

Forty years later, his son, Australian Ollie Saxton, achieved the same result in the 94kg division in Glasgow.

Saxton senior went on to win three golds in Auckland — back then you got a medal for the snatch, clean and jerk, and overall — something that would only earn him one medal today.

He represented England in those two Games, but four years after that, in Victoria, British Colombia, he won a silver for Australia.

Something for Ollie to aspire to in four years in Ahmedabad.

5. Bobsleigh 'bootcamp' for Welsh shot putter

Keeping busy during the athletics off-season is not a problem for Adele Nicoll.

The Welsh shot putter has one of the more unusual sporting crossover stories, mixing shot putt with bobsleigh.

And she's pretty good at both. In February she was flying down on the Pista Olimpica Eugenio Monti in Cortina d'Ampezzo at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where she finished 18th in the monobob and 15th in the two-woman.

She thinks the rigours and unglamorous life of a bobsled athlete places her in good stead for athletics.

"In athletics, we just get our kit bag and we turn up to the track, but with the bobsleigh we're driving the vans around the world," Nicoll told the BBC.

"You race, you pack up all the equipment and you drive to the next location, which could be a 24-hour journey.

Adele Nicoll competed in Milano-Cortina in the monobob and two-woman bobsleigh events. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

"It's just you and your teammates. You're doing all the servicing of the sleds, you're doing everything.

"Bobsleigh is basically a boot camp that makes you the most resilient, hard-working, grafting athlete.

"I've come back into athletics now with that discipline and that's what I think has made me a much better track and field athlete."

Nicoll finished fifth in the women's shot put today, AEST, with a best effort of 16.33m.

Nicoll is not the only crossover athlete to combine bobsledding with the Commonwealth Games.

Four-time medallist in track cycling from Birmingham 2022 and 2021 Tokyo Olympic sprint champion, Canadian Kelsey Mitchell, is also partial to bobsledding and finished 13th in the two-woman event in Cortina — and even acted as some inspiration for Aussie track cyclist Kristina Clonan.

World.title: Weightlifter Cikamatana claims Glasgow gold after Paris pain
World.content:
Australian weightlifter Eileen Cikamatana struggled through days when she wanted to give up and "be a baby in my mum's arms".

But the 26-year-old has found consolation after her Paris Olympics heartbreak, bouncing back in Glasgow to win her third Commonwealth Games gold medal.

Cikamatana was a class above in the women's 86kg event, nailing a 108kg snatch and a 140kg clean and jerk for a Games record total of 248kg.

England's silver medallist Madias Ngake lifted a total of 239kg, while Canadian teenager Rose Beaudoin (230kg total) took bronze.

Eileen Cikamatana in action during the weightlifting in Glasgow. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

In tears after narrowly missing out on a bronze medal when she finished fourth on Olympic debut at Paris 2024, Cikamatana was in tears again in Glasgow, just of a different kind.

"Mission accomplished. I came for one thing, and I got that one thing," Cikamatana beamed.

"I had days that I just wanted to go back home and be a baby in my mum's arms.

"I had days that I wanted to exit the door, but I'm glad I pulled that left leg back in.

"The original plan was to finish off after the Paris Olympics, but we (with coach Paul Coffa) didn't get what we wanted."

Madias Ngake (left), Eileen Cikamatana, and Rose Beaoudin celebrate their medals. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Cikamatana is the third female weightlifter in history to achieve the Commonwealth Games feat of three titles in a row, joining India's Mirabai Chanu (women's 48kg) and Canadian weightlifter Maude Charron (63kg) after they also won gold in Glasgow.

The 26-year-old has dominated her weightlifting categories since winning gold for Fiji in the 90kg event at the 2018 Gold Coast Games.

Cikamatana then switched allegiance to Australia the following year due to a local dispute with Fiji's weightlifting governing body, and to keep working with Coffa and his wife Lily.

Eileen Cikamatana (centre) representing Fiji at the 2015 Commonwealth Youth Games. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

Taking out the 87kg title at the 2022 Birmingham edition, Cikamatana is also the first woman to win Commonwealth Games gold for two countries in an individual sport.

Cikamatana is adamant about making the podium at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, but has pressing matters to attend to first.

"I'm going to go have some cake, because I've been wanting to have them ever since I got here," Cikamatana said.

"Cheesecake, obviously. I'm a cheesecake girl."

Ngake's incredible journey to silver

Ngake took silver in a remarkable career comeback.

The Cameroon-born English weightlifter was belatedly awarded a bronze medal from the 2012 Olympics after multiple rivals returned positive drug tests.

But the medal was sent to Cameroon, and she has never seen it.

Madias Ngake absconded from the Cameroon Olympics team in 2012. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Ngake, fearing persecution in her birth country because of her sexuality, absconded from the Cameroon team during the London Games.

Living homeless in London before working as a cleaner for 10 years, Ngake rekindled her desire to compete after a chance meeting with her former Cameroonian coach during the 2022 Commonwealth Games.

The 34-year-old, sporting sparkling red hair that matched her England uniform, threatened to pull off an upset after setting a Games snatch record of 111kg, but fell short of setting a clean-and-jerk benchmark of 135kg.

Cikamtana's win is Australia's third weightlifting medal in Glasgow, with youngster Ollie Saxton emulating his father and four-time Games medallist Andrew Saxton by winning bronze in the men's 94kg event earlier on day six of the Games.

Saxton had logged a total of 336kg, pulling off a 156kg snatch and a 180kg clean-and-jerk lift.

Saxton finished on the podium 40 years after his father won 100kg sub-heavyweight bronze for England at his debut Games in Edinburgh.

World.title: FIFA hits Argentina with World Cup charges for scuffle, 'Malvinas' banner
World.content:
FIFA has lodged disciplinary charges against two Argentina players for striking Spain opponents moments after the World Cup final and have charged Argentina's soccer federation for players showing a political banner about the Falkland Islands after beating England in the semifinals.

A list of disciplinary cases FIFA has opened against Argentina also include "discriminatory chants and gestures" by fans, alleged assault by an assistant coach after the final and "throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches" at the World Cup.

Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes faces three charges of assault over the post-game clashes after Spain's 1-0 win on July 19, defender Nahuel Molina faces two charges and coach Roberto Ayala one.

Molina and Thiago Almada also are charged with unsporting behaviour. The same charge has been levelled against Spain player Gavi.

Argentina's players carried a banner with the slogan "Las Malvinas son Argentinas", meaning "The Malvinas are Argentine", after beating England 2-1 in the semifinals.

UK urges action over Falklands banner The British government urges FIFA to investigate after Argentine players held up a banner declaring the Falkland Islands were Argentinian.

Argentina refers to the Falkland Islands as Islas Malvinas. The islands were invaded in 1982 under orders from Argentina's then-military dictatorship, triggering a 10-week war won by Britain.

British government officials urged FIFA to investigate the display of the banner, and the soccer body said on Wednesday the formal charge was "using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature."

FIFA said all the people charged had "now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the FIFA Disciplinary Committee in due course".

AP

World.title: 'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance': The Aussie Dolphins' way
World.content:
There's a ritual for Australians before every night of swimming at the Commonwealth Games: we run a rule down the schedule and count how many gold medals are locked in and how many others might be possible.

We did it on Tuesday, when the Dolphins' all-time gold medal record was in peril, ultimately equalled in the mixed 4x100m medley relay. And again on Wednesday, we knew the record would be broken, but by who?

The women's 50m freestyle was the first lock of the night, followed quickly by the men's 50m butterfly.

Trust this team to get greedy and nab three golds for the price of two races, with Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster winning matching golds, trailed by Cameron McEvoy, just after Meg Harris led Alex Perkins and Shayna Jack in the first podium sweep of the night.

Two for the price of one as Kyle Chalmers and Ben Armbruster touched at the same time in the 50m butterfly. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

But neither were the first gold of the evening and the record-breaking 29th of the meet.

That honour went to young Kai Taylor, who won his first international individual gold medal with a wire-to-wire victory in the men's 200m freestyle.

Despite Taylor entering these Games as an elite 200m practitioner, he fell into the "possibly if not likely" category during that pre-night perusal.

More fool us, as his last 200m swim three days prior was one of the moments of the campaign for Australia.

Live: Commonwealth Games day six We are past the halfway mark in Glasgow, which means the end of the swimming program as athletics kicks into high gear. Follow live.

After being a lead-off heat swimmer in the 4x200m freestyle relay at the Paris Olympics two years ago, the 22-year-old was chosen to anchor the final swim in Glasgow.

He entered the water about a body length and 0.24 seconds behind England's Max Litchfield and not only caught and put a gap on him within a lap, but powered ahead to a victory by 3.51 seconds.

But on Wednesday he swam a 1:47.23, two seconds slower than his personal best at June's trials, to qualify in seventh place.

He was placed in lane one for the final, and it seemed he simply wasn't feeling it on the day.

Taylor wasn't alive when Kieren Perkins famously won 1,500m gold from lane eight at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics. But many of us were.

Taylor's mum, Hayley Lewis, certainly was as a member of many of the same teams as Perkins.

All that to say, we should have known better. And Kai did.

Kai Taylor is an international individual medallist for the first time. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"If you've got a lane, you've got a chance," he said.

"I managed to get myself into the final tonight after a bit of a slow swim this morning, but you've always got a chance when you're in the race, and I just went out there with no fear."

Unlike his stunning relay swim, he led the entire way, first staying clear of Jack McMillan and then the rest of the field that swallowed up the Northern Irishman but couldn't catch the Commonwealth Games debutant on his desperate charge for history.

Taylor's victory was followed by the aforementioned podium sweeps and victories in five of the final six races of the night.

That started with a swimmer at the other end of the spectrum as Lakeisha Patterson, one of only two swimmers returning to Glasgow after competing in 2014, flew home in the 100m freestyle S9 for her third Commonwealth crown.

Still somehow 27, it feels like "Lucky" has been around and will be around forever.

Australia has come to expect gold rushes from the Dolphins for decades, so much so that the epic victories and unrivalled dominance are frequently met by little more than a thumbs-up, while minor medals elsewhere at the Games are welcomed as historic events.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

But Chalmers urged Australians not to take this moment for granted.

"We are in a golden era of swimming and it's not normal for swimmers to stand up and win gold medals and break world records, break Commonwealth Games records night in and night out," he said.

"But we draw so much inspiration from each other … we've got some generational talents on the team right now and I think we as a country really need to enjoy that while we can because it's not going to last forever."

Chalmers would know, having made his debut as a 17-year-old at the 2016 Olympics and winning one of Australia's three gold medals in the pool in Rio.

Ten years on, he is a seasoned veteran of the team with one eye on retirement.

Nothing is permanent in this game, so as the swimming ends and attention turns away from Tollcross, take a moment to recognise the brilliance we just witnessed.

Thirty-seven gold medals, 16 silver and 23 bronze. New names unearthed, old crowns getting a spit-shine and another reminder of this team's perpetual performances of the least appreciated but most anticipated feats of brilliance.

World.title: F1 confirms contingency plans if Middle East races are cancelled
World.content:
Formula 1 will end the season in Europe if races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi cannot be held, and has set a mid-September deadline, the Liberty Media-owned sport's chief executive Stefano Domenicali has said.

Races scheduled for Saudi Arabia and Bahrain in April were called off due to the war in Iran, with Malaysia's Sepang circuit now due to host the latter on October 4, with the Gulf kingdom paying most of the costs.

The FIA-sanctioned World ‌Endurance Championship (WEC) has already moved its last two rounds in Qatar and Bahrain to Barcelona's Circuit de Catalunya and Italy's Monza in October and November.

"We will take the maximum time for us to see how the situation will develop and we will take the ‌decision at the right time," Domenicali told reporters on Wednesday, local time.

"The deadline for the decision of any possible change of the actual calendar ⁠is the middle of September.

"For us today, the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi ‌are confirmed. By the way, they are already sold out," he added.

"If this will not ‌be possible, the end of the season will be in Europe because we cannot go in other places."

Qatar is due to host F1 on November 29 and Abu Dhabi on December 6.

Imola confirmed on list of candidates

The Italian confirmed Italy's Imola circuit, his birthplace and home to Ferrari as well as Mercedes' F1 leader Kimi Antonelli, was on the ‌list of possible replacements.

Informed sources have touted Imola, dropped from the calendar this year, as a leading candidate despite the weather at that time of year.

Domenicali said the temperatures in Las Vegas during the Saturday night race in ⁠November were colder than in Europe.

"There was a possibility of having ‌two races in Las Vegas (to end ‌the season), but we don't want to ruin a jewel that is growing," he said, adding that there would also be added competition ‌with the regular NFL season.

The 2027 calendar has yet to be published, but Bahrain had been expected to take back its slot as season opener from Australia in March before the conflict erupted.

Domenicali said ‌F1 planned to publish a schedule later ⁠in the year.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Of course, in case the situation in the Middle East would not be solved, we have options, different plans," said the chief executive. "But the trigger for that, of course, is at the end of the year. So we still have a lot of time."

"We will keep, in any case, the target of ⁠24 grands prix also for next year."

Portugal and Turkey will return as new rounds on the calendar next year, and Domenicali said longer term there were positive ‌negotiations with possible hosts ‌in Africa and interest from Asia and South America.

"We have more requests in China, and Japan, but for the moment we want to stay with one race in China because we need to consolidate the market before thinking to have another option there," he added.

Reuters

World.title: 'Total conflict': Infantino sets deadline for controversial FIFA scheme
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino set a September 19 deadline for the 211 member federations to accept one-off $US20 million ($28.7 million) offers as part of a $US20 billion project to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

The $US20 billion FIFA subsidiary was blasted by international soccer organisations.

European soccer body UEFA aims to call its 55 member federations to an emergency online meeting, likely today. The organisation said, "there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme".

The effort is being bankrolled by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

The effort marks Mr Infantino's latest effort to align with those in the orbit of Mr Trump: by creating the FIFA peace prize, letting Mr Trump intervene in a process that led to United States forward Folarin Balogun playing at the World Cup, and now trying to lock in Joshua Kushner's investment firm to a 12-year ownership deal with the Switzerland-based not-for-profit soccer body.

Joshua Kushner, founder of Thrive Capital with model and partner Karlie Kloss. (Getty Images: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg)

Mr Infantino set out the "singular and unique funding opportunity" in a letter detailing why he wants to create the $US20 billion FIFA subsidiary — 20 per cent owned by private investors — that would run the soccer body's competitions and events like World Cups and Club World Cups.

"It is my duty and responsibility as FIFA president to present such game-changing opportunities to you, our members," Mr Infantino wrote in the letter.

The effort elevates the status of Joshua Kushner, who has long been connected financially to his brother Jared.

When Joshua Kushner founded a venture capital firm rather than follow into the family's real estate business, his elder brother was an early investor and a board member.

Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Joshua Kushner at an event in New York in 2013. (Getty Images: Patrick McMullan)

The brothers are reportedly close, and their father, Charles Kushner, received a pardon from Mr Trump and now serves as the US ambassador to France.

But the younger Kushner has a history of six-figure donations to Democrats, and his wife, the model and entrepreneur Karlie Kloss, attended last month's opening of the Obama presidential library and told Bloomberg earlier this year she's never met Donald Trump.

The proposal revealed and backed by Joshua Kushner's investment firm Thrive Capital was met with immediate fury from Mr Infantino's former colleagues at UEFA, which said the World Cup "is not FIFA's to sell".

Gianni Infantino has been overtly trying to find favour with US President Donald Trump and his inner-circle.

One option open to European soccer is to threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions — a tactic used in 2021 when UEFA-led opposition helped stop Mr Infantino's plan to play the World Cup every two years instead of four.

UEFA and its president, Aleksander Čeferin, hosted a video conference between its five member federations and the biggest soccer leagues: England, Spain, Italy, Germany and France.

"President Čeferin expressed his stance against this (FIFA) project," Giovanni Malagò, the new president of Italian soccer, said during the presentation of new Italy coach Roberto Mancini.

"The situation is really total conflict."

Infantino's ambitions

FIFA's private equity plan is the latest ambitious project proposed during Mr Infantino's 11-year presidency, in which he has increasingly seemed to be an executive leader acting without consulting with soccer's major stakeholders.

Previous plans include creating a FIFA Peace Prize — awarded to Mr Trump in December at the World Cup draw — and trying to push through a secretive $US25 billion private equity plan in 2018 to create new and bigger men's competitions. That was resisted by UEFA.

Gianni Infantino (right) with then FIFA President Sepp Blatter and UEFA President Michel Platini at the UEFA Champions League final in 2007. (Getty Images: Etsuo Hara)

Concerns about the latest and previously secret plan were aired Wednesday by the continental soccer bodies for Asia and the North American region known as CONCACAF.

"We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process," CONCACAF said in a statement.

The Kuala Lumpur-based Asian Football Confederation said it was "disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it."

What's on offer to FIFA member federations

If a majority of the 211 members approve the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary, they also each are promised $US20 million in funding from the four-year commercial cycle tied to the men's 2030 World Cup.

That would lead, Mr Infantino wrote, to "a pool of diverse international investors" joining Joshua Kushner's Thrive as the anchor investor: "This process will be led by J.P. Morgan."

If Mr Infantino's plan is rejected, those members will get their previously promised $US10 million over the next four years, his letter stated.

Gianni Infantino supported the European Super League idea, which was deeply unpopular with football fans. (Getty Images: Adam Davy/PA Images)

The cash difference on offer to FIFA members appears to be $US86 million over 12 years compared to about $US36 million in existing promised funding for rejecting the private equity deal.

The rushed deadline to claim an initial $US20 million "says everything you need to know about this plan," UEFA said. "FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."

Dozens of member federations typically rely on FIFA for funding, have national teams with little realistic chance of qualifying for World Cups, and whose best players rarely, if ever, join clubs playing at the highest level of international competitions.

FIFA's one-member, one-vote democratic system means the most powerful soccer nations on the field easily can be outvoted by those who rarely play top-level games.

Resistance in Britain

FIFA's plan met quick opposition from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose government is preparing to support hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. FIFA is set to confirm that lone bid for 2035 at an online meeting in November.

"Football does not belong to investors," Mr Burnham, a longtime soccer fan, said in a video message on Instagram.

FIFA boss reveals $US20b plan to sell World Cup FIFA president Gianni Infantino earns more criticism after unveiling a brazen plan to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup.

"Once you have sold a piece of [the World Cup], you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will."

Resistance by British lawmakers — including threats of legislation by then-prime minister Boris Johnson in 2021 — previously helped stop the divisive European Super League project that was an existential threat to UEFA's Champions League, and which Mr Infantino had discreetly supported.

J.P. Morgan bankers also worked with top European clubs on that project, which collapsed within 48 hours.

Mr Infantino has seemed to be cruising toward being re-elected unopposed as FIFA president for a fourth and final term through 2031.

Promising more FIFA funds to member federations was a decisive part of his initial election-day speech in February 2016, and at his unopposed re-elections in 2019 and 2023.

Some observers have long suspected Mr Infantino wants a longer-term role running the sport. A CEO or commissioner role at a FIFA subsidiary, FFE, would fit that bill.
